documents.title: Acute Stroke Treatment

chunks.content: Introduction Stroke encompasses a group of acute cerebral circulatory disorders stemming from limited or comprehensive cerebral impairment syndrome, including two categories: ischemic stroke and hemorrhagic stroke. This condition is characterized by high morbidity, high disability, high mortality, high recurrence rates, and a significant economic burden, all of which severely impact patients’ health status and quality of life [ – ]. According to some data [ , ], 70% to 80% of stroke survivors experience varying degrees of functional limb movement disorders, which severely limit their daily abilities and impose a heavy burden on their families and society. Several studies have concluded that hemiplegia, as the primary limb dysfunction, does not stem from the destruction of the motor system itself. Instead, it results from the acute neurological dysfunction caused by the disease, also known as disuse disorder. Moreover, the brain’s neurons exhibit plasticity after a stroke, making early rehabilitation training an effective means of promoting the recovery of patients’ neurological functions, thereby reducing disability and enhancing the quality of life [ , ]. The survey found that the level of exercise rehabilitation for stroke patients was far below the guideline recommendations [ ]. As the disease progressed, patients gradually exhibited the “three lows” of lack of initiative, weakened adherence, and reduced willingness to participate. Therefore, an in-depth understanding of the actual experiences and needs of stroke patients during physical rehabilitation is of great significance for optimizing rehabilitation strategies and enhancing rehabilitation outcomes. However, employing a single qualitative research method makes it challenging to comprehensively reflect on the genuine experiences of exercise rehabilitation for stroke patients and their real-life dilemmas in the participation process due to limitations in the representativeness of the sample group, the interview process design, and potential subjective biases present during the interviews. Previous systematic reviews and meta-synthesis have explored related research questions. For example, one systematic review examined the experiences of stroke patients during physical rehabilitation [ ], but the included studies were all published before 2015. The incidence of stroke has been rising in recent years, as has the number of studies investigating patients’ experiences with rehabilitation. Furthermore, as society evolves and patients’ rehabilitation strategies may shift—from traditional methods to those based on handheld games, virtual reality, or rehabilitation robots—their experiences and needs during physical rehabilitation may also differ. Another systematic review examined the rehabilitation needs of patients after departing from medical institutions [ ]. But the study did not concentrate on physical rehabilitation and lacked insights into patients’ experiences during hospitalization and rehabilitation in specialized facilities. Patients typically opt for treatment in a professional institution during the acute or subacute stages, and only when their condition is relatively stable do they choose to leave the medical institution in favor of home or community rehabilitation. However, the feelings and needs of patients vary across different illness stages and settings. Given this, the present study conducted another systematic assessment and meta-synthesis of studies related to the real experiences and needs of stroke patients in physical rehabilitation. It aims to dig deeper into their inner feelings, practical needs, and real barriers in the process of exercise rehabilitation, and to address the shortcomings of previous reviews in terms of timeliness, specificity to physical rehabilitation, and inclusion of technology-mediated interventions. In order to provide a scientific basis of reference framework for the subsequent development of targeted strategies to promote exercise rehabilitation and optimise practice pathways for stroke patients. The review Aim This study aims to systematically evaluate and integrate the real experiences and unmet needs of stroke patients in the process of physical rehabilitation, to reveal the patients’ inner feelings, practical barriers, and core demands when participating in exercise rehabilitation, to provide a scientific basis for optimizing personalized and patient-centered rehabilitation intervention strategies, and ultimately to enhance rehabilitation adherence and long-term rehabilitation outcomes. Methods This study follows the Enhancing Transparency in Reporting Qualitative Research Reviews (ENTREQ) [ ] and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) [ ], to ensure transparency in research reporting (Supplementary Material 1). The program was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42024594929). Search strategy A systematic search was conducted in Embase, Web of Science, CINAHL, PubMed, SinoMed, Google Scholar, CNKI, WanFang databases, and VIP for qualitative research on the experiences, experiences, and related needs of stroke patients during physical rehabilitation, with a timeframe of the database being established until September 2024, and an updated search in January 2025 was conducted. Using the three-step search strategy recommended by Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI), an initial limited search was conducted on PubMed and CNKI, followed by an analysis of the words contained in the title and abstract and the index terms used to describe the article. A second search was then conducted in all selected databases using the identified keywords and relevant indexing terms. Finally, a complete retrospective search

research on the experiences, experiences, and related needs of stroke patients during physical rehabilitation, with a timeframe of the database being established until September 2024, and an updated search in January 2025 was conducted. Using the three-step search strategy recommended by Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI), an initial limited search was conducted on PubMed and CNKI, followed by an analysis of the words contained in the title and abstract and the index terms used to describe the article. A second search was then conducted in all selected databases using the identified keywords and relevant indexing terms. Finally, a complete retrospective search of the bibliographies of all references selected for inclusion in the literature was performed, and a search of Google Scholar for unpublished reports and related articles was performed. The complete search strategy is described in Supplementary Material 2. Eligibility criteria The PICoS (Population, Phenomenon of Interest, Context, Study design) model recommended by JBI was used to develop the screening criteria for this study. Inclusion criteria were as follows: P (population) was stroke patients ≥ 18 years of age with residual limb dysfunction who had received rehabilitation for limb function, and excluded stroke patients with preexisting limb dysfunction before stroke or limb dysfunction that occurred after stroke but was not caused by stroke.; I (phenomenal interest) was the experiences, feelings, or needs of the physical rehabilitation process; Co (context) was any setting (e.g., home, hospital, community, rehabilitation facility, etc.), and cultural context, and in any geographic location; and S (study design) was a qualitative study, including phenomenological research, grounded theory, ethnography, and other qualitative research methods. Exclusion criteria were as follows: articles not in English or Chinese, reviews, conference abstracts, qualitative research data that could not be extracted from mixed-methods approaches, and articles for which the full text was not available. Study selection The results of the literature search will be imported into Endnote X9, a literature management software, and after removing duplicate articles, two study members (XTS and XYZ) identified potentially eligible studies by reading the titles and abstracts according to the inclusion–exclusion criteria of the literature, and then two researchers conducted a full-text reading to assess whether the inclusion criteria were met. Any disagreements that arose between reviewers were resolved through discussion or with a third reviewer (HMZ). Assessment of methodological quality Two authors (XTS and KP) independently assessed the quality of the included studies using the 10-item Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) tool [ ], which evaluates the purpose of the study, methodology, recruitment, data collection, researcher reflection, ethical considerations, data analysis, rigor of findings, and appropriateness of the study’s value, ethical considerations, data analysis, rigor of findings, and appropriateness of the study’s value. Any discrepancies in the quality assessment are discussed between the two authors until a consensus is reached. Data extraction Data extraction was carried out using a pre-prepared data extraction form that included: authors, year of publication, country, sample size, phenomenon of interest, study design, methods of data collection and analysis, and main conclusions. Two authors (XTS and XYZ) extracted the data independently, and a third author (HMZ) was responsible for checking the accuracy of the data. The three authors discussed any discrepancies in the extracted data until a consensus was reached. Data synthesis Thematic synthesis was used to generalize and synthesize the qualitative data following the recommendations of the Cochrane Handbook [ ]. Coding and thematic development were carried out in three stages, each of which was independently considered, discussed, and agreed upon by two or more researchers. Data extracted from the results of all included studies were entered verbatim into the NVivo 12 Plus for coding and data management. In the first stage of the analysis, the text of the study was coded. In the second stage, the codes were grouped into logical and meaningful clusters in a hierarchical tree structure to form descriptive themes. Finally, the relationships between the descriptive themes were explained and elaborated, resulting in analytic themes. Thematic integration was done independently by two research team members (XTS and XYZ) who, after discussion, each incorporated their findings into a preliminary thematic framework. This was critically reviewed by a third panelist (HMZ) and revised accordingly by two members. Any disagreement among the three panelists about the final thematic framework was discussed face-to-face until all authors reached a consensus on the thematic framework. Results Search results A total of 4074 documents were initially retrieved. After removing duplicates, 3,312 articles remained, 3,251 records were excluded by browsing titles, abstracts, and keywords, and 35 articles were excluded by reading the remaining articles in their entirety(Reasons for exclusion 1: no physical dysfunction was present in the study population n = 13; Reason 2: the study design was a mixed study but it was not possible to extract the qualitative component n = 5; Reason 3: only patients’ willingness to be rehabilitated was explored but patients had not yet actually been involved in rehabilitation n = 9; Reason 4: the focus was on caregivers or medical staff n = 6; Reason 5: incomplete data n = 2). A follow-up search of the list of participating literature for the included studies and earlier related reviews identified 2 articles that met the inclusion criteria, and a total of 28 articles were ultimately included in this systematic review. The literature screening flowchart is shown in Fig. (PRISMA flowchart showing study selection progress). Characteristics of included studies Of the 28 papers included, 6 were in Chinese, and 22 were in English, published between 2005 and 2024, and reporting data from 468 participants from 13 countries (including high- and middle-income countries). The most common were China [ ] and Australia [ ], while other countries included the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Turkey, Canada, Sweden, Norway, Iceland, Switzerland, Denmark, and New Zealand. 2 articles explored patients’ needs during the physical rehabilitation process [ , ], and 12 articles explored patients’ feelings about using an extranet-based rehabilitation platform for physical rehabilitation (5 explored patients’ feelings about utilizing VR for physical rehabilitation [ – ], 2 explored the experience of handheld gaming-based rehabilitation [ , ], and 5 focused on the experience of utilizing a telerehabilitation platform or assistive device for rehabilitation [ – ] 2 studies explored patients’ feelings during intensive upper extremity exercise or high repetition upper extremity exercise [ , ]. The specific characteristics of the included studies are described in Supporting Material 3. Quality of included studies Table (Quality assessment of the included literature) shows the risk of bias ratings of the included studies, with the majority of studies meeting more than 8 of the 10 quality assessment criteria and all of them having some or all of the following values. However, it is worth noting that some of the studies did not describe the methods used for qualitative data analysis, such as thematic or content analysis, or lacked an in-depth description of the analysis process. In addition, few studies considered the relationship between the researcher and the participants, and the researcher did not critically examine his or her role, potential biases, and influences when analyzing and selecting data. These missing details can lead to biased or misleading interpretations of the data, and the lack of relevant details in recruitment strategies in some of the studies further exacerbates the potential for introducing bias. Synthesis results A total of 117 findings were distilled in this study, which were repeatedly read, analyzed, and grouped into 24 new categories, and finally summarized into 4 integrated findings. The relationships between themes and sub-themes are shown in Fig. (The relationships between themes and sub-themes), and a detailed thematic synthesis is shown in Supporting Material 4. Body perception and dynamic adaptation Limb loading During physical rehabilitation, participants often struggle to sustain exercise due to fatigue and pain caused by somatic loading. Six studies have indicated that post-stroke patients frequently experience decreased muscle strength and abnormal muscle tone, along with fatigue and pain during physical rehabilitation [ , , , – ], which can impact the duration and effectiveness of rehabilitation training. Poorly designed rehabilitation equipment Inadequate setup of rehabilitation equipment results in a negative rehabilitation experience for participants. Twelve articles explored physical rehabilitation based on various elements, including Internet technology, and five studies noted that the variety and hierarchical nature of the system often motivated patients. However, technical problems with rehabilitation equipment (e.g., frequent machine malfunctions, poorly configured interfaces resulting in delayed or shifted images) or ergonomic design issues (e.g., overly tight harnesses that cause binding or pain due to friction, bulky sensors, and skin sensitivities) often result in a less than optimal patient experience [ , , , , ], and patients often face various discomforts. Dynamic changes A longitudinal phenomenological study exploring stroke survivors’ perceptions of upper extremity rehabilitation priorities revealed that patients’ rehabilitation priorities shift as rehabilitation progresses [ ]. In the early stages of rehabilitation, patients typically prioritize restoring or improving their ability to walk, focusing on lower extremity function; around six months post-stroke, patients begin to concentrate more

shifted images) or ergonomic design issues (e.g., overly tight harnesses that cause binding or pain due to friction, bulky sensors, and skin sensitivities) often result in a less than optimal patient experience [ , , , , ], and patients often face various discomforts. Dynamic changes A longitudinal phenomenological study exploring stroke survivors’ perceptions of upper extremity rehabilitation priorities revealed that patients’ rehabilitation priorities shift as rehabilitation progresses [ ]. In the early stages of rehabilitation, patients typically prioritize restoring or improving their ability to walk, focusing on lower extremity function; around six months post-stroke, patients begin to concentrate more on restoring upper extremity function, except for those who cannot walk independently; and by eighteen months post-stroke, all patients aim to restore upper extremity function. Improvement in physical function As the rehabilitation process advances, the limb function of stroke patients improves (e.g., balance function, joint mobility, and gait) with the aid of both spontaneous and specialized rehabilitation [ , , , ]. These improvements enable stroke patients to better integrate into daily life and enhance their self-care and quality of life. Psychological course and emotional experience Negative emotions and social avoidance Due to the sudden onset of the disease, abnormal limb movements, and concerns about the prognosis, patients often experience strong negative psychological effects such as fear and anxiety [ , ]. Before the disease, patients fulfilled various social roles; however, after its onset, their self-care abilities are impaired, leading to a replacement of their original roles and a decrease in family functions. “roles” refer to the positions individuals occupy within social structures (e.g., family, work, community) and the associated behavioral expectations, responsibilities, and obligations (e.g. returning to work or assuming family responsibilities). For stroke patients, the illness often forces significant disruption or transformation of their core social roles. Consequently, patients frequently feel self-blame, resulting in a heavy emotional burden [ , , ]. Additionally, some participants expressed concern about how they were perceived by bystanders. They often felt stigmatized due to physical and speech impairments following a stroke, leading to feelings of low self-esteem and reluctance to engage in daytime outings [ , ]. Desire for restoration of limb function Participants generally conveyed a strong desire for functional recovery, expressing the wish to regain their physical abilities to self-manage and lessen their dependence on others [ , ]. They aspire to return to participation in daily activities, continue their valued hobbies, and resume family and social roles [ , ]. Confusion However, due to a lack of experience in physical rehabilitation and knowledge about the disease, many patients feel confused and helpless during this process. Over time, they may forget the rehabilitation techniques taught by medical staff, causing uncertainty and confusion when they face challenges during rehabilitation exercises [ , , , , , , , ]. This uncertainty not only amplifies the patients’ psychological burden but also impacts their rehabilitation outcomes and adherence. Furthermore, three studies indicate that patients often exhibit psychological dependence when confronted with multiple rehabilitation options, with some typically following the decisions of family heads, elderly parents adhering to their children’s advice, and others delegating decision-making to therapists [ , , ]. Fear and self-doubt Stroke patients frequently endure a psychological state of fear intertwined with self-doubt during rehabilitation. This state is marked by significant uncertainty regarding falls and other adverse events, low self-efficacy caused by post-stroke limb dysfunction [ , , ], fear of causing injury or inconvenience to others [ ], and apprehension towards new rehabilitation methods [ , , ]. Lack of therapeutic care Three studies noted that the transition from therapist-led to patient-directed rehabilitation occurred prematurely after discharge [ , , ]. As treatment frequency diminishes, patients often feel unsupported, neglected, and abandoned by healthcare services. Loss of patience Gait rehabilitation for stroke is lengthy and varies by individual, and during this period, patients may have insufficient understanding of their condition or overly high expectations for their rehabilitation progress. Therefore, when actual outcomes fall short of their expectations, it frequently leads to frustration [ , , , ]. Some participants expressed resistance to rehabilitation as they observed no immediate improvement in their limb functionality and considered rehabilitation futile or unattainable [ , , ]. Additionally, a singular rehabilitation strategy often leads to boredom and frustration, causing patients to lose patience during the prolonged rehabilitation process [ , , ]. Psychological adaptation and emotional transformation Enhancements in physical functioning and regular communication with medical staff alleviated negative emotions and fostered a recognition of rehabilitation’s value. In the acute phase, patients showed intense anxiety and despair for fear of lifelong disability, describing hospitalisation as ‘the sky is falling’; in addition, patients’ inability to assume their original social roles due to the loss of limb function often resulted in deep self-blame, etc. [ ,

, , ]. Additionally, a singular rehabilitation strategy often leads to boredom and frustration, causing patients to lose patience during the prolonged rehabilitation process [ , , ]. Psychological adaptation and emotional transformation Enhancements in physical functioning and regular communication with medical staff alleviated negative emotions and fostered a recognition of rehabilitation’s value. In the acute phase, patients showed intense anxiety and despair for fear of lifelong disability, describing hospitalisation as ‘the sky is falling’; in addition, patients’ inability to assume their original social roles due to the loss of limb function often resulted in deep self-blame, etc. [ , , , , , ]. However, with the assisted rehabilitation by healthcare professionals, the patients’ limb functions gradually improved, which enhanced their self-confidence in the rehabilitation process and made them participate more actively in rehabilitation exercises. Additionally, some participants recognized the beneficial role of religious beliefs throughout their recovery journey [ ], viewing them as a source of liberation and hope and offering spiritual support to patients. Multidimensional motivations and facilitators Positive feedback Positive feedback, whether it is verbal encouragement from the therapist, visual indicators of progress (e.g., walking speed/distance), or automatic rewards in rehabilitation techniques (e.g., ‘good job’ messages, points), is a powerful facilitator that helps to enhance self-efficacy promoting a sense of accomplishment related to achieving goals. “Self-efficacy” refers to an individual’s confidence and belief in their capability to successfully execute specific behaviors and achieve desired outcomes. In the rehabilitation context, it specifically denotes the patient’s confidence in their ability to effectively engage in and adhere to rehabilitation exercises, overcome challenges, and ultimately achieve functional recovery. This information provides them with a clearer understanding and higher expectations of their rehabilitation progress [ , , , ]. Integrated incentives and feedback mechanisms within rehabilitation platforms further reinforce this confidence, preventing discouragement during the recovery process [ , ]. Diverse external support Physical, emotional, and social support from medical staff, peers, family, and the community motivates persistence [ , , ]. They not only offer essential physical assistance but also foster a sense of care and understanding through encouragement and support, thereby enhancing patients’ motivation to face recovery challenges positively. Group-based activities further cultivate a sense of belonging, transforming rehabilitation into a collectively meaningful endeavor [ , , , , , , , ]. Participants found communication with others facing similar illnesses to be beneficial, as they exchanged firsthand knowledge of stroke and rehabilitation and sought mutual motivation and psychological support. Participants frequently felt more secure and confident exercising with a peer group and being part of a team, which not only fostered a positive sense of connection but also encouraged a positive outlook on life. Challenging design Hierarchical and competitive designs (e.g., leaderboards, increasing difficulty) tap into patients’ intrinsic motivation by designing rehabilitation as an engaging pursuit of achievement [ – , ]. Task designs (e.g., virtual flight simulations) are often more engaging through real-time reward cycles (e.g., points, visual feedback) and immersive tasks (e.g., virtual flight simulations) [ , , , ]. Internet-based rehabilitation platforms (e.g., virtual reality, tablet-based games) are often considered more innovative and interesting than traditional approaches. Goal setting and sense of achievement Setting clear goals and gaining a sense of accomplishment positively affect a patient’s recovery. Goals based on the patient’s identity (e.g., beliefs, values, or culture) and meaningful aspects of life (e.g., relationships, hobbies, and occupations) transform abstract recovery into value-driven action [ , ]. Patients gain motivation from self-observed improvements in functioning (e.g., improved performance at daily tasks), which validates the achievability of goals [ , , , ], in contrast to unmonitored progress, which leads to frustration and weakens the nature of adherence [ ]. Positive emotional attitudes and personality traits Positive emotional attitudes and personality traits enhance patients’ motivation to recover, influencing recovery outcomes. Inherent traits like humor and perseverance function as psychological buffers, enabling patients to reframe setbacks. These traits also drive rehabilitation integration, embedding exercises into daily routines (e.g., using stairs as therapy) to reduce willpower dependency [ , , ]. Avoiding disability labeling and functional degradation Avoiding disability labeling and functional decline emerged as crucial motivations for participants to continue their rehabilitation. They strongly rejected the stigma and pity associated with disability, wanting to be recognized as capable individuals rather than disabled. This mindset motivates them to challenge themselves continually and strive to regain function, preserving their dignity and independence. Additionally, concerns about functional decline further motivate adherence in stroke patients, who hope to maintain their current functioning and independence through ongoing rehabilitation and thus avoid falling into a detrimental cycle of functional loss [ , ]. This mindset motivates them to challenge themselves continually and strive to regain function, preserving their dignity and independence. Additionally, concerns about functional decline further motivate adherence in stroke patients, who hope to maintain their current functioning and independence through ongoing rehabilitation and thus avoid falling into a detrimental cycle of functional loss [ , ]. Self-responsibility Many participants recognized during their recovery journey that they had an obligation to actively manage their health recovery and to reassume their pre-stroke social roles (e.g., returning to work or family duties) [ , ]. Furthermore, Therapist oversight (e.g., progress tracking) adds an external layer of responsibility that utilises social commitment to motivate patients to adhere to recovery [ , , ]. Unmet needs and directions for optimizing intervention strategies Convenient and continuous demand for rehabilitation services Nine studies point to patients’ desire for convenient and consistent rehabilitation services that provide flexibility to practice according to their daily living plans [ , , , , , , , , ]. Although municipalities offer a variety of services, access to them is often complicated by time or frequency constraints [ ], particularly for patients in rural and remote areas, where distance, travel time, therapist turnover rates, and other limitations render participation in rehabilitation training very challenging or impossible [ , , ]. They expressed frustration with the commuting time involved, and stroke survivors showed a strong desire for rehabilitation services closer to home or available within their communities. Simultaneously, patients are eager for post-discharge follow-up, professional guidance, and to maintain close contact with healthcare professionals for improved rehabilitation outcomes [ , , ]. Additionally, varying literacy and skill levels among patients led some participants to express concerns about difficulties with technology due to hardware limitations or personal conditions. Some elderly stroke patients found operating tablets and other devices too complicated and indicated a need for training support or technical guidance from medical staff [ , ]. Access to rehabilitation information and resources Low accessibility of rehabilitation-related information, a lack of supporting rehabilitation facilities, irrational design of rehabilitation assistance appliances, and a shortage of community workers hinder patients from undergoing limb function rehabilitation. Stroke patients and their families often remain unaware of the correct methods for functional exercise after leaving medical or rehabilitation institutions, and the out-of-hospital exercise routines lack professional guidance and team support from medical staff. In contrast, information regarding stroke physical rehabilitation in daily life and on the internet is limited, generalized, and hardly accessible [ , ]. With an extended discharge time, patients often feel uncertain about their rehabilitation and struggle to effectively resolve challenges encountered during rehabilitation exercises, which negatively impacts their adherence to rehabilitation and its effectiveness. Patients hope that hospitals or rehabilitation institutions can provide professional and personalized rehabilitation guidance and offer more specific information about the pros and cons of rehabilitation programs so they can choose a suitable rehabilitation method for themselves [ , , ]. Furthermore, the lack of rehabilitation opportunities and the inadequate facilities or assistive devices have created a scarcity of opportunities for patients, and stroke patients are eager for more exercise instruments, devices, and venues that cater to their needs to aid them in performing rehabilitation exercises [ , , , , , ]. Individualized rehabilitation guidance Five studies reported participants’ desire for personalized guidance from healthcare professionals during recovery [ , , , , ]. Participants reported a lack of targeted guidance on how to perform the exercises or how long to continue them. During rehabilitation, patients sometimes experience fatigue and even severe pain, yet they often choose to tolerate this discomfort, seeking help from healthcare professionals only when it becomes unbearable. This endurance stems not only from the pain but also partly from the fear of being perceived as “weak” or “uncooperative” by others [ ]. There is a strong desire among patients for healthcare professionals to pay more attention to their individual needs and to develop and adapt rehabilitation treatments to each patient’s specific situation. Socialization and group interaction between patients with similar experiences Four studies emphasized the participants’ need for social and group interactions with others who have similar experiences [ , , , ]. Group therapy is recognized as a more cost-effective form of long-term support and treatment, where stroke survivors can mutually encourage and resource each other. Survivors expressed enthusiasm for the prospect of socializing and exercising together, stating they hoped dedicated spaces, such as activity rooms or public fitness centers, could be arranged for socializing and learning from one another and fellow survivors, which could aid in recovery [ , ]. others who have similar experiences [ , , , ]. Group therapy is recognized as a more cost-effective form of long-term support and treatment, where stroke survivors can mutually encourage and resource each other. Survivors expressed enthusiasm for the prospect of socializing and exercising together, stating they hoped dedicated spaces, such as activity rooms or public fitness centers, could be arranged for socializing and learning from one another and fellow survivors, which could aid in recovery [ , ]. Economic support and policy guarantees Patients often experience varying degrees of limb dysfunction post-stroke, which may lead to loss of financial income as they can no longer engage in their former occupations. Additionally, post-stroke treatment, medication, and rehabilitation represent a chronic process that demands long-term adherence and incurs high costs, ultimately deterring most patients. Many have expressed feelings of helplessness and distress regarding having to abandon treatment due to financial pressure [ , , , , ]. Patients generally hope that the government can offer more subsidies to reduce treatment and rehabilitation costs, particularly advocating for the inclusion of rehabilitation-related expenses within the scope of health insurance reimbursement to alleviate the financial burden on individuals and their families [ , ]. Real-time feedback and intelligent adjustments Eight studies noted participants’ desire to monitor their progress and receive timely feedback throughout the recovery process [ , , , , , , , ]. Whether through online telerehabilitation using an extranet platform or offline, face-to-face rehabilitation with a therapist, participants expressed a desire to visualize their exercises and utilize visual and auditory feedback to gauge whether they need to intensify their efforts or adjust their approach. As progress in rehabilitation is often gradual, effective monitoring and feedback help them recognize if they are proceeding correctly and track their improvements, which can enhance their confidence and motivate them further. Discussion Patients’ self-efficacy in rehabilitation increases as they perceive improvements in their physical abilities during the recovery process. Physical rehabilitation that utilizes Internet technology, such as handheld games or virtual reality, is more engaging and convenient than traditional face-to-face rehabilitation sessions with a therapist [ ]. However, patients’ attitudes towards and acceptance of digital technology often vary widely, likely due to factors like varying levels of education and age differences [ ]. Elderly stroke patients with lower literacy frequently feel confused, especially during the initial phase of using these technologies [ ]. Therefore, when implementing Internet-based interventions, healthcare professionals should take into account the diversity among patients from different cultural backgrounds and age groups, focusing specifically on the acceptance of older stroke patients with lower literacy levels. Additionally, poorly designed rehabilitation equipment can lead to unpleasant experiences for patients [ , , ]. In the future, when designing limb rehabilitation aids for stroke patients, it is essential to prioritize creating aids that are compact and user-friendly, with appropriate ergonomics and a clear, simple interface. It is important to recognize that there are variations in the focus on upper and lower limb function among stroke patients at different rehabilitation stages. It has been suggested that in the early stages of rehabilitation, patients often prioritize lower limb function to restore or improve their walking ability; around six months post-stroke, patients begin to shift their focus toward recovering upper limb function, except for those unable to walk independently; and by eighteen months post-stroke, all patients concentrate on regaining upper limb function [ ]. This pattern may relate to the evolution of an individual’s core needs as described in Maslow’s hierarchy of needs theory. In the early rehabilitation stage, patients’ core needs focus on physiological safety, which is evident in their fixation on gait recovery, motivated by fear of falling and embarrassment of over-relying on others for toileting. In the middle stage, patients’ core needs shift towards belongingness and respect, reflected in their desire for independence in managing daily personal tasks (e.g., shaving, cooking) to avoid appearing entirely dependent. In the late stage of rehabilitation, the core need becomes self-actualization, expressed through the pursuit of occupational rehabilitation or the return to hobbies. This indicates that healthcare professionals should not only recognize the visible dysfunctions of patients but also understand the dynamically shifting core needs underlying them. Through a phased, multidimensional intervention program, we can assist patients in achieving a holistic reconstruction of their physical, mental, and social functions. Stroke patients face complex and diverse psychological and social challenges during the rehabilitation process. Studies have shown that disease onset, abnormal limb function, and prognostic concerns together induce strong negative psychological experiences in patients [ , ]. These psychological reactions not only stem from the disease itself but are also closely related to the social environment. The disruption of patients’ social roles has led to a dual psychological impact: on the one hand, the loss of self-worth resulting from the weakening of family functions; on the other hand, the stigma attached to post-stroke dysfunction has created a vicious cycle of “self-stigma-social withdrawal”, whereby patients’ social participation is limited. Medical professionals need to help patients rebuild their sense of self-worth and improve their psychological status through early screening and timely intervention from a biopsychosocial perspective. In addition, patients’ lack of knowledge about rehabilitation and the uncertainty created by forgetting methods often place them in a passive role in the decision-making process. Especially in the family decision-making model, elderly patients tend to follow the advice of their children or therapists [ , ]. This phenomenon of psychological dependence also reveals the inadequacy of the stroke rehabilitation education system. Medical personnel can adopt a phased approach to education, focusing on disease mechanisms and prognosis in the acute phase, and rehabilitation skills (e.g., mobility skills) in the recovery phase, as well as using tools such as videos and graphic manuals to reduce forgetfulness. To address the passive decision-making tendency of elderly patients, medical staff can use ‘decision-making aids’ (e.g., option lists, risk comparison charts, and pros and cons analysis tables) to help patients understand the advantages and disadvantages of different rehabilitation options, encouraging them to participate in developing personalized training plans to enhance their autonomy [ ]. Seeing progress and receiving positive feedback are factors that promote recovery, and ongoing monitoring and evaluation are key to long-term adherence. Many studies indicate that patients feel “marginalized” and “abandoned” after being discharged from hospitals, often facing challenges such as unclear channels of help, lack of professional support, uncertain progress, and difficulty confirming whether they are following the right pathway. This can lead to a loss of patience and a tendency to give up during the long-term recovery process [ , , ]. Consequently, they lose patience and opt to abandon long-term rehabilitation efforts. In the future, we should enhance the “hospital-community-family” three-way linkage extended care model, improve the social support system for full-cycle rehabilitation of stroke, and provide multi-channel, easily accessible professional support resources [ , ]. Implementing a regular monitoring and evaluation mechanism can provide patients with timely positive and clear feedback, allowing them to see the progress of their rehabilitation. At the same time, extranet-based rehabilitation platforms or assistive devices should improve their monitoring and feedback mechanisms so that patients can feel in real time whether their rehabilitation actions are correct and make timely adjustments based on the feedback content. Additionally, presenting patients with stage-by-stage assessment reports can help them visualize the extent of improvement in their physical function and the progress made, thereby enhancing their confidence in adhering to long-term rehabilitation [ ]. Interaction and social support among peers with similar experiences can positively impact a patient’s recovery process [ ]. Peer socialization promotes learning and communication among patients, and in group therapy, they can observe each other’s recovery progress, which motivates them to work harder. They can also share their experiences and insights to learn from each other, fostering positive interactions. This aligns with several studies [ – ]. In the future, it is essential to provide dedicated rehabilitation exercise spaces, organize diverse group activities, strengthen rehabilitation education and publicity, and establish peer support networks among stroke patients, utilizing both online and offline methods. For instance, organizing rehabilitation lectures and experience-sharing sessions can promote communication and interaction among patients, enrich their rehabilitation experience, and enhance their sense of social belonging [ ]. A systematic review of older adults’ participation in dance fitness games showed that those who participated as a group reported higher adherence and a stronger sense of belonging compared to individuals who participated alone [ ]. Therefore, designing future extranet-based rehabilitation platforms or assistive devices should include social elements and create rehabilitation devices or games that allow multiple participants to enhance patient compliance. A lack of accessible rehabilitation resources and robust policy support will inhibit patients from participating in or adhering to physical rehabilitation in the long term [ , ]. In the future, the allocation of rehabilitation resources and services needs optimization, social security policies such as medical insurance should be strengthened to support rehabilitative medical care, and the implementation of family rehabilitation strategies should be promoted. A lack of accessible rehabilitation resources and robust policy support will inhibit patients from participating in or adhering to physical rehabilitation in the long term [ , ]. In the future, the allocation of rehabilitation resources and services needs optimization, social security policies such as medical insurance should be strengthened to support rehabilitative medical care, and the implementation of family rehabilitation strategies should be promoted. For example, it is crucial to enhance the number and scale of rehabilitation medical institutions, develop remote rehabilitation services to overcome geographical constraints, expand the scope of medical insurance coverage, increase reimbursement rates, simplify the reimbursement process, and establish a family rehabilitation support system to promote the integration of family and community rehabilitation, thereby facilitating the rehabilitation process and improving the quality of life for patients. The most important advancement of this review is the integration of patient experience with digital rehabilitation technologies (e.g., virtual reality systems and tele-rehabilitation platforms) and the demonstration that gamified design elements (e.g., challenge tiers, real-time rewards) significantly increase patient motivation, an effect absent in traditional settings. Furthermore, our review reveals how unmet needs (e.g., real-time feedback, financial support) interact with psychosocial factors (e.g., avoidance of disability labelling), which could contribute to the future development of targeted and diverse interventions. Implications for research and practice Some of the studies were qualitative studies nested within quantitative studies without integrating the results. Future reporting of results from mixed studies should draw on relevant methodological guidelines to avoid fragmentation of quantitative and qualitative components. In the future, evidence-based decision-making aids for the physical rehabilitation of stroke patients can be developed to help patients make scientific decisions according to their actual situation and to reduce the sense of confusion and uncertainty in the rehabilitation process. Healthcare professionals need to pay attention to the individual differences and personalized needs of patients, and develop and promptly adjust rehabilitation strategies according to the specific conditions of patients. Currently, Internet-based physical rehabilitation is gradually beginning to be applied to the patient rehabilitation process, and the number of studies on this type of research has gradually increased in recent years, but it is very different from traditional rehabilitation, and in the future, we can conduct a review of the patient experience of physical rehabilitation based on the Internet technology to explore the patient’s feelings in this particular situation. Stroke patients at different stages of the disease may have different experiences and needs, and future longitudinal follow-up studies could be conducted to inform the provision of more targeted interventions where possible. Limitations Only articles published in English and Chinese across nine databases were included in this systematic review, which potentially overlooked other articles that met the criteria. To more comprehensively assess the real experiences and unmet needs of patients with residual limb dysfunction after stroke, this study did not exclude several articles with lower quality ratings. Furthermore, several studies were qualitative studies nested within interventional studies, where patients may be influenced by the specific intervention, leading to the possibility of biased results. Additionally, the literature included in this study did not cover low-income country settings, limiting the applicability of the findings to areas facing extreme resource deprivation. There is a strong need for future localized research on stroke rehabilitation in low-income countries to explore innovative strategies (e.g., community-led rehabilitation models, low-cost technology adaptation) to meet patient needs with limited resources. Conclusions This meta-synthesis of 28 qualitative studies reveals that stroke patients experience physical rehabilitation as a dynamic adaptation process, navigating physical challenges and shifting functional priorities over time. They simultaneously grapple with significant psychological and social challenges. Success in this journey is fueled by multidimensional motivators such as strong support networks, meaningful feedback, clear goals, and intrinsic resilience. Critically, patients report substantial unmet needs, particularly concerning continuous services, personalized information and guidance, opportunities for peer connection, and economic/policy support. Furthermore, technology-mediated rehabilitation (e.g., VR, gamified platforms) emerges as offering unique motivational advantages but also faces challenges related to design usability and patient acceptance, especially among older or less literate individuals. To translate these findings into practice, we recommend a staged rehabilitation programme based on patients’ changing needs, prioritising functional goals. Provide embedded psychological scaffolding through decision aids and collaboration with family physicians, and scale up community group interventions to reduce treatment abandonment. Co-design technology-assisted solutions with patients, taking into account the differences between patients with different literacy levels and meeting their individual needs, and subsidizing rehabilitation costs in national insurance schemes through policy advocacy. Introduction Mixture Markov Model (MMM) is a well-known clustering technique in order to cluster event sequences where each event is coming from a state-space given by a collection of finite events. In literature several statistical applications of MMM and Mixture Hidden Markov Markov Model (MHMM) can be found for clustering event sequence data in various fields ( ; ; ; ). A few applications of MMM can also be found in the field of biostatistics ( ; ). However, one of the challenging aspects of estimating MMM parameters remains in optimizing the mixture likelihood. Due to the multi-modal nature of the mixture likelihood, it is difficult to maximize using derivative-based methods as these tend to converge at local maxima. Although the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm can be used for parameter estimation for MMM ( ), its performance largely relies on the initial point solution ( ). Several articles addressed the convergence issues of using EM algorithm for estimating parameters in mixture model ( ) which might pose a challenge in obtaining the maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) in case of MMM as well. proposed a faster alternative to the EM algorithm for optimizing the MMM likelihood, but this was later shown to under-perform when compared to the EM algorithm in terms of predictive performance. Therefore, exploring alternative approaches to maximize MMM likelihood would be helpful in improving the estimation performance, resulting in improved inference and related prediction performances as well. As an alternative to EM algorithm and other convex optimization techniques, evolutionary global optimization techniques ( ) can be considered as a natural choice in order to address the complex and multi-modal nature of the objective function that is, the MMM likelihood. For optimizing multi-modal functions, several evolutionary global optimization techniques have been proposed in the last few decades, for example, “Genetic Algorithm (GA)” ( ; ; ) and “Simulated Annealing (SA)” ( ; ), which are widely used nowadays. These methods were first developed for unconstrained global optimization, later they were extended for optimizing objective functions with constraints ( ; ). Among other non-deterministic global optimization techniques, Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) ( ; ) remains popular for unconstrained global optimization. proposed a different evolutionary based global optimization technique called “Generalized Pattern Search” (GPS) which is a more generalized version of the Direct search method earlier proposed by . In GPS, using an “exploratory moves algorithm” ( ), the objective function values at a set of neighboring points around the current solution are evaluated and the point with the best (i.e., the maximum or minimum, based on requirement) objective function value is selected as the updated solution. Later GPS has been extended to solve global optimization problems on several constrained spaces and shown to outperform other related evolutionary based algorithms ( ; ). In this article, we propose a Pattern search based algorithm to maximize the MMM likelihood, compare the performance of the proposed optimization algorithm to other existing evolutionary global optimization techniques, and eventually demonstrate the estimation performance of the proposed algorithm while maximizing MMM likelihood to outperform the results obtained using EM algorithm based on simulation experiments. The parameter space of the MMM likelihood for known (finite) number of clusters is composed of a set of transition matrices, initial state probability vectors and the vector of mixture proportions. Now, the parameters of the collection of transition matrices can be also observed as a collection of simplexes since each row of a transition matrix belongs to a simplex space. Also, note that, the mixture proportion vector and each of the initial state probability vectors are simplexes as well. Therefore, the whole parameter space of the MMM likelihood can be expressed as a collection of simplexes. In order to solve the MMM likelihood, we come up with a Pattern search based global optimization technique to solve any objective function whose parameter space is given by a collection of simplexes, called multiple simplex constrained optimization routine (MSiCOR). We also explore some of its theoretical properties. As an application to MSiCOR in the context of MMM, we cluster Multiple sclerosis (MS) patients based on their disease-modifying treatment (DMT) prescription history. MS is an autoimmune disease of the the central nervous system (CNS) that leads to neurodegeneration in the brain and spinal cord. In MS, the immune system damages the protective sheath (myelin) that covers nerve fibers, causing dysfunctional communication between the CNS and the rest of the body For most people with MS (pwMS), the disease starts with relapses resulting in episodes of new or worsening symptoms due to acute focal inflammation of the CNS. MS is generally diagnosed in early adulthood. Major symptoms of MS include muscle stiffness, paralysis, cognitive impairment, fatigue, depression, visual disturbance, balance and gait difficulty, and problems with bladder, bowel, or sexual function. Although there is no cure

In MS, the immune system damages the protective sheath (myelin) that covers nerve fibers, causing dysfunctional communication between the CNS and the rest of the body For most people with MS (pwMS), the disease starts with relapses resulting in episodes of new or worsening symptoms due to acute focal inflammation of the CNS. MS is generally diagnosed in early adulthood. Major symptoms of MS include muscle stiffness, paralysis, cognitive impairment, fatigue, depression, visual disturbance, balance and gait difficulty, and problems with bladder, bowel, or sexual function. Although there is no cure for MS, there are 20 FDA-approved DMTs that reduce inflammatory disease activity and delay disease progression. DMTs can be divided into several mechanistic categories, including interferon-beta, glatiramer acetate, fumarates such as dimethyl fumerate and natalizumab, sphigophine-1-phosphate modulators such as fingolimod, and B-cell depletion agents such as rituximab. Over the course of this chronic disease, pwMS typically receive serial DMTs as monotherapies. Common reasons for switching DMTs include therapeutic failure (e.g., relapse), intolerance or adverse events. Prior research efforts identified various demographic, clinical, genetic and neuroimaging features associated with disease activity of pwMS ( ; ). Further, several research works focused on the time series analysis of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) intensity ( ) and volumetric medical image sequences ( ; ) of the MS patients. showed the dependence of DMT preference on socio-demographic and clinical features. However, to the best of our knowledge, few studies have examined DMT prescription sequence data. These prior studies have focused on either a single best patient-specific DMT option ( ), or the criteria for switching or stopping DMTs ( ). Moreover, emphasis has remained mostly on possible treatment options of a patient at a given time point based on response to previous DMTs. To the best of our knowledge, DMT prescription sequence remains an unexplored clinical space in MS. As an example, it is possible to estimate transition probabilities of moving from one DMT to another DMT based on patient history both at a personal and at a population level under certain statistical model assumptions. We hypothesize that the variation among these transition probabilities across patients is governed by clinical, demographic, and/or other factors. Since the choice of DMT prescription largely depends on patient disease status, the prescribed DMT at any given time can be mapped to a set of clinical conditions and observations. Thus, analysis of DMT transitions and patient clusters based on how transitions across DMT options occur over individual timelines can provide insights on the associations of the clinical features and observations with DMT prescription sequence. Different statistical models can be used to cluster event sequences in logitudinal data ( ; ). One potential approach is marked point processes (MPP; ). However, there is generally a lag between the actual onset of new neurological symptoms (i.e., relapses indicative of disease activity) and the observed date of DMT prescription. The lag can occur when patients visit their physicians a few days after the onset of symptoms/relapses. Given the typical time that it takes for insurance authorization process, there can be further lags between prescription date and the actual DMT start date. Thus, in the scenario of MS DMTs, incorporating the observed time periods between any two prescription dates into the model might be misleading, making MPPs unsuitable for modeling. However, the order in which a patient has been prescribed DMTs over their observation period is still useful and can be modeled in other ways using state-space models (SSMs). In the literature, hidden Markov chain models (HMMs) have been used to cluster event sequences ( ). However in our scenario we do not have any hidden underlying variable like in HMMs. In this article, we model MS DMT prescription sequences using a mixture of discrete state-space Markov chain models. There are a few notable reasons for clustering pwMS based on DMT sequences. First, over the disease course, pwMS are serially treated with multiple DMTs that might change over time. As such, estimating the transitional probabilities of changing across different pairs of DMTs across MS patients or any sub-populations will have clinical relevance. Second, after the individuals are clustered based on DMT sequences, cluster-specific summary statistics of clinical and demographic features can inform prescription guidance for future patients. Further, patient-specific covariates can also be used for clustering along with DMT sequences. We thus incorporate patient-specific covariates within MMMs to explain cluster memberships as in latent class analysis. MMM Likelihood Without Covariates Suppose the observed data consist of medication sequences on N treatments from K patients, { Y i = ( Y i , 1 , … , Y i , h i ) } i = 1 K , where Y i , t ∈ { 1 , … , N } represents the treatment received by patient i at time t ∈ { 1 , … , h i } , and h i denotes the length (or the total number of time-points) of the medication sequence for the i th patient. We assume that the medication sequences are generated from L time-homogeneous Markov chain processes, or clusters. Let M = [ M 1 , … , M L ] denote L Markov transition matrices corresponding to the L clusters, and s = [ s l ( k ) ] N × L = [ s 1 , … , s L ] denote the corresponding initial state probability vectors where s l = [ s l ( 1 ) , … , s l ( N ) ] ⊺ for l ∈ { 1 , … , L } . Then (1) P ( Y i ∣ z i = l , X i ) = s l ( Y i , 1 ) M l ( Y i , 1 , Y i , 2 ) ⋯ M l ( Y i , h i − 1 , Y i , h i ) , where z i denotes the cluster membership of the i th patient, M l ( y t , y t + 1 ) denotes the transition probability from y t to y t + 1 and s l ( y t ) denotes the initial state probability of the state y t in the l th cluster, for y t ∈ { 1 , … , N } . The likelihood is given by (2) L M , s ( Y 1 , … , Y K ) = ∏ i = 1 K ∑ l = 1 L w l s l ( Y i , 1 ) M l ( Y i , 1 , Y i , 2 ) ⋯ M l ( Y i , h i − 1 , Y i , h i ) , where { w l } l = 1 L denotes the mixture probability of the l th cluster such that ∑ l = 1 L w l = 1 , w l ≥ 0 . 2.2. We assume that the medication sequences are generated from latent class models of L time-homogeneous Markov chain processes with latent class membership z also depending on the covariates X i but that Y i is independent of X i ∣ z . ( ) holds true in this case as well, and additionally we assume (3) w i l ≡ P ( z i = l ∣ X i ) = exp ( X i ⊺ γ l ) 1 + ∑ l ′ = 2 L exp ( X i ⊺ γ l ′ ) , l = 1 , … , L , where Γ = ( γ 1 , … , γ L ) denotes the cluster-specific coefficient vectors of the covariates. First cluster is considered as the baseline cluster, so we take γ 1 ≡ 0 . Here the likelihood is given by (4) L M , s , Γ ( Y 1 , … , Y K ) = ∏ i = 1 K ∑ l = 1 L w i l s l ( Y i , 1 ) M l ( Y i , 1 , Y i , 2 ) ⋯ M l ( Y i , h i − 1 , Y i , h i ) . The posterior probability of a patient belonging to cluster l can be obtained as (5) P ( z i = l ∣ Y i , X i ) = P ( Y i ∣ z i = l , X i ) P ( z i = l ∣ X i ) ∑ l ′ = 1 L P ( Y i ∣ z i = l ′ , X i ) P ( z i = l ′ ∣ X i ) . Once we estimate the cluster-specific parameters, we can use ( ) to identify where any given patient belongs. Thus, after estimating the clusters, we may summarize the available statistics for the patients to explore the cluster characteristics and differences. In , after the clusters are estimated based on real data, we summarize the patient relapse rate and rates of a few other relevant medical codes for each cluster. These include the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) code, Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) code, and the Concept Unique Identifiers (CUIs). 3. Computation 3.1. The Estimation Problem We maximize ( ) in order to estimate the parameters for each Markov chain component. To begin with, the ( d − 1 ) -dimensional simplex is defined as Δ d − 1 = { ( x 1 , … , x d ) ∈ R d : x i ≥ 0 , i = 1 , … , d , ∑ i = 1 d x i = 1 } . In ( ), s l and each row of M l belongs to ( N − 1 ) dimensional simplexes, and α ∈ Δ L − 1 . Apart from the coefficient vector Γ , the remainder of the parameter space consists of L ( N + 1 ) simplexes of size ( N − 1 ) and one simplex of size ( L − 1 ) . In order to maximize ( ), one may use the EM algorithm ( ), however, EM algorithm tends to get stuck at poor local solutions due to the possible multi-modal nature of the mixture likelihood. Moreover, the estimation performance of EM also depends on the initial starting point, as discussed in . An alternative is to apply a direct numerical maximization procedure on the objective function. Widely used algorithms for constrained optimization include interior point (IP) methods ( ), sequential quadratic programming (SQP; ), and the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) algorithm. However, these algorithms typically require good initial starting points in order to reduce the risk of being trapped at poor local maxima. In addition, popular global optimization techniques include the genetic algorithm (GA; ) and simulated annealing (SA; ). However, a major disadvantage of these algorithms is that they can be computationally slow, and thus there remains a tradeoff between estimation accuracy and computation time. Among other global optimization methods, a generalized pattern search algorithm was proposed by , and variations have been proposed for various constrained parameter spaces ( , ). Variants of PS have been shown to outperform existing GA or SA algorithms (see, e.g., ). In order to

However, a major disadvantage of these algorithms is that they can be computationally slow, and thus there remains a tradeoff between estimation accuracy and computation time. Among other global optimization methods, a generalized pattern search algorithm was proposed by , and variations have been proposed for various constrained parameter spaces ( , ). Variants of PS have been shown to outperform existing GA or SA algorithms (see, e.g., ). In order to maximize the likelihood, we first develop a Pattern search ( ) based algorithm to maximize any objective function whose parameter space is given by a collection of simplexes, called multiple simplex constrained optimization routine (MSiCOR). Then, we further modify it to perform updating steps of the unconstrained coefficient vector Γ , with an end goal to maximize ( ) overall. Thus, we consider a variation of PS that can be used to optimize objective functions over parameter spaces that are a collection of simplexes and of unconstrained parameter spaces, as is the case for the MMM likelihood with covariates based on MS DMT sequences and patients’ clinical data. 3.2. Multiple Simplex Constrained Optimization Routine (MSiCOR) Consider a non-convex objective function f : Δ n 1 − 1 × ⋯ × Δ n B − 1 ↦ R which we wish to minimize. In pattern search (PS), within an iteration while optimizing over a M -dimensional space, 2 M candidate points in the neighborhood of the current solution are explored. These are obtained by changing one coordinate at a time, both in positive or negative direction, keeping other coordinates unchanged. For example, in case we want to optimize a function f over an unconstrained space R M , given the step-size s and current solution z = ( z 1 , … , z M ) , the objective function f is evaluated at 2 M new candidate points, given by { z i + } i = 1 M and { z i − } i = 1 M where z i + = ( z 1 , … , z i − 1 , z i + s , z i + 1 , … , z M ) and z i − = ( z 1 , … , z i − 1 , z i − s , z i + 1 , … , z M ) . At each iteration, the best solution out of these ( 2 M + 1 ) points is selected based on the objective function values at those points. In PS, the step-size s is chosen adaptively. Unlike the case of unconstrained pattern search, in our problem, the parameter space is composed of multiple simplexes, and the general PS needs to be modified for our scenario. MSiCOR consists of several runs . Iterations are performed within each run until a convergence criteria is met, which is detailed in the sequel. Each run starts from the solution returned by the previous run and attempts to find a better solution, with the initial solution for the first run being user-provided. The algorithm terminates and returns the final solution when the solutions obtained by two consecutive runs are close. Having multiple runs aids in jumping out of local minima. 3.2.1. Tuning Parameters Each run depends on the following tuning parameters: initial global step-size s initial > 0 , step decay rate ρ > 1 , step-size threshold ϕ > 0 , and sparsity threshold λ ≥ 0 . The values of these tuning parameters are set by the user and are kept unchanged across runs. We consider two additional tuning parameters τ 1 , τ 2 to control the convergence criteria. Finally, the maximum number of iterations within a run and the maximum number of runs can be fixed as M iter and M run , respectively. 3.2.2. Global and Local Step-Sizes The parameter space consists of multiple unit-simplex blocks. Suppose there are B unit-simplex blocks, and that the j th simplex block is ( n j − 1 ) -dimensional and denoted by P j = ( p j , 1 , … , p j , n j ) ∈ Δ n j − 1 for j = 1 , … , B . The total number of parameters is M = ∑ j = 1 B n j . Within each run, we consider a global step-size η and 2 M local step-sizes { { ( s j , i + , s j , i − ) } i = 1 n j } j = 1 B which are chosen adaptively depending on the tuning parameter values as

by P j = ( p j , 1 , … , p j , n j ) ∈ Δ n j − 1 for j = 1 , … , B . The total number of parameters is M = ∑ j = 1 B n j . Within each run, we consider a global step-size η and 2 M local step-sizes { { ( s j , i + , s j , i − ) } i = 1 n j } j = 1 B which are chosen adaptively depending on the tuning parameter values as well as the improvement in the values of objective function. Inside a run, in the first iteration the value of the global step-size is set to be η ( 1 ) = s initial , where η ( h ) denotes the value of global step-size in the h th iteration in a run. The value of η remains the same throughout an iteration. At the end of each iteration, its value either remains same or gets divided by ρ ( > 1 ) based on a criteria described later in . At the beginning of an iteration, the values of the local step-sizes s j , i + and s j , i − are set to be the value of the global step-size η of that iteration. 3.2.3. Exploratory Movements Suppose the current value of the parameters at the beginning of the h th iteration is P = P ( h ) = ( P 1 ( h ) , … , P B ( h ) ) , where P j ( h ) = ( p j , 1 ( h ) , … , p j , n j ( h ) ) ∈ Δ n j − 1 for j = 1 , … , B . During the iteration, the objective function is evaluated at 2 M feasible points in the neighborhood of P ( h ) . These feasible points are obtained by taking steps around P ( h ) modulated by the local step-sizes s j , i + , s j , i − for j = 1 , … , B , and i = 1 , … , n j . These can be divided into M “positive” movements ( j , i , + ) and M “negative” movements ( j , i , − ) for j = 1 , … , B and i = 1 , … , n j . We call a coordinate of a unit-simplex box “significant” if its value is greater than λ . Suppose that there are m j ( < n j ) significant positions in the j th simplex block P j ( h ) excluding the i th position p j , i ( h ) . The ( j , i , + ) th movement consists of updating p j , i ( h ) to ( p j , i ( h ) + s j , i + ) and subtracting s j , i + ∕ m j from the m j significant positions, thus keeping the sum of the values of the j th simplex block one. We then check whether the updated P j ( h ) is in the unit-simplex. If so, we set P j ( h ) ( i , + ) equal to the updated P j ( h ) , and if not (since it is possible if either p j , i ( h ) + s j , i + > 1 or at least one of the updated values at the significant positions is negative), we update the local step-size by setting s j , i + = s j , i + ∕ ρ and repeat the same step until the updated P j ( h ) is in unit-simplex. However, we do not allow s j , i + to be smaller than ϕ . In case s j , i + becomes smaller than ϕ (by dividing it multiple times by ρ ), we set P j ( h ) ( i , + ) = P j ( h ) . The ( j , i , − ) th movement is performed in a very similar manner by subtracting s j , i − from p j , i ( h ) and adding s j , i − ∕ m j to the other significant positions, and we refrain from detailing it here. 3.2.4. Sparsity Control We incorporate a sparsity control step in order to encourage possibly sparse solutions. For each of the obtained modified simplex blocks { P j ( h ) ( i

h ) ( i , + ) = P j ( h ) . The ( j , i , − ) th movement is performed in a very similar manner by subtracting s j , i − from p j , i ( h ) and adding s j , i − ∕ m j to the other significant positions, and we refrain from detailing it here. 3.2.4. Sparsity Control We incorporate a sparsity control step in order to encourage possibly sparse solutions. For each of the obtained modified simplex blocks { P j ( h ) ( i , + ) } i = 1 n j and { P j ( h ) ( i , − ) } i = 1 n j for j = 1 , … , B , we set the values of the “insignificant” coordinates (that is, coordinates less than λ ) to zero. This is adjusted for in the “significant” positions by incrementing each of them by the same amount in order to keep the sum of all the coordinates to be one. After the sparsity control step, if the modified P j ( h ) ( i , + ) (or P j ( h ) ( i , − ) ) remains in unit-simplex, we denote it by p ¯ j ( h ) ( i , + ) (or p ¯ j ( h ) ( i , − ) ). If not, we set p ¯ j ( h ) ( i , + ) = P j ( h ) ( i , + ) (or p ¯ j ( h ) ( i , − ) = P j ( h ) ( i , − ) ). Remark 1 . λ should be taken relatively large in case of prior knowledge that the final solution is sparse. If not, it can be chosen relatively small or zero. 3.2.5. Selecting the Best Candidate Solution Corresponding to the modified simplex block p ¯ j ( h ) ( i , + ) , the candidate solution is given by P ( h ) ( j , i , + ) = ( P 1 ( h ) , … , P j − 1 ( h ) , p ¯ j ( h ) ( i , + ) , P j + 1 ( h ) , … , P B ( h ) ) . Similarly, corresponding to the modified simplex block p ¯ j ( h ) ( i , − ) , the candidate solution is given by P ( h ) ( j , i , + ) = ( P 1 ( h ) , … , P j − 1 ( h ) , p ¯ j ( h ) ( i , − ) , P j + 1 ( h ) , … , P B ( h ) ) . Note that { p ¯ j ( h ) ( i , + ) } j = 1 n j and { p ¯ j ( h ) ( i , − ) } j = 1 n j belong to the unit-simplex. Thus we obtain 2 M candidate solution points P ( h ) ( j , i , + ) and P ( h ) ( j , i , − ) for j = 1 , … , B and i = 1 , … , n j . The objective function is evaluated at these 2 M candidate solutions and the best solution point (i.e., the solution point where the value of the objective function is the lowest) out of the ( 2 M + 1 ) points including current solution P ( h ) is set as the updated solution P ( h + 1 ) . 3.2.6. Loop Termination Criteria As mentioned in , at the end of each iteration, the value of η either remains the same or gets divided by ρ . If ∣ f ( P ( h + 1 ) ) − f ( P ( h ) ) ∣ < τ 1 at the end of the ( h + 1 ) th iteration, we set η = η ∕ ρ , and leave it unchanged otherwise. Moreover, we set the minimum allowable value of η to be ϕ , and terminate a run if η becomes smaller than ϕ . For example, consider a situation where η > ϕ at the start of the h th iteration within the R th run. However, at the end of h th iteration, ∣ f ( P ( h ) ) − f ( P ( h − 1 ) ) ∣ < τ 1 ,

end of the ( h + 1 ) th iteration, we set η = η ∕ ρ , and leave it unchanged otherwise. Moreover, we set the minimum allowable value of η to be ϕ , and terminate a run if η becomes smaller than ϕ . For example, consider a situation where η > ϕ at the start of the h th iteration within the R th run. However, at the end of h th iteration, ∣ f ( P ( h ) ) − f ( P ( h − 1 ) ) ∣ < τ 1 , and so we set η = η ∕ ρ , but it happens to be that η ∕ ρ < ϕ . We then terminate the R th run at the h th iteration and return the solution obtained at the end of h th iteration as the solution of the R th run, which then serves as the starting point for the ( R + 1 ) th run. Recall that we set η = s initial at the beginning of each run. Suppose P ^ ( R ) denotes the solution returned by the R th run. The algorithm terminates when ∣ f ( P ^ ( R ) ) − f ( P ^ ( R − 1 ) ) ∣ < τ 2 and returns P ^ ( R ) as the final solution. In we provide a flowchart of the runs executed within MSiCOR. Pseudo-code for MSiCOR is provided in . 3.3. Comparative Performance Using Benchmark Functions In order to evaluate the comparative performance of MSiCOR, we consider the minimization problem of four benchmark functions ( ) namely Rastrigin function, Ackley’s function, sphere function and Griewank function whose parameter spaces are modified to be a collection of simplexes (see of the for function expressions). The benchmark functions are quite challenging to minimize because of their typical complex structure along with presence of multiple minimums (generally) which pose challenges in finding the global minimum. It is impossible to design an optimization algorithm which can always find the global minimum for any black-box function. Although some global optimization algorithms are backed up with theoretical evidence on global convergence (e.g., on genetic algorithm), however, those convergence properties are derived based on a lot of assumptions regarding the properties of the objective function. First those properties might not hold true in practice. Second there is no way to verify if those properties hold true for a black-box function since the function is already “black-box” by nature. Therefore, to comprehend the performance of any heuristic, global or black-box optimization technique, a common practice is to conduct experiments based on minimizing benchmark functions; and eventually based on average computation time and quality of the obtained solutions, one may get an idea about the relative performance of an algorithm. In this context, along with MSiCOR we also consider Genetic Algorithm (GA), Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) and Interior Point (IP) optimization techniques to minimize the aforementioned benchmark functions (see of the for details). IP and SQP algorithms search for local minimum while optimizing any function and in general they are less time consuming. On the other hand GA tries to find global minimum being more time consuming. These above-mentioned well-known algorithms are available in Matlab via the Optimization Toolbox functions fmincon (for IP and SQP algorithm) and ga (for GA). While using IP and SQP algorithms, the upper bound for maximum number of iterations and function evaluations have been set to be infinity each. For GA, the default options of “ga” function in Matlab has been considered. MSiCOR is implemented in Matlab. The comparative study has been performed for the cases n = 5, d = 5 and n = 5, d = 10 for all the above-mentioned algorithms, where n is the number of simplexes and ( d − 1 ) is the dimension of each simplex blocks. All the computations have been performed in a computer with 64-Bit Windows 8.1, Intel i7 3.6GHz processor, 32GB RAM. For each case, all the algorithms have been initialized from 100 randomly generated starting points. The true minimum of all considered modified benchmark functions is 0. The average computation time (in seconds, also standard deviation in parenthesis), obtained minimum value of the objective functions and standard deviations of obtained objective function values for each cases have been noted down in . It is observed that MSiCOR provides better solution for considered benchmark functions compared to other methods, except for modified sphere function. The sphere function being convex, it is expected for IP and SQP to perform well while optimizing it. But MSiCOR outperforms GA for all considered benchmark functions. Although MSiCOR took more time on average to converge compared to IP and SQP, it took

The sphere function being convex, it is expected for IP and SQP to perform well while optimizing it. But MSiCOR outperforms GA for all considered benchmark functions. It is also noted that the standard deviation of the objective function values at the obtained solutions is the least for MSiCOR, which implies that MSiCOR algorithm is more robust and less dependent on starting points compared to other algorithms. To check the performance of the proposed algorithm in higher dimensional problems, additional simulation studies have been performed. Theoretical Properties The greatest challenge of solving a non-convex optimization problem is that in general algorithms cannot be designed to guarantee reaching the global optima. However, it is a desirable property of any algorithm that it should reach a global minimum when the function is convex. In this section, via , it is shown that taking the values of the parameters ϕ , τ 1 and τ 2 significantly small, the stopping criteria of the proposed algorithm ensures that the solution obtained is a global minimum in case the objective function is convex.
