documents.title: Tics Tourette Syndrome Treatment

chunks.content: Brief overview in historical context In 1498, Jakob Sprenger and Heinrich Kraemer published “Maleus maleficarum” (hammer of witches) and described a priest with motor and vocal tics, thought to be caused by demonic influence. In 1825, Jean Marc Gaspard Itard described “the case of a cussing Marquise,” (with) premonitory sensation, echolalia and coprolalia. Gilles de la Tourette in 1895 described 9 patients who suffered from a disorder characterized by involuntary movements, echolalia, echopraxia, coprolalia, and strange, uncontrollable sounds [ ]. Tourette surmised this was a “degenerative disorder of the nervous system, which was partially due to the immoral behaviors of previous generations”Later, Charcot (Tourette’s mentor) would rename this disorder Tourette syndrome [ ]. Characteristics and course Historically, Tourette syndrome (TS) has primarily been considered a disorder of childhood. The Tourette International Consortium reported a mean age of onset of 6.4 years in 6805 patients with TS with a mean age at diagnosis of 13.2 years, demonstrating a 7-year gap before diagnosis was made. They noted a 4.4:1 male to female predominance. Associated comorbidities included attention deficit and hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in 55.6%, obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) in 54.9%, anger issues (27.6%), learning problems (22%), mood disorders (16.9%), anxiety (16%), conduct disorder (12.3%), and pervasive developmental disorder (4.6%). A positive family history of tic disorder was present in 51.7% [ ]. The Danish National Tourette Clinic reported on 314 patients with age ranging from 5 to 19 years with a diagnosis of TS. They noted that tic severity commonly tended to decline gradually during adolescence. After the age of 16 years, tic resolution had occurred in 17.7%, mild residual tics persisted in 59.5% and moderate to severe tics continued in 22.8%. There was a strong tendency for neuropsychiatric comorbidities to persist (63%). They concluded that the “severity of tics, OCD, and ADHD were significantly associated with age and declined during adolescence; however, considerable comorbidities and coexisting psychopathologies tended to persist through later adolescence” [ ]. The European Clinical Guidelines for Tourette Syndrome indicated 80% of individuals who present with tics at under age 10 experienced a significant decrease in tic frequency and severity during adolescence by the age of 18 years will most commonly no longer experience impairment from tics; however, tics persisted in 20%, and in some circumstances worsened and became debilitating [ ]. Tourette spectrum Our understanding of TS is rapidly changing. “The perception of TS as a rare, bizarre psychological disorder began to change in the 1960s”, and is now “recognized as a relatively common, biological, genetic disorder with a spectrum of neurobehavioral manifestations that wax and wane during over time during its natural course. The marked fluctuations in the severity and frequency of symptoms, coupled with the striking variation in manifestations from one patient to another, however, contribute to frequent misdiagnosis” (Jankovic, 2001) Many medical providers primarily consider TS to be a tic disorder that often includes neuropsychiatric comorbidities, and place their treatment emphasis on minimizing tics; however, TS is a clinical spectrum and the therapeutic approach should be more comprehensive. The relationship between neuropsychiatric symptoms and tics is complex and intertwined. Each child or individual presents as a unique case within the spectrum. Jankovic stated that “because of the broad range of neurological and behavioral manifestations and their varying severity, therapy for TS must be individualized and tailored specifically to the needs of the patient, and the most troublesome symptoms should be targeted first.” (Jankovic, 2001) Hartmann added, “personalized treatments in Tourette syndrome are both necessary because of the width of the clinical spectrum, making every patient unique from a symptom-oriented perspective; yet, difficult to achieve because of the lack of large prospective cohorts which may inform on prognostic factors and disease-modifying interventions.” (Hartman) When considering the potential neuropsychiatric disorders within the Tourette spectrum, all diagnostic criteria may not be met for a given disorder independently, but associated clinical characteristics may be present to some degree. A child might not meet all diagnostic criteria for ADHD, yet still have varying degrees of hyperactivity or problems with attention/focus. Similarly, a child might not meet diagnostic criteria for generalized anxiety disorder, yet still show signs of excessive worrying. The diagnostic criteria for OCD might not be met, yet the individual may obsess over certain routines or feel compelled to perform rituals to avoid something bad from happening. Stern said, “less intrusive obsessionality is clearly very common, and represents obsessive-compulsive behavior. Tourettic obsessionality is clinically distinct from pure obsessive-compulsive disorder” [ ]. Assessment for signs and symptoms of common neuropsychiatric problems will allow the treatment team to comprehend the complexity of each child in order to create an optimal individualized therapy plan. Patient/Family education The first recommendation in the American Academy of Neurology (AAN) Practice Guideline: The Treatment of Tics in People with Tourette Syndrome and Chronic Tic Disorders

the individual may obsess over certain routines or feel compelled to perform rituals to avoid something bad from happening. Stern said, “less intrusive obsessionality is clearly very common, and represents obsessive-compulsive behavior. Tourettic obsessionality is clinically distinct from pure obsessive-compulsive disorder” [ ]. Assessment for signs and symptoms of common neuropsychiatric problems will allow the treatment team to comprehend the complexity of each child in order to create an optimal individualized therapy plan. Patient/Family education The first recommendation in the American Academy of Neurology (AAN) Practice Guideline: The Treatment of Tics in People with Tourette Syndrome and Chronic Tic Disorders , is to provide families with information about “the natural history of a disorder (to) help inform treatment decisions [ ]. As Quezada and Coffman stated, “a critical first step in the treatment of TS is proper education of the patients, family members, teachers, and others who interact with the patient about the broad range of clinical features and variable course of the disorder” [ ]. Families often have misconceptions about TS that have been shaped by public syndicated and social media. Thus, it is essential that a multidisciplinary TS clinic allocates a significant portion of the first visit to education and answering questions. Educational endeavors should extend beyond that first visit with ongoing provision of information for the patient, family, and everyone with a significant influence in his or her life. The school should develop a customized educational or 504 plan for each child as a safety net to ensure services are provided as indicated to maximize success and well-being. Accommodations will not be necessary for every child, but it is important that the school be prepared to identify issues and offer solutions. TS education actually should begin prior to the first clinic visit. There is a need to improve public awareness, and knowledge among healthcare and education professionals. “Despite greater awareness of TS as a result of increased educational efforts directed at physical and other health care providers, psychologists, educators, and the general public, many cases still remain undiagnosed, or patients’ symptoms are wrongly attributed to hyperactivity, nervousness, habits, allergies, asthma, dermatitis, and other conditions” (Jankovic, 2001). The American Academy of Neurology Guideline states “psychoeducation about TS with peers can result in more positive attitudes toward a person with TS, while psychoeducation about TS with teachers can improve knowledge about the condition. Improving peer attitudes and teachers’ knowledge regarding TS may positively affect people with TS [ ]. General considerations for treatment Once education has been achieved, the discussion can move to the therapeutic approach and treatment options. The first determination is if tic severity warrants treatment. Are the tics bothering the child and causing a negative impact or dysfunction? Often, especially with younger children, the child may not even be aware of the tics. The tics may bother the parent, but not the child. Essentially, if negative impact on the child is absent or minimal, medication is not warranted. Medical therapy should be considered when the tics negatively impact the child’s self-esteem or ability to function, or if tics produce discomfort or pain. If medical therapy is considered, it is critical to establish appropriate expectations, and ensure that patients and families understand it is rare for treatment to result in complete tic resolution. On average, medications for tics can reduce symptoms by about 25–50% [ ]. The goal should be reasonable tic control and reduction of associated impairment, to maximize the child’s quality of life and ability to function [ ]. The treatment plan should be developed with consideration of the potential need to also treat neuropsychiatric morbidities, and to avoid treatment options that may adversely impact comorbidities. The treatment approach should include consideration for all factors. Tourette spectrum with ADHD ADD with or without hyperactivity is quite common occurring in 7 to 15% of school-aged children [ ]. The prevalence is considerably higher in children with TS. Studies have revealed that ADD/ADHD occurs as a comorbidity in 30–50% or perhaps as high as 75% of children with TS [ ]. ADHD impairs learning to varying degrees, and may be associated with language problems [ ]. The AAN recommends clinicians assess, evaluate, and ensure appropriate treatment of ADHD in children with Tourette syndrome. It is essential that physicians monitor heart rate and blood pressure in patients treated with alpha-2 adrenergic agonists, and counsel families about sedation [ ]. Historically, many clinicians have considered stimulants to be contraindicated in children with TS, due to concern for tic exacerbation. This is no longer the dominant theory. Cochrane Reviews concludes “although stimulants have not been shown to worsen tics in most people with tic disorders, they may, nonetheless, exacerbate tics in individual cases” [ ]. Stimulants may also worsen OCD symptomatology in some individuals. When treating children with TS and

ADHD in children with Tourette syndrome. It is essential that physicians monitor heart rate and blood pressure in patients treated with alpha-2 adrenergic agonists, and counsel families about sedation [ ]. Historically, many clinicians have considered stimulants to be contraindicated in children with TS, due to concern for tic exacerbation. This is no longer the dominant theory. Cochrane Reviews concludes “although stimulants have not been shown to worsen tics in most people with tic disorders, they may, nonetheless, exacerbate tics in individual cases” [ ]. Stimulants may also worsen OCD symptomatology in some individuals. When treating children with TS and ADHD, it is best to strive for a balanced response. If the ADHD symptoms are impairing, it will likely be necessary to use a stimulant medication in order for the child [ ] succeed academically. Tics are sometimes noted to improve in response to stimulant therapy as the stress of academic struggles and negative attention to behavior are reduced. If tics or other problems worsen significantly, then benefits vs. drawbacks must be compared, and an alternative medication may need to be considered. Treatment for Tourette spectrum with ADHD, Tics dominant Central α<sub>2</sub> adrenergic agonists Clonidine and guanfacine are central α 2 adrenergic agonists used to treat ADHD and tics when they occur in combination. These medications can be given alone or in combination with a stimulant if ADHD symptoms are prominent. Clonidine is often prescribed as a first line treatment for tic prevention, and may also have a positive impact on inattention and hyperactivity with a relatively low side effect profile. Formulations include immediate release tablets and an extended release transdermal patch. In prior studies, the most significant improvement occurred in response to combination therapy [ ]. The clonidine transdermal patch was evaluated as therapy in a randomized double blind, multicenter, placebo-controlled trial for the treatment of tic disorders conducted in China. There were 437 patients, diagnosed with either transient tic disorder (5%), chronic tic disorder (40%), or Tourette syndrome (55%). The tic severity score decreased by 69% in response to clonidine patch, but also decreased by 47% in the placebo group [ ]. The recommended starting dose is 0.05 mg per day. The dose should be titrated slowly to effect to a total dose of 0.1–0.3 mg per day in adults and children, divided 3–4 times per day. Hypotension and bradycardia can occur and blood pressure and heart rate should be monitored [ ]. Guanfacine is supplied as immediate and sustained release tablets. In a randomized, double blind, 8-week trial in a group of 34 subjects with ADHD combined type and tic disorder, guanfacine reduced tic severity by 31% compared to no significant change in the placebo group. The authors concluded that guanfacine was “safe and effective in short term treatment of ADHD and tic disorder, and a combination of these medications might allow lower doses of stimulant” [ ]. It is important to monitor for possible QTc prolongation when treating with guanfacine, especially when the patient has a history of cardiac condition, is taking other medications that might lengthen QTc, or has a positive family history of QTc prolongation. The recommended starting dose is 0.5 mg per day and can be titrated to up to 4 mg per day [ ]. Abrupt cessation of guanfacine can produce rebound hypertension, thus the dosage should be tapered prior to discontinuation [ ]. The rate limiting adverse event as the dosage of clonidine or guanfacine is increased is drowsiness/sedation. On the other hand, stimulants commonly cause sleep disturbance/insomnia. Combined therapy with an α 2 -agonist and a stimulant may result in a relative balance of these effects. Tricyclic antidepressants Tricyclic antidepressants have been used to treat tics and ADHD in children. Most trials evaluated the use of desipramine with some evidence for improvement in core symptoms of ADHD and relatively weak evidence for tic reduction, but with concern for potential cardiovascular symptoms. One trial with Nortriptyline exhibited improvement in ADHD symptoms [ ]. Treatment for Tourette spectrum with ADHD, ADHD dominant Punja in a comprehensive review of the treatment of ADHD with amphetamines concluded “although amphetamines seem efficacious at reducing the core symptoms of ADHD in the short term, they were associated with a number of adverse events”. No single amphetamine was found to be superior to another, nor was there a significant difference between immediate release and sustained release formulations. The most common side effects were decreased appetite, sleep problems, and abdominal pain [ ]. Storebo’s group examined 185 trials, with over 12,000 participants, comparing methylphenidate with placebo. They concluded that “methylphenidate may improve teacher-reported ADHD symptoms, teacher-reported general behavior, and parent-reported quality of life among children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD”. They also recognized low quality evidence. Most prominent adverse effects tended to be sleep problems and decreased appetite

associated with a number of adverse events”. No single amphetamine was found to be superior to another, nor was there a significant difference between immediate release and sustained release formulations. The most common side effects were decreased appetite, sleep problems, and abdominal pain [ ]. Storebo’s group examined 185 trials, with over 12,000 participants, comparing methylphenidate with placebo. They concluded that “methylphenidate may improve teacher-reported ADHD symptoms, teacher-reported general behavior, and parent-reported quality of life among children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD”. They also recognized low quality evidence. Most prominent adverse effects tended to be sleep problems and decreased appetite [ ]. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) has issued clinical guidelines for the diagnosis, evaluation, and treatment of ADHD. They recommend that any child from 4 to 18 years of age, who has “academic or behavioral problems and symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, or impulsivity” be evaluated for ADHD. The AAP recommends behavioral-based therapy before age 6, and consideration in severe cases for use of methylphenidate at a very low dose, due to decreased metabolism in children under age 5. For children 6 to 12 years old, they recommend stimulants as first line, followed by atomoxetine, extended release guanfacine, and clonidine. Again, there is no strong evidence to suggest one stimulant is better than another. Atomoxetine has been associated with somnolence, suicidal thoughts, and rare cases of hepatitis [ ]. Treatment for Tourette spectrum with mood disorders: anxiety/OCD/depression Significant elements of anxiety are present in up to 80% of kids with TS, and OCD is expressed to some degree in up to 90% [ ]. There is also increased risk for depression and suicidality. A matched case-cohort study using a national registry revealed increased risk for suicide attempt and death by suicide in people with TS compared with controls. Suicide risk was diminished, but remained substantial after adjusting for psychiatric comorbidity. The strongest predictors of death by suicide included persistence of tics beyond young adulthood, and previous suicide attempt [ ]. The AAN Guideline stressed the importance that clinicians perform appropriate screening for anxiety, mood, and disruptive behavior disorders in people with tic disorders. Clinicians must inquire about suicidal thoughts and suicide attempts during interviews with TS patients, and refer them for appropriate evaluation and intervention if present [ ]. Treatment of TS is best provided with a strong multidisciplinary approach to care with psychiatry and/or psychology participation. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are first-line treatment options for anxiety, OCD, and depression. As a group, SSRIs are the only medications FDA approved for the treatment of OCD. In the Cochrane review of the treatment of anxiety disorders in children and adolescents, 15 of 22 included studies evaluated SSRs vs. placebo. The authors concluded medication was more effective than placebo in reducing overall symptom severity in OCD. Drug adverse events were reported in only 4.9% [ ]. A separate Cochrane review evaluated the results of 19 clinical trials focused on the treatment of depressive disorders in children and adolescents with “newer antidepressants” and included over 3000 subjects. Anyone with high risk of suicide was excluded as were many co-morbid conditions. Treatment with antidepressants lowered depression severity scores and produced higher rates of response and remission, but raised the possibility of an increased risk of suicide-related outcome for those on antidepressants compared with placebo. Fluoxetine was recommended medication of first choice. Clinicians need to keep in mind that there is evidence of an increased risk of suicide-related outcomes in those treated with antidepressant medications [ ]. Cannabinoids Cannabadiol (CBD) and cannabis have been reported via limited studies and mostly anecdotally to be potentially effective in the treatment of tics, OCD, anxiety and depression people with Tourette syndrome. Objective evidence is limited. Studies in patients with PTSD have shown reduced symptoms. There is limited evidence that CBD can reduce baseline anxiety [ ]. In a Cochrane review from 2009, 2 trials with a total of 28 patients were analyzed. The studies compared CBD monotherapy, CBD as adjuvant therapy, and placebo. One was a double blind, single dose, crossover, and the other was a double blind, parallel group. Improvements in tic frequency and severity were very small [ ]. There have been a few case reports, but completed controlled trials are generally lacking. Cannabinoid therapy is currently very popular for number of diagnoses and problems, but overall efficacy and safety of these therapies are not well defined. The AAN recommends against the use of cannabis in adolescence due to “potentially harmful cognitive and affective outcomes in adulthood”. Use of cannabis during pregnancy or breastfeeding is not recommended, and it may be harmful if used in patients recommends against use in women who are pregnant or breastfeeding, or in patients with active “psychosis” [ ]. Considering OCD apart from Tourette syndrome,

have been a few case reports, but completed controlled trials are generally lacking. Cannabinoid therapy is currently very popular for number of diagnoses and problems, but overall efficacy and safety of these therapies are not well defined. The AAN recommends against the use of cannabis in adolescence due to “potentially harmful cognitive and affective outcomes in adulthood”. Use of cannabis during pregnancy or breastfeeding is not recommended, and it may be harmful if used in patients recommends against use in women who are pregnant or breastfeeding, or in patients with active “psychosis” [ ]. Considering OCD apart from Tourette syndrome, there are limited case reports of using cannabinoids to treat OCD with both CBD [ ] and cannabis [ ] with positive results. Controlled trials using cannabinoids to treat tics and OCD are needed to further assess both safety and efficacy. Behavioral therapy A Cochrane review evaluated cognitive behavioral therapy for anxiety disorders in children and adolescents that included results from 41 studies and 1806 participants. The authors reached the conclusion that, “Cognitive behavioral therapy is an effective treatment for childhood and adolescent anxiety disorders; however, the evidence suggesting that CBT is more effective than active controls or TAU or medication at follow-up, is limited and inconclusive” [ ]. Treatment for Tourette with aggression/anger/rage or medication refractory Tics Anti-psychotics Antipsychotic drugs work by modifying the effect of dopamine in the brain primarily by blocking dopamine receptors, especially D2 receptors. These mechanisms have been thought to be responsible for reduction in tics [ ]. Multiple studies indicate varying degrees of effectiveness. The limitation is the extensive side effect profile. There is a relatively highe incidence of extrapyramidal, hormonal, and metabolic side effects. Abrupt discontinuation can cause withdrawal dyskinesia. For pimozide and ziprasidone, the EKG should be monitored with attention to the QTc interval before and after starting the medication [ ]. Treatment with an anti-psyhotic should be reserved for medication-refractory tics, and in children with dominant features of anger, aggression, rage attacks, autism spectrum disorder with significant behavioral issues, etc. Aripiprazole Published in 2017, a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 133 patients aged 7–17 years with a diagnosis of TS were randomized to low dose aripiprazole (5 mg/day if <50 kg; 10 mg/day if ≥50 kg), high-dose aripiprazole (10 mg/day if <50 kg; 20 mg/day if ≥50 kg), or placebo. They were scored at baseline and after 8 weeks using the YGTSS (Yale Global Tic Severity Scale). Significant improvement was experienced 69% of the low dose Aripiprazole group, 74% of the high dose group, and 38% of the placebo group. Most common side effects were sedation, somnolence, and fatigue. The authors concluded it was both safe and effective [ ]. Results from a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of aripiprazole in children and adolescents with Tourette’s disorder was published 2013, and included 61 subjects with a treatment phase of 10 weeks [ ]. There was a significant reduction in YGTSS. Aripiprazole was FDA approved for the treatment of TS in 2014. The recommended initial dose is 2 mg per day with a maximum of 10 mg/day if <50 kg or 20 mg/day if ≥50 kg [ ]. Fluphenazine Fluphenazine is a phenothiazine, antipsychotic medication. It does not have a specific indication for the treatment of TS. A 2014 retrospective chart review included 268 patients and reported improvement in 80.5%. The average duration of therapy with fluphenazine was 2.6 years. Adverse effects were reported 26% of patients, [ ]. Fluphanazine is not FDA approved ro therapy in childnre with TS and should be used with caution since adverse effects can be significant. Haloperidol Haloperidol was the first neuroleptic drug approved by the FDA for the treatment of adult patients with TS in 1969 and for children in 1978. In its class, it is one of the more studied medications. Pimozide Pimozide is another well-studied medication within this class that was FDA approved for treatment of adolescents with TS in 1984 as a second-line therapy when other treatments had failed. It was recognized there is potential for prolongation of the QT interval and ventricular arrhythmias have been rarely reported. It is critical to obtain an electrocardiogram to check the QTc interval before and after starting the medication [ ]. In a Cochrane review of treatment options for TS, pimozide was noted to be superior to placebo in three clinical trials, similar to haloperiodol in two trials, and inferior to haloperiodol in one trial. Pimozide and respiridone appeared to be equally efficacious. Pimozide induced less dyskinesia and sedative effect compared to haloperidol. [ , ]. Risperidone The results of 5 clinical trials utilizing risperidone in the treatment of TS were included in a review in CNS Drugs , and indicated positive efficacy, but also prominent adverse effects including dyskinesia and metabolic abnormalities. They

and after starting the medication [ ]. In a Cochrane review of treatment options for TS, pimozide was noted to be superior to placebo in three clinical trials, similar to haloperiodol in two trials, and inferior to haloperiodol in one trial. Pimozide and respiridone appeared to be equally efficacious. Pimozide induced less dyskinesia and sedative effect compared to haloperidol. [ , ]. Risperidone The results of 5 clinical trials utilizing risperidone in the treatment of TS were included in a review in CNS Drugs , and indicated positive efficacy, but also prominent adverse effects including dyskinesia and metabolic abnormalities. They concluded that risperidone may be a best option for children/adolescents with TS with a tendency for prominent aggression, anger and violence [ ]. Olanzapine There are few studies and limited evidence to support the use of olanzapine in the treatment of TS. There have been one open label, one randomized single blind trial, and one randomized cross over study that reported decreased severity of tics [ ]. Quetiapine There have been two open label studies (1 adult and 1 pediatric) that evaluated quetiapine in the treatment of TS that did indicate decreased severity of tics on YGTSS (Yale Global Tic Severity Scale) [ ]. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) Due to the invasive nature of DBS, it is not an option to be taken lightly, but may be a consideration for patients with severe TS that is resistant to medical and behavioral therapy. They should have failed multiple classes of medications before consideration of DBS. “The AAN highlights recommendations from the Movement Disorders Society: when DBS is used in TS, best practices used for other DBS applications are followed, including confirmation of diagnosis, use of multidisciplinary screening, and stabilization of psychiatric comorbidities inclusive of active suicidality” [ ]. DBS with stimulation within the thalamus dates back to 1999, and has been studied for treatment of multiple disorders including Parkinson’s, essential tremor, epilepsy, and others. The most common targets lie within the medial thalamus and include centromedian nucleus, parafascicular nucleus and ventralis oralis nucleus. Additional targets include the anteromedial or posterior ventrolateral GPi, anterior internal capsule, nucleus accumbens, subthalamic nucleus, fields of Forel (H1), and globus pallidus externus [ ]. A meta-analysis of 57 studies and 156 cases of TS report significant improvement of 53% in YGTSS. Significant reductions were found with stimulation of anterior limb of internal capsule and nucleus accumbens. There were no significant differences in improvement in comparison of these targets. (Baldermann) The International Tourette Syndrome Deep Brain Stimulation Public Database and Registry included a total of 185 patients from 10 countries between 2012 and 2016. Results were reported from 163 patients with medically refractory symptoms who received DBS implantation in the centromedian thalamic region (93 or 57%), anterior globus pallidus internus (41 or 25%), posterior globus pallidus internus (25 or 15%), or anterior limb of the internal capsule (4 or 2.5%). Impact on tic severity was performed using YGTSS. Mean age was 29.1 years, with a range of 13–58 years. OCD was present in 97 of 151 pts (64.2%), and 32 of 148 (21.6%) had self-injurious behavior. A significant reduction in the mean YGTSS from 75.0 to 41.2 had occurred at 1 year after implantation. Adverse events occurred in 35.2% (56 patients) including two with intracranial hemorrhage and infection in four. The most common adverse effects were dysarthria in 10 (6.3%) and paresthesia in 13 (8.2%) [ ]. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) TMS is newer therapy with more limited evidence. Kleimaker offered the following description of TMS: “TMS electric currents through magnetic fields produced by electromagnetic coils. Lower frequency rTMS around 1 Hz typically includes net decrease of excitability of targeted areas and higher frequencies cause net increase. Can last minutes to hours. Over time creates long-term plasticity which can create long-term rehabilitation, learning, memory. Encompasses changes within membranes of synapses leading to enhanced (long term) potentiation or reduces (long term depression) synaptic transmission” [ ]. The supplemental motor area (SMA) has a high degree of interconnection with basal ganglia and is considered a central hub within the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits. It is believed, that the central role of SMA in tic generation is underpinned by increased metabolic activity and increased GABA levels correlating with tic severity. SMA function is likely not involved in the learning, formation and propensity to develop tics, which more likely resides within the basal ganglia. One limitation is of TMS is anatomical location. Higher frequency stimulation will hit neighboring areas. There are a number of “possible targets” still being studied. Bilateral SMA simulation produced improvement in 5 of 7 studies, and bilateral PreSMA stimulation has demonstrated showed significant improvement [ ]. More investigation utilizing TMS in the treatment of TS is indicated before this becomes a solid option. Treatment for Tourette spectrum: Tic dominant

and increased GABA levels correlating with tic severity. SMA function is likely not involved in the learning, formation and propensity to develop tics, which more likely resides within the basal ganglia. One limitation is of TMS is anatomical location. Higher frequency stimulation will hit neighboring areas. There are a number of “possible targets” still being studied. Bilateral SMA simulation produced improvement in 5 of 7 studies, and bilateral PreSMA stimulation has demonstrated showed significant improvement [ ]. More investigation utilizing TMS in the treatment of TS is indicated before this becomes a solid option. Treatment for Tourette spectrum: Tic dominant Cognitive behavioral intervention for Tics (CBIT) In the AAN and Tourette Association of America recommendations that have also been endorsed by the Child Neurology Society, CBIT is recommend as first line treatment for tics and impairing symptoms. CBIT is primarily used in children over age 9; however, there are patients under the age of 9, who might benefit from behavioral therapy. One study looked at children ages 5 to 8, and adapted CBIT for use in younger children. The results revealed high levels of satisfaction and retention, significant decrease in YGTSS, and reduction in comorbidities that were maintained at 3 month and 1 year follow ups [ ]. A randomized, observer-blinded, controlled trial, with 126 children aged 9 to 17, with impairing TS, or other chronic tic disorder, concluded that CBIT produced significant improvement in symptom severity, based on YGTSS [ ] CBIT increases the ability of the patient to “perform response inhibition” [ ]. Baclofen Baclofen has been evaluated in the treatment of TS with overall weak evidence for improvement [ ]. Botulinum toxin Botulinum toxin (Botox) is sometimes used for specific focal tics that cause impairment. There was one randomized placebo controlled trial with 20 patients that exhibited low-quality evidence, and uncertain benefit [ ]. The AAN’s official guideline ascribes level C evidence for the treatment of tics in TS. They did strongly recommend (level A), that physicians “counsel individuals with tics that botulinum toxin injections may cause weakness and hypophonia, and that all effects are temporary”. Often the procedure would need to be repeated at 3, 4 month intervals, as the effects typically only last 12–16 weeks [ ]. Topiramate One randomized, double-blind, placebo controlled trial evaluated topiramate in the treatment of TS and included 29 patients with a mean age of 16.5 years. Total daily dose ranged from 25 to 200 mg. There was statistically significant improvement on YGTSS, and no significant adverse events [ ]. The AAN recommends that Topiramate might be helpful in treatment of mild, but troublesome tics as an alternative to other medications. They recommend physicians counsel patients on possible side effects, which include cognitive and language problems, somnolence, decreased appetite, weight loss, and possible increased risk of renal stones [ ]. Tetrabenazine In one open label study using tetrabenazine for tic prevention in 10 patients with average treatment of 9.4 months, 4 of 10 experienced “marked improvement”. Another open label study of 120 adults and children indicated improvement, although results were skewed because 93% of participants were on other medications [ ]. A third study included 92 patients with a tetrabenazine dose range of 6.25 mg to 150 mg per day. Nearly 78% of patients experienced complete or nearly complete abolishment of tics [ ]. Recently, Teva pharmaceuticals announced that their phase 2 and 3 ARTISTS 1 and Phase 3 ARTISTS 2 trials both failed to meet their primary endpoint aimed at reduction of both motor and phonic tics using the YGTSS to assess the children. This was released via: https://www.nasdaq.com/press-release/teva-announces-registration-trials-of-deutetrabenazine-in-pediatric-patients-with . Deutetrabenazine The −OCH3 (methoxy) group is replaced with −OCD3 (trideuter-omethoxy) in deutetrabenazine which results in both increaseed half-life and decrease side effects. One 6-week open label trial included TS patients 12–18 years of age with a resultant decrease in YGTSS in response to deutratrabenazine [ ]. Another study included evaluation of 23 patients over 8 weeks, and deutetrabenazine therapy significantly reduced YGTSS. Side effects included headache, fatigue, irritability, nasopharyngitis, somnolence, hyperhidrosis, and diarrhea [ ]. We have found relaxation therapy and breathing exercises, combined with medication tailored to their symptoms works best. CBIT is great option, if available. Ultimately, these children represent a subclass of TS that should be treated with the same strategy as those in each of the other sections. Conclusion Tourette syndrome is a spectrum disorder. It is primarily a disorder of childhood. Within this spectrum, we find a range of neuropsychiatric comorbidities of varying degrees, all of which are intertwined. When we create our treatment plan, we have to account for all associated problems. That will allow us to have the best chance for success. A multidisciplinary approach is optimal when caring for children and adolescents with Tourette syndrome.

documents.title: Practice guideline update efficacy and tolerability of new antiepileptic drugs treatment resistant epilepsy

chunks.content: Introduction Epilepsy is a chronic non-communicable disease of the brain that affects people of all ages. There are ~50 million patients with epilepsy worldwide, making it one of the most common neurological diseases in the world ( ). Nearly 80% of epileptic patients live in low- and middle-income countries. China has ~6 million patients with active epilepsy (AE, defined as two or more unprovoked seizures in the past year) every year, and 60% of them suffer from partial-onset seizures ( , ) with a mortality risk of 2–3 times that of the general population ( ). Epilepsy accounts for 5% of the global economic burden of mental illnesses ( ). Long-term administration of anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs) and other costs of diagnosis and treatment impose a heavy economic burden to families. In 2009, a study conducted in Southwest China showed that the average annual cost (in US dollars) of epileptic patients was $773, in which the cost of AEDs amounted to $243 ( ). In 2015, another study on the disease burden in central China showed that the average annual cost of epileptic patients reached $949 ( ). Moreover, the stigma of epilepsy brings about a serious psychological burden to patients and their families, which discourages the patients from seeking treatment and reduces their quality of life ( ). As for children and adolescents, suffering from epilepsy imposes a lifelong impact on their social, emotional, and occupational development ( ). Therefore, the prevention and treatment of epilepsy is not only a medical problem, but also a vital public health and social problem. Epilepsy is a treatable disease, with AEDs being the preferred therapeutic option and the most important treatment approach. Up to 70% of epileptic patients achieve seizure remission for a relatively long time through proper diagnosis and standardized use of AEDs ( ). However, in developing countries, most epileptic patients cannot receive reasonable and effective treatment. In China, the treatment gap for AE patients is ~60% ( , ). Epileptic patients therefore have significant unmet medical needs. As recommended drugs for the treatment of refractory focal epilepsy in adults, third-generation AEDs including perampanel (PER) and lacosamide (LCM) show advantages in terms of efficacy, safety, and tolerability over first- and second-generation AEDs ( ). PER (Fycompa®, Eisai Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan) is a first-in-class non-competitive highly selective α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole propionic acid receptor antagonist. Several multi-center, randomized-controlled, phase III clinical trials have shown that compared with placebo, PER (4–12 mg/day) considerably reduces seizure frequency and improves response rate with acceptable tolerability in epileptic patients ( – ). LCM is one of the sodium channel blockers in AEDs. Two phase III clinical trials have shown that compared with placebo, LCM substantially reduces seizure frequency with good tolerability ( , ). In the 2018 guidelines from the American Academy of Neurology and the American Epilepsy Association (AAN/AES), the grades of evidence-based recommendation for PER and LCM are A and B, respectively ( ). Cost-effectiveness (CE) evidence and budget impact analysis (BIA) of PER have been reported in other countries ( , ). Some studies have also explored the CE of LCM as an add-on to conventional AED therapy ( , ). All these studies have demonstrated that PER or LCM as an add-on therapy for uncontrolled or refractory epilepsy is a cost-effective regimen ( , , ). In 2019, China approved PER for add-on therapy in adults and children over 12 years of age with partial-onset seizures (with or without secondary generalized seizures). In December 2020, PER was included in China's latest National Reimbursement Drug List (NRDL; LCM was released to the market in 2018 and included in the NRDL in 2019). Due to the limitations of the public budget, economic efficiency has become one of the most important factors for inclusion in the NRDL of China since 2018. The economic efficiency of LCM compared with conventional therapy was proven in 2010. Bolin et al. showed that LCM was cost-effective as an add-on therapy for uncontrolled partial-onset seizures ( ). In 2018, the economic efficiency of PER as an add-on therapy for primary systemic tonic-clonic seizures was confirmed in Spain ( ). However, the economic efficiency of PER therapy for partial-onset seizures in China remains unknown, and there is a lack of comparison between PER and LCM. From the perspective of resource allocation, even if the drugs are economical, whether they can be afforded by public funds is still the threshold for inclusion. According to the Institute for Clinical and Economic Review (ICER) Value Framework 2.0, the economic efficiency and affordability of a drug should be simultaneously included in its value evidence ( ). Since 2019, the evidence from CE analysis (CEA) and BIA has also become economic evidence that is compulsory to be submitted for inclusion in the NRDL of China. The aim of

According to the Institute for Clinical and Economic Review (ICER) Value Framework 2.0, the economic efficiency and affordability of a drug should be simultaneously included in its value evidence ( ). Since 2019, the evidence from CE analysis (CEA) and BIA has also become economic evidence that is compulsory to be submitted for inclusion in the NRDL of China. The aim of this study is to evaluate the value of PER as an add-on regimen to the treatment of partial-onset seizures in China and provide evidence on both its CE and affordability. Materials and Methods Model Structure As epilepsy is a lifetime chronic disease, we used the Markov model to evaluate lifelong effectiveness and costs of PER + AEDs vs. LCM + AEDs in patients with partial-onset seizures in China. The health state was classified according to seizure frequency, namely: ≥53 times/year, 13–52 times/year, 1–12 times/year, and no seizures. The seizure frequency was dependent on the response level after medication (the scale of the decrease in baseline number of seizures). More specifically, distribution of response levels over each cycle period were mapped to health states defined by seizure frequency. The mapping calculation was based on clinical trials. There are six response levels: seizure-free, response rate of 75–99%, response rate of 50–74%, response rate <50%, increased seizures, and maintenance therapy (including patients withdrawn from the trial due to adverse reaction or other reasons). The cycle period of the model was set to 4 months (consistent with the medication regimen). This model adopted a lifetime horizon, and the cycle of the model was terminated when the proportion of dead patients reached 99.9%. According to latest guidelines for pharmacoeconomic evaluation in China ( ), health outputs and costs were discounted at an annual discount rate of 5%. In particular, two dose comparison groups were set up in this study, namely PER 8 mg/day vs. LCM 400 mg/day and PER 4 mg/day vs. LCM 200 mg/day, as adjunctive treatment. This design was based on comprehensive consideration of the defined daily dose (DDD) recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) ( ), the availability of clinical trial data ( , ), and the actual clinical dose used in China indicated by clinicians ( ). The model structure is shown in . Health Outcomes and Data Sources Health outcomes included the number of epileptic seizures, life years (LYs), and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs). For the first cycle in the model, response rates were derived from clinical trials 335 (trial registration number: NCT01618695 , sample size: 704) and EP0008 (trial registration number: NCT01710657 , sample size: 548), both of which include reasonably large sample sizes in Chinese populations (199 Chinese in trial 335, 406 Chinese in trial EP0008). The baseline seizure distribution of patients by health state was displayed in , as LCM 4 mg/day and LCM 8 mg/day was assumed to have the same baseline seizure frequency with PER 4 mg/day and PER 8 mg/day, respectively. Other baseline information of patients involved in the clinical trials is listed in . Because the two trials were not head-to-head trials, we used an indirect comparison method in this study and acquired the risk ratio values of PER and LCM response rates with conventional therapy as the bridge. Because LCM lacked data on the proportion of patients with increased epileptic seizures, we assumed the proportion of patients whose seizures increased by <25% to be equal to that of the PER group. We obtained the proportion of patients whose seizures increased by ≥25% from the data reported in another clinical trial of LCM ( ). The initial distributions of response rates are detailed in . From the second cycle, transition probabilities of response rate were obtained from long-term follow-up data ( ). The model converted 5-year transition probabilities according to the following equation ( ): P 4 month = 1 - exp [ ( 1 / 15 ) * [ ln ( 1 - P 5 year ) ] ] where P 5year denotes the 5-year probability, P 4month denotes the 4-month probability, and 4 months accounts for 1/15 of 5 years. Neligan et al. only reported the probability of response rates transitioning from <50 to 50–99% ( ). Here, we allocated the transition of response rates from <50 to 50–74% or 75–99% according to the proportion of patients corresponding to the response rates of 50–74% and 75–99% in the trial EP0008 ( ). The transition probabilities of response rates are listed in . Natural mortalities were obtained from the life table of natural mortalities in China published by the WHO (

Neligan et al. only reported the probability of response rates transitioning from <50 to 50–99% ( ). Here, we allocated the transition of response rates from <50 to 50–74% or 75–99% according to the proportion of patients corresponding to the response rates of 50–74% and 75–99% in the trial EP0008 ( ). The transition probabilities of response rates are listed in . Natural mortalities were obtained from the life table of natural mortalities in China published by the WHO ( ). The seizure-free population was considered to have the same mortality risk as the general population. Mortality risks for different seizure frequencies were based on the data reported by Nilsson et al. ( ), and the RR values are listed in . Costs From a health system perspective, only direct medical costs were taken into account in this study, including drug costs and medical service costs (covering outpatient, emergency, and inpatient treatment costs). For drug costs, the unit price of drugs was multiplied by their daily dose to obtain the unit cost. AED costs were derived from the unit price multiplied by the use ratio of various drugs in clinical trials (335, EP0008). The unit price of drugs was derived from the median national price in the China Drug Bidding Database ( shuju.menet.com.cn ). In all cases, it was included as the price of the largest sales specification and converted into the unit price of the smallest dose. Medical service costs were derived from the unit price multiplied by the frequency of medical visits, and details are displayed in . Because of the lack of data on medical visits for epilepsy, the items of medical services and the frequency of medical visits were acquired from the opinions of 18 clinicians from different hospitals in China. The unit price of medical services was derived from the median of documented data in the medical insurance bureaus of nine provinces and cities in China. Because the service prices were inconsistent among different levels of hospitals, we adjusted the service prices according to the proportion of medical visits to second- and third-level medical institutions ( ). All costs used in this study were converted from Chinese yuan to US dollars [1 dollar = 6.5408 yuan ( )]. Details are provided in . Health Utilities Health state utility values were acquired from the National Health and Wellness Survey of Kantar Health ( ). Details are summarized in . Base-Case Analysis Costs were calculated by simultaneously taking into account the usage of all drugs (including PER, LCM, and AEDs) and medical service resources by the patients in different states. Finally, the number of seizures, LYs, QALYs, and incremental CE ratio (ICER) related to PER + AEDs vs. LCM + AEDs were obtained. Uncertainty Analysis We performed one-way deterministic sensitivity analysis (DSA) using the 95% confidence interval reported in the literature as the variation range. The discount rate ranged from 0 to 8% ( ). The impact of the extreme discount rate (effectiveness: 8%, cost: 0%; effectiveness: 0%, cost: 8%) on the results was taken into account. Assuming that the distribution proportion of PER entering maintenance therapy, response rate of 75–99%, and seizure-free state fluctuates by 20% for DSA. The variation range of other parameters that lacked documented reports was assumed based on KOL (Key Opinion Leader) opinions. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) was performed using Monte Carlo simulation with 10,000 iterations. The standard deviation of utility values was derived from the literature ( ). The standard deviation of costs was obtained from the standard deviation of AED prices and the distribution range of KOL opinions. Parameter distributions came from classical assumption ( ). The parameter characteristics of mortality, cost, and utility value are listed in . In addition to the parameters listed in , we assumed that LY conforms to a normal distribution, with its mean and standard deviation derived from the model. In basic analysis, we assumed that there was no transition from <50% response rate to increase in seizure. However, we found this assumption was uncertain compared with other studies. Considering that the transition patterns of response rates are the basis of the cycle in the model, we designed a scenario analysis according to the pharmacoeconomic study of Tremblay et al. ( ): assuming that there are probabilities for patients with a response rate of <50% transitioning to the state of increased seizures, and the transition is expressed by the following equation: P <50% to increase in seizures = P increase in seizures * (1 – P responsive). ( ): assuming that there are probabilities for patients with a response rate of <50% transitioning to the state of increased seizures, and the transition is expressed by the following equation: P <50% to increase in seizures = P increase in seizures * (1 – P responsive). Budget Impact We analyzed the impact of the inclusion of PER in the NRDL on the medical insurance budget in 2021–2023. The target population comprised participants in basic medical insurance aged ≥12 years with partial-onset seizures and undergoing standardized drug treatment ( ). Taking into account the substitution of other similar drugs by PER, we added zonisamide (ZNS) as a reference drug in addition to LCM. The market share of the three drugs in 2020–2023 was obtained by Eisai Co., Ltd. based on the actual market situation ( ). Cost data were derived from the CEA results, and the distribution proportion of patient health states before and after treatment is summarized in . For the two groups of daily doses, we obtained the use ratio of clinical patients for different daily doses of PER and LCM by consulting KOL, and this set of data was used for weighting in the cost calculation. The medical insurance reimbursement policy is provided in . DSA was performed on epidemiological parameters, use ratio of clinical doses, and cost parameters that may affect budget impact (BI). The distribution ranges of the parameters are given in . Results Base-Case Analysis The results of base-case analysis ( ) show that PER has an dominate advantage over LCM in terms of CE. Compared with LCM 400 mg/day, PER 8 mg/day reduces the number of seizures per capita by 141 times, with an incremental LY of 0.061, an incremental QALY of 0.054, and a direct medical cost saving of $2,390. Compared with LCM200 mg/day, PER 4 mg/day reduces the number of seizures per capita by 72 times, with an incremental LY of 0.012, an incremental QALY of 0.010, and a cost savings of $860. Uncertainty Analysis Deterministic Sensitivity Analysis The DSA results ( ) show that the ICER of PER 8 mg/day vs. LCM 400 mg/day group ranges from $150,911 to $8,418/QALY, with the extreme discount rate having the greatest impact on ICER. The ICER of PER 4 mg/day vs. LCM 200 mg/day group ranges from $556,653 to $119,970/QALY, with the utility value having the greatest impact on ICER. The price of AEDs and the unit price of medical services have little impact on ICER in both groups. Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis The PSA results ( ) show that the different dose groups of PER have a large probability of being economical at various levels of willingness-to-pay. The one-to-three times gross domestic product (GDP) per capita was $10,838–$32,515 in China in 2019 ( data.stats.gov.cn ). Scenario Analysis The results of scenario analysis ( ) show that compared with LCM 400 mg/day, PER 8 mg/day achieves an incremental QALY of 0.039 and a cost saving of $2,747, which is still the regimen with dominate advantage. However, compared with PER 4 mg/day, LCM 200 mg/day results in an incremental QALY of 0.005 and an incremental cost of $554. The ICER is $105,194/QALY, higher than three times GDP per capita [$32,515], indicating that LCM is not cost-effective. This result may be attributed to the relatively small incremental QALY, which may not meet the minimal clinically important difference. Budget Impact Analysis Base-Case Analysis After the inclusion of PER in the NRDL, it is expected that the target population using PER will increase by 1,918; 4,287; and 8,983 in 2021–2023, respectively, with a total population increase from 6,557 to 21,774. In contrast, the target populations of LCM and ZNS will decrease by a total of 3,531 in the 3 years. Before and after the inclusion of PER in the NRDL, the absolute BI over 2021–2023 will be $17.30, $27.78, and $39.08 million and $18.58, $30.61, and $43.65 million, respectively ( ). The incremental BI (including drug and medical service costs) over the 3 years will be $1.28, $2.83, and $4.56 million, respectively, accounting for 0.00037, 0.00082, and 0.00132% of the total expenditure of national medical insurance in that year (total medical insurance expenditure was acquired from medical insurance bureau reports. Among them, drug costs will increase by $1.39, $3.02, and $4.99 million, whereas medical service costs will be reduced by $0.10, $0.19, and $0.42 million ( ). Medical insurance reimbursement costs per capita (including drug and medical service costs) will increase by $110.72, $151.59, and $169.14. Deterministic Sensitivity Analysis The BI results are relatively robust. The factors that have the greatest impact on the results are the market share after inclusion of

accounting for 0.00037, 0.00082, and 0.00132% of the total expenditure of national medical insurance in that year (total medical insurance expenditure was acquired from medical insurance bureau reports. Among them, drug costs will increase by $1.39, $3.02, and $4.99 million, whereas medical service costs will be reduced by $0.10, $0.19, and $0.42 million ( ). Medical insurance reimbursement costs per capita (including drug and medical service costs) will increase by $110.72, $151.59, and $169.14. Deterministic Sensitivity Analysis The BI results are relatively robust. The factors that have the greatest impact on the results are the market share after inclusion of PER in the NRDL, the prevalence of AE, and the distribution of patients using different daily doses of PER (4/8 mg). The price of PER also has a relatively large impact on the results ( ). Discussion This is the first study to calculate the value of PER as an add-on regimen to the treatment of patients with partial-onset seizures in China with respect to CE and medical insurance affordability. Currently, there are limited documents on the economic evaluation of PER. An economic evaluation based on the perspective of Spain showed that the ICER of PER as an adjuvant therapy to AEDs was €16,557/QALY over a 33-year study period; with the willingness-to-pay of €30,000/QALY, PER had an 89.3% probability of being the cost-effective option for primary generalized tonic-clonic epileptic seizures ( ). Here, our study from the perspective of China's health system shows that using PER as an adjuvant therapy to AEDs has an dominate advantage over LCM in terms of CE. This result is also relatively stable within the one-two-three times GDP per capita of $10,838–$32,515. Moreover, the time horizon of our model is the patient's lifetime. Based on the BIA, this study is in agreement with the results of Tremebly et al. ( ) for PER; that is, PER as an add-on brings about an increase in BI year by year while also resulting in a medical service cost savings. This result is mainly attributed to the improvement of health state after the use of PER, which in turn reduces the direct medical costs. In clinical trials 304, 305, and 306 with PER, 4.4% and 3.5% of the patients achieved a seizure-free state owing to an add-on therapy with PER at 4 or 8 mg/day (1.0% in the AEDs placebo group) ( ), whereas in the clinical trial 335, the proportion of seizure-free patients in the Chinese population was even higher in the PER group (8.8 vs. 0%). This study is novel in several ways. First, this study simulates the lifetime effectiveness and cost data of patients through a Markov model, with full consideration of long-term simulation and health state classification of epileptic patients. Epilepsy is a chronic disease that may be lifelong ( ). It is therefore necessary to investigate the long-term health outcomes of epilepsy and distinguish the costs from different frequencies of epileptic seizures. In an economic evaluation of LCM compared with conventional therapy, Simoens and Bolin et al. adopted a decision tree model to simulate the outcomes of short-term therapy in epileptic patients without considering the seizure-free state ( , ). Furthermore, no head-to-head studies on PER and LCM have been found, which is also one of the innovative points of this study. Second, this study gives a comprehensive consideration to the daily dose of drugs. The WHO recommends the adult daily doses of PER and LCM to be 8 and 300 mg/day, respectively ( ). Clinical trial 335 of PER involved three daily dose groups of 4, 8, and 12 mg, respectively ( ). However, clinical trial EP0008 of LCM only consisted of two daily dose groups of 200 and 400 mg, respectively ( ). According to KOL opinions, we finally determine to explore the CE of PER 8 mg/day vs. LCM 400 mg/day and PER 4 mg/day vs. LCM 200 mg/day. We did not include PER 12 mg/day in the analysis because this dose is mainly used in patients with refractory epilepsy as indicated by KOL. In the BIA, the distribution of patients using different doses is taken into account comprehensively in accordance with the actual use ratio in the clinic given by KOL, aiming to be more in line with the real-world situation. Third, this study also takes into account multiple aspects of cost data to better reflect the current situation in China. All the drugs analyzed in this study are included in the latest NRDL (announced by medical insurance bureau at the end of December 2020). Considering the fairness of the control and the origin of efficacy data from original drugs, we obtain the price of LCM from the price of the original drug, whereas for the remaining AEDs, both original and generic drugs are taken into account to make

by KOL, aiming to be more in line with the real-world situation. Third, this study also takes into account multiple aspects of cost data to better reflect the current situation in China. All the drugs analyzed in this study are included in the latest NRDL (announced by medical insurance bureau at the end of December 2020). Considering the fairness of the control and the origin of efficacy data from original drugs, we obtain the price of LCM from the price of the original drug, whereas for the remaining AEDs, both original and generic drugs are taken into account to make the price close to the market. In China, the price of medical services is set by medical insurance bureaus of various provinces and cities, leading to the differences in medical service price across regions. Here, we select nine provinces and cities based on their geographical locations in East, Central, and West China, and then take the medians of their prices. In addition, considering that epileptic patients usually visit second- and third-level medical institutions, we have the prices of second- and third-level medical institutions weighted according to the proportion of the number of medical visits ( ). In the BIA based on the perspective of medical insurance payers, we not only distinguish the difference in the reimbursement of various insurance categories (URRBMI and UEBMI), but also consider the difference in the reimbursement policies of outpatient, emergency, or inpatient, and Class A or Class B of drugs. Our study is not without limitations. First, the lack of local data in China may introduce potential bias in the results. For example, because no data are available on the utility value and mortality risk caused by epilepsy in the Chinese population, the utility value ( ) and mortality risk ( ) of foreign population are used in this study. There are also no data on the long-term transition probability of epileptic patients in the Chinese population. We therefore use the transition of response rates in epileptic patients of a 5-year follow-up investigation conducted in the United Kingdom ( ). Moreover, with regard to whether there will be a certain probability for epileptic patients with a response rate of <50% transitioning to increased seizures during actual drug use in the clinic, we take this situation as a scenario analysis for supplementation, because follow-up data are lacking for the Chinese population. Further, we have to make certain assumptions because of the objective lack of some data. For example, LCM lacks the proportion of patients with increased seizures reported in clinical trials. We therefore assume that the proportion of patients whose seizures increased by <25% is equal to that of the PER group, whereas the proportion of patients whose seizures increased by ≥25% is based on another clinical trial ( ). In the BIA, reports on the annual growth rate of the prevalence of AE is lacking. Thus, we select the annual growth rate of the lifetime prevalence of epilepsy reported in a meta-analysis in China ( ) and perform a sensitivity analysis on this parameter. In addition, because no available clinical research reports on ZNS are found, we assume in the BIA that the proportion of AEDs and therapeutic efficacy of patients in the ZNS group are at the average levels of PER and LCM. We consult pharmacoeconomic experts and clinicians to deal with all the assumptions as much as possible. Finally, some factors are not taken into account in this study, such as compliance and adverse reactions. Frequent administration of AED affects patient compliance. When AED is administered once a day, patient compliance is 87%; when AED is administered twice a day, patient compliance drops to 81% (PER once a day and LCM twice a day) ( ). However, because the two drugs are both add-on therapy in this study and the daily administration frequency of AEDs also affects compliance, the measurement of compliance value is not included in the model. Previous research has reported that PER and LCM cause relatively mild adverse reactions in a short term ( , ), whereas ZNS is currently a generic drug in the Chinese market which lacks reliable research reports. Long-term adverse reactions to PER and LCM need to be determined through further follow-up monitoring of the Chinese population. Conclusion Our study demonstrates that PER is valuable as an add-on therapy for patients with partial-onset seizures in China. PER has a dominate advantage of CE compared with LCM (8 vs. 400 mg/day; 4 vs. 200 mg/day), and its incremental BI for medical insurance payers is relatively acceptable. In this study, the BIA as a supplement to CEA achieves a relatively comprehensive evaluation of the value of PER in the treatment of partial-onset seizures in China. China has not yet developed a value framework that integrates CE and BI

to be determined through further follow-up monitoring of the Chinese population. Conclusion Our study demonstrates that PER is valuable as an add-on therapy for patients with partial-onset seizures in China. PER has a dominate advantage of CE compared with LCM (8 vs. 400 mg/day; 4 vs. 200 mg/day), and its incremental BI for medical insurance payers is relatively acceptable. In this study, the BIA as a supplement to CEA achieves a relatively comprehensive evaluation of the value of PER in the treatment of partial-onset seizures in China. China has not yet developed a value framework that integrates CE and BI proposed by foreign researchers ( ). Nevertheless, evidence on the CE and affordability of drugs has received increasing attention in this country. The present study also provides a reference for stakeholders to judge the value of PER. Data Availability Statement Publicly available datasets were analyzed in this study. This data can be found here: https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT01618695?term=NCT01618695&draw=2&rank=1 ; https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/results/NCT01710657?term=NCT01710657&draw=2&rank=1 . Ethics Statement Ethical review and approval was not required for the study on human participants in accordance with the local legislation and institutional requirements. Written informed consent for participation was not required for this study in accordance with the national legislation and the institutional requirements. Author Contributions DZ and XL were mainly responsible for research model building, data collection, and manuscript writing. WT was responsible for research design, model building, and manuscript review and modification. XK, WD, and YR contributed to the collection of model data and model building. HX provided beneficial help to the initial model building. JD confirmed the clinical and epidemiological inputs. All authors have contributed substantially to the study and approved the final submitted version of the manuscript. Conflict of Interest The authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.

documents.title: Practice guideline summary disorders of consciousness

chunks.content: Introduction Level of consciousness assessed by bedside clinical examination is an established predictor of recovery from brain injury [ , ] and is widely implemented in prediction scores affecting major decisions about aggressiveness of care and withdrawal of life-sustaining therapies [ – ]. More recently, brain activation to motor commands has been detected in clinically unresponsive patients with brain injury using functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) [ , ] and machine learning analysis of electroencephalogram (EEG) [ , ]. This state, which is called cognitive motor dissociation (CMD) and has been demonstrated in 15% of clinically unresponsive patients with acute brain injury, has been linked to long-term recovery of independence [ , ]. Clinical assessments and CMD detection are typically performed by asking patients to act out or imagine a motor movement (e.g., “keep moving your right hand”). Understanding such a command may be challenging for patients with acute brain injury in a distracting intensive care unit (ICU) context, and particularly for patients with impaired speech comprehension (e.g., receptive aphasia) [ ]. Recent guidelines for the assessment of patients with disorders of consciousness from the American [ ] and European [ ] Academies of Neurology have endorsed advanced assessments for responsiveness such as CMD, if available. However, the practical and moral risk of erroneously failing to detect CMD is enormous if CMD testing is introduced into clinical practice [ ]. The concern for false negative CMD results has been raised in studies that included healthy volunteers [ – ], but the risk of occult aphasia in behaviorally unresponsive patients is poorly understood, as highlighted in a recent gap analysis [ ]. Here, we aimed to provide estimates of false negative CMD testing among patients with aphasic in the ICU to allow care providers to manage this risk. Brain activation using CMD paradigms has been reported in a wide range of brain injuries, including trauma [ ], cardiac arrest [ ], and stroke [ ]. Patients with stroke are at particularly high risk of aphasia, ranging from 19 to 62% for acute ischemic and 9% to 32% for acute hemorrhagic strokes [ ]. Our study, which examines the relationship between aphasia and brain activation in patients with spontaneous ICH, departs from previous CMD studies [ , ] in focusing on patients who are awake and able to follow commands or mimic. This is a necessity because clinically evaluating for aphasia is impossible in behaviorally unresponsive patients, and a diagnosis cannot be made based on imaging alone given that anatomical localizations of aphasia types are increasingly understood to vary [ ]. Our objective was to quantify the risk of failing to show brain activation in the context of aphasia. To achieve this, we performed a prospective study of patients with acute primary ICH who were able to follow verbal commands or mimic to visual cues [ ] within 48 h of bleeding. All patients underwent standardized aphasia testing and assessments using an EEG-based motor command paradigm used to detect CMD while in the ICU. We tested the hypothesis that patients with impaired comprehension (e.g., receptive or global aphasia) would be less likely to show brain activation to the motor command paradigm. Methods Study Design From September 2019 to December 2023, we screened every patient admitted with a diagnosis of acute ICH to the neurological ICU at Columbia University Irving Medical Center in New York City. Inclusion criteria were the following: (1) diagnosis of primary ICH (e.g., hypertension, anticoagulation); (2) lobar (frontal, temporal, partial, or occipital) or subcortical (thalamic, capsular, or basal ganglia) location of ICH verified by computerize tomography and/or MRI; (3) age 18 years or older; (4) consciousness within 48 h of bleeding, defined as the ability to consistently follow a simple command (e.g., “stick out your tongue” or “show me two fingers”) and/or mimic the commanded action from visual cues (patients who made errors on some but not all of their responses were included); and (5) premorbid fluency in English or Spanish. Exclusion criteria were (1) secondary cause of ICH (e.g., trauma, neoplasm, vascular malformation, hemorrhagic transformation of ischemic stroke), (2) ICH location in the cerebellum or brainstem, (3) ongoing seizures, (4) severe cardiorespiratory compromise, (5) premorbid aphasia, (6) premorbid deafness, (7) pregnancy, (8) imprisonment, or (9) refusal to participate in the study on the part of the patient or health care agent. All patients meeting inclusion and exclusion criteria underwent an EEG-based motor command paradigm assessment developed to detect CMD [ ] and formal aphasia testing on the same day and as soon as possible after admission to the ICU. EEG-based motor command paradigm testing was performed using a standardized approach [ , ]. deafness, (7) pregnancy, (8) imprisonment, or (9) refusal to participate in the study on the part of the patient or health care agent. All patients meeting inclusion and exclusion criteria underwent an EEG-based motor command paradigm assessment developed to detect CMD [ ] and formal aphasia testing on the same day and as soon as possible after admission to the ICU. EEG-based motor command paradigm testing was performed using a standardized approach [ , ]. Briefly, digital EEG was recorded using a standard 21-electrode montage, and commands were provided using single-use headphones (six blocks of eight commands each, duration approximately 25 min). Motor commands alternated between “keep opening and closing your right hand” and “stop opening and closing your right hand” for the right hand (as well as corresponding commands for the left hand). Digital EEG tracings was clipped (each into five 2 s long EEG segments following command presentations), and power spectral density in predefined frequency spectra (delta [1–3 Hz], theta [4–7 Hz], alpha [8–13 Hz], and beta [14–30 Hz]) were calculated for each recording electrode. EEG features were analyzed using a support vector machine learning algorithm with a linear kernel to identify systematic differences between clips following “keep …” and “stop …” commands. Performance of the support vector machine classifier was judged based on the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Significance testing involved a one-tailed permutation test (500 times randomly shuffled labels). Significance was set at area under the receiver operating characteristic curve > 0.5. Each patient only underwent one recording, so false discovery rate correction for multiple recordings was not required. All EEG analyses were performed with the use of open-source packages, including MNE-Python ( www.martinos.org/mne/stable/index.html ) and Scikitlearn ( http://scikit-learn.org/stable/index.html ). Aphasia Testing Aphasia testing was available in English and Spanish. Aphasia in English-speaking patients was diagnosed using three subtests of the Multilingual Aphasia Examination (MAE) [ , ]—auditory comprehension, visual naming, and sentence repetition—together with the Western Aphasia Battery-Revised [ ]. Aphasia in Spanish-speaking patients was diagnosed using the three MAE subtests alone (the Western Aphasia Battery-Revised is unavailable in Spanish). A team of researchers trained and supervised by a neuropsychologist (SA) administered the questionnaires at the bedside and recorded patients’ answers. The neuropsychologist reviewed the answers to determine which patients were aphasic and to classify patients by aphasia type (i.e., expressive, receptive, global, transcortical motor, transcortical sensory, transcortical mixed, conduction, or pure anomia) [ ]. Second, each case of aphasia was rated as mild, moderate, or severe with respect to each affected domain—that is, comprehension, naming, and/or repetition. Ratings were based on a percentile rank [ ] determined by comparison with a normative group of patients with aphasia described in the MAE manual [ ]. Third, to capture subtle language changes beneath the threshold of clinical aphasia, the same scale was used to determine percentile ranks (although not mild, moderate, or severe rating) for patients without aphasia and for domains in patients with aphasia that were not frankly impaired. For purposes of primary analysis, patients with aphasia were grouped into those with impairment of language comprehension (i.e., receptive aphasia, global aphasia, transcortical sensory aphasia, or transcortical mixed aphasia) and those without (i.e., all other types of aphasia). Ambiguous cases were jointly adjudicated by the neuropsychologist and principal investigator (JC). The research team, the neuropsychologist, and the principal investigator were blinded to the results of the EEG-based motor command paradigm during data collection and data preparation. The neuropsychologist was masked to all demographic, clinical, imaging, and outcome data throughout the study. Clinical and Outcome Measures Basic demographic data were obtained directly from patients and families (e.g., primary language, level of education, and handedness). Admission head computerized tomography was used to obtain characteristics of each hemorrhage (e.g., laterality, volume, intraventricular extension). Outcome prediction scores (primary ICH score [ ]; Functional Outcome in Patients with Primary ICH [FUNC] score [ ]) were based on the ICU team’s initial calculation. Additional data were prospectively obtained from chart review including likely ICH etiology per SMASH-U [ ] criteria, anxiolytic and sedative medications present during motor command paradigm testing, and attentiveness to the examiner during motor command paradigm testing. Outcomes were assessed at 3, 6, and 12 months after bleeding using the Glasgow Outcome Scale extended (GOS-E) [ ] and modified Rankin Scale (mRS) [ ]. Withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy and cause of death were recorded. Statistical Analysis Categorical variables are shown as counts (percentages), and continuous variables as means (standard deviations) or medians (interquartile ranges [IQRs]), as appropriate. Univariable associations were assessed with a Wilcoxon rank-sum test for quantitative variables or χ 2 test for qualitative variables. Variables found to be significantly associated with an outcome at the p < 0.05 level were then included in the multivariable analysis using logistic regression modeling.
