Related theory and technical foundation Theoretical foundation of multimodal computer graphics Multimodal perception technology fundamentally relies on the integration of multiple sensory channels to create comprehensive and intuitive user experiences that transcend the limitations of single-modality interfaces . The theoretical foundation encompasses the principles of cross-modal sensory processing, where visual, auditory, and haptic information streams are simultaneously captured, processed, and synthesized to generate coherent perceptual experiences. This approach leverages the natural human tendency to process information through multiple sensory pathways, thereby enhancing comprehension and engagement in digital environments . The multi-sensory information fusion mechanism addresses the critical challenge of integrating heterogeneous sensor data streams with varying reliability and temporal characteristics in elderly care environments. When visual, auditory, and haptic sensors simultaneously capture user interactions, the system must determine which sensory modality provides the most reliable information at each moment. For example, when ambient noise interferes with voice commands, the system should prioritize visual gesture recognition while reducing audio input weight. The fusion process can be mathematically represented as: where F(t) represents the fused multimodal output at time t, S_i(t) denotes the preprocessed input from the i-th sensory modality (i = 1: visual from RGB-D camera, i = 2: auditory from microphone array, i = 3: haptic from pressure sensors, i = 4: environmental context from IoT sensors), w_i(t) represents the dynamic weight assigned to each modality based on signal-to-noise ratio and historical accuracy, and n = 4 is the total number of sensory channels. The weights are normalized such that ∑w_i(t) = 1 and updated every 100ms using an adaptive Kalman filter that adjusts based on sensor confidence scores derived from variance analysis of recent measurements. This equation enables the system to automatically shift reliance from unreliable sensors (e.g., camera in low-light conditions) to more dependable modalities (e.g., haptic feedback), ensuring consistent user experience across varying environmental conditions . This mathematical framework enables adaptive weighting mechanisms that can prioritize certain sensory inputs based on environmental conditions or user preferences. Computer graphics plays a pivotal role in multimodal interaction systems by providing the visual foundation upon which other sensory modalities are anchored and synchronized. Advanced rendering techniques enable real-time generation of visually compelling content that responds dynamically to user interactions while maintaining consistency across different sensory channels . The integration of computer graphics with multimodal systems requires sophisticated coordinate transformation algorithms that ensure spatial and temporal alignment between visual elements and corresponding auditory or haptic feedback. Three-dimensional modeling and rendering technologies form the core infrastructure for creating immersive multimodal environments. Modern 3D rendering pipelines incorporate physically-based rendering (PBR) techniques that simulate realistic material properties and lighting conditions, thereby enhancing the believability of virtual environments. The rendering equation, fundamental to photorealistic image synthesis, can be expressed as: where L_o represents outgoing radiance, L_e denotes emitted radiance, f_r is the bidirectional reflectance distribution function, L_i represents incoming radiance, and Ω represents the hemisphere of directions . Virtual reality and augmented reality technologies provide the technological foundation for creating immersive multimodal experiences that can adapt to diverse user needs and environmental conditions. We formally define a resilient AI system R as a tuple R = (S, A, T, M, θ) where S represents the set of system states (normal, degraded, failed), A denotes the set of adaptive actions (resource reallocation, quality reduction, service failover), T is the state transition function under perturbations, M is the performance metric function (response time, accuracy, availability), and θ represents resilience threshold parameters. Resilience is quantified through three measurable dimensions: (1) Fault Tolerance measured as P(system operational | failure event) ≥ 0.95, indicating the probability of maintaining service during component failures; (2) Adaptive Recovery measured as Mean Time To Recovery (MTTR) ≤ 180 s, representing the average duration from failure detection to service restoration; and (3) Performance Degradation measured as M(degraded)/M(normal) ≥ 0.85, ensuring that performance during stress conditions remains within 15% of optimal levels. These thresholds were established based on elderly care application requirements where system unavailability exceeding 3 min causes user frustration and discontinuation rates above 40% (based on pilot testing with 50 users). In our experimental validation, we measure these dimensions through controlled failure injection: network latency perturbations (50ms→500ms step increases), server load stress tests (10→500 concurrent users), and component failure simulations (camera disconnection, database timeout). The resilience score R_score = 0.35·FT + 0.40·AR + 0.25·PD aggregates these dimensions with empirically determined weights reflecting relative importance for elderly user satisfaction, where FT (fault tolerance), AR (adaptive recovery), and PD (performance degradation) are normalized to [0,1] scales. This theoretical framework encompasses fault tolerance, graceful degradation, and adaptive recovery mechanisms that enable systems to continue providing essential services even when operating under suboptimal conditions. The core principle of resilience extends beyond traditional reliability metrics by incorporating the system’s ability to learn from failures and adapt its operational strategies to prevent similar disruptions in the future. Adaptive learning algorithms form the cornerstone of resilient AI systems by enabling continuous modification of computational models based on real-time feedback and changing operational conditions . These algorithms utilize online learning techniques that update model parameters incrementally as new data becomes available, allowing systems to respond dynamically to evolving user needs and environmental conditions. Meta-learning approaches further enhance adaptability by enabling systems to learn how to learn more effectively, thereby improving their capacity to adapt to novel situations with minimal additional training data. Machine learning applications in personalized service delivery leverage sophisticated pattern recognition and predictive modeling techniques to tailor system responses to individual user preferences and behavioral patterns . Collaborative filtering methods analyze user interaction histories to identify similar preference profiles and generate personalized recommendations, while content-based filtering techniques extract feature representations from service attributes to match user preferences with appropriate service options. These approaches enable the development of recommendation systems that can adapt to changing user preferences while maintaining high accuracy in personalized service delivery. The emotion recognition and evaluation models utilize multimodal data fusion techniques to assess emotional states through facial expression analysis, voice pattern recognition, and physiological signal monitoring . The emotion detection framework addresses the challenge of recognizing subtle emotional expressions in elderly populations where facial mobility decreases by approximately 30% compared to younger adults and cultural factors (Korean emotional restraint norms) influence expression intensity. Training data comprised 68,559 total images from three sources: FER2013 dataset (35,887 images, distribution: 4,593 angry, 547 disgust, 5,121 fear, 8,989 happy, 6,077 sad, 4,002 surprise, 6,198 neutral), RAF-DB dataset (29,672 real-world annotated faces), and custom elderly dataset (2,400 images collected from 5 senior centers in Busan with IRB approval, ages 65–89 years, gender-balanced, annotated by 3 expert raters achieving inter-rater reliability Cohen’s κ = 0.81). Testing employed hold-out set of 13,592 images (20% of combined data) stratified by age group, gender, and emotion category, supplemented with 15,000 synthetic images generated using StyleGAN2 for data augmentation. The neural network architecture consists of four components: (1) Visual feature extraction using ResNet-50 base model pre-trained on ImageNet (1.2 million images) and fine-tuned on elderly-specific dataset, accepting 224 × 224 RGB input and outputting 2048-dimensional feature vectors through convolutional layers (conv1: 64 filters 7 × 7 kernel stride 2, Layer1-4: [64,64,256]×3, [128,128,512]×4, [256,256,1024]×6, [512,512,2048]×3 residual blocks); (2) Facial landmark detection using Dlib 68-point detector tracking 10 eyebrow landmarks (points 17–26), 12 eye landmarks (points 36–47), and 20 mouth landmarks (points 48–67), computing 25 geometric features including mouth opening ratio=(upper_lip-lower_lip)/face_height and eye aspect ratios; (3) Audio feature extraction from 16 kHz 16-bit mono audio preprocessed with α = 0.97 pre-emphasis filter, extracting 40 Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs) using 25ms windows with 10ms hop, pitch via YIN algorithm, log energy per frame, and voicing probability via spectral flatness, aggregating into 128-dimensional audio vectors over 3-second sliding windows; (4) Multimodal fusion concatenating visual (2048-dim) + audio (128-dim) + geometric (25-dim) features into 2201-dimensional vectors, passing through fully-connected layer reducing to 1024 dimensions with ReLU activation and 50% dropout regularization, followed by batch normalization. Temporal modeling employs bidirectional LSTM processing 10-frame sequences (1-second windows at 10fps) through two LSTM layers (1024→256→256 hidden units) capturing temporal dynamics of emotional expressions, with bidirectional processing providing both past and future context totaling approximately 2.1 million trainable parameters. Classification head consists of fully-connected layer (512-dim from bidirectional LSTM → 256-dim with ReLU and 30% dropout) followed by output layer (256-dim → 7 classes with softmax activation) predicting angry, disgust, fear, happy, sad, surprise, and neutral emotions. Training procedure utilized Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with learning rate 0.0001, β_1 = 0.9, β_2 = 0.999, ε = 1e-08, weight decay 0.0001 for L2 regularization, batch size 32 limited by GPU memory, training for 150 epochs with early stopping patience = 20 epochs monitoring validation loss, gradient clipping at maximum norm 5.0, and learning rate schedule with linear warm-up from 0 to 0.0001 over first 5 epochs followed by cosine annealing to minimum 1e-07. Data augmentation included random rotation ± 15°, horizontal flip probability 0.5, color jitter (brightness ± 20%, contrast ± 20%), random crop 90–100% then resize to 224 × 224, and Gaussian noise σ = 0.01 added to 10% of samples. The therapeutic effect evaluation system implements a comprehensive assessment framework that combines quantitative metrics with qualitative indicators to measure intervention effectiveness across multiple dimensions including engagement levels, emotional state changes, cognitive performance indicators, and social interaction patterns . The evaluation metric E_effectiveness is derived from established psychometric assessment frameworks used in geriatric care: Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II) for mood assessment, Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) for cognitive function, and Lubben Social Network Scale for social engagement. The evaluation algorithm processes longitudinal data collected at weekly intervals to identify trends and patterns that indicate therapeutic progress: where E_effectiveness represents overall therapeutic effectiveness normalized to 0–5 scale (0 = no effect, 5 = maximal benefit), Δmood indicates emotional state changes measured as difference between pre-intervention and current Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15) scores normalized to [0,1] range where higher values indicate greater mood improvement, engagement_score quantifies user participation frequency and duration calculated as (actual_sessions/recommended_sessions)×(average_duration/target_duration) capped at 1.0, cognitive_improvement represents percentage change in digital cognitive assessment scores (attention, memory, executive function subtests) from baseline with 15% improvement corresponding to 1.0 value, and social_interaction measures community feature usage including forum posts, collaborative art sessions, and peer feedback frequency scaled to [0,1] where 0.5 represents baseline expectation of 2 interactions per week. Task assignment employed stratified randomization: each synthetic user randomly assigned 8 of 12 tasks with difficulty matching to cognitive ability using algorithm that assigned users with MMSE 18–20 to 6 low-difficulty and 2 medium-difficulty tasks, MMSE 21–25 to 4 low, 3 medium, and 1 high-difficulty tasks, and MMSE 26–30 to 2 low, 3 medium, and 3 high-difficulty tasks. Throughput testing employed Apache JMeter load testing tool simulating realistic usage patterns (70% read operations, 20% write operations, 10% complex queries) ramped from 10 to 500 concurrent users over 30-minute period, holding peak load for 10 min, measuring requests processed per second averaged over 5-minute stable periods. Limitations of synthetic user modeling approach This study acknowledges critical limitations inherent to synthetic data validation that constrain external validity and generalizability to real elderly populations. Synthetic models cannot fully capture the complexity of human behavior including unpredictable emotional responses, day-to-day cognitive fluctuations (good days/bad days not modeled), cultural nuances beyond parameterized variables, individual idiosyncrasies in technology interaction styles, and contextual factors such as family dynamics, living conditions, daily routine variations, health crises, medication effects, and motivation fluctuations influenced by external events. The 300 synthetic profiles, while diverse in age (65–95 years), education (elementary to university), and cognitive function (MMSE 18–30), employ averaged motor control parameters that oversimplify physical capability diversity including severe arthritis, Parkinsonian tremors, visual field defects, and assistive device usage (magnifiers, hearing aids, mobility aids) not explicitly modeled. Cognitive variability limitations include assumption of stable decline trajectories following predictable patterns whereas real elderly exhibit non-linear cognitive changes, transient delirium episodes, diurnal attention fluctuations (morning alertness peaks, sundowning effects), and fatigue accumulation varying individually. Emotional authenticity represents a fundamental limitation: computational mood models based on valence-arousal dimensions lack subjective experiential depth, cannot capture complex emotions like nostalgia or existential concerns, and simplify coping mechanisms and resilience factors that real users employ when facing technology frustrations. Cultural representation limitations include narrow focus on Korean elderly population parameters with limited generalizability to other East Asian cultures (Japanese, Chinese with different collectivism norms), Western individualistic cultures (European, North American with distinct aging perspectives), or Global South populations (different socioeconomic contexts, health literacy levels, technology access). The synthetic generation process relied on published literature ( n = 25 studies, total 8,947 participants) and government statistics that may contain sampling biases toward healthier, more educated elderly who participate in research, potentially underrepresenting frail, institutionalized, or socially isolated subgroups. Behavioral parameter independence assumption (e.g., treating cognitive function, motor control, and emotional state as separate variables) ignores known correlations: cognitive impairment often co-occurs with motor decline (correlation r = 0.42 in real populations), depression correlates with reduced technology engagement ( r =-0.38), and sensory impairments compound cognitive challenges through information processing bottlenecks. Validation efforts to address these limitations included consultation with five geriatric care specialists (mean 12.4 years clinical experience) who evaluated 50 randomly selected synthetic scenarios rating realism mean 7.8/10 (SD = 1.2), with identified gaps including inability to model complex social interactions (family conflicts, caregiver burden), unpredictable mood fluctuations (grief, joy from unexpected events), and learned helplessness behaviors (repeated failures leading to technology avoidance). Gender differences emerged with females showing 76% increase (1.9→3.3) versus males 57% increase (1.7→2.7), potentially reflecting stronger social orientation in female elderly populations (gender-by-time interaction F(1,298) = 4.21, p = 0.041). Technology experience moderated social engagement gains: high-experience users (score ≥ 7, n = 78) increased 91%, medium-experience (score 4–6, n = 147) increased 69%, and low-experience (score ≤ 3, n = 75) increased 38%, with significant interaction (F(2,297) = 8.94, p < 0.001) suggesting need for enhanced social feature onboarding for technology-naive users. Progressive improvement occurred throughout intervention: Week 4 mean = 11.2 (20% improvement), Week 8 mean = 13.1 (41% improvement), Week 12 mean = 14.7 (58% improvement), indicating continued learning without plateau. Sensitivity analyses examine result robustness under varying assumptions. Optimistic scenario assumes 30% higher savings effectiveness (healthcare utilization reductions 1.3× larger): emergency room visits decline to 0.75/year (savings $360), GP visits to 2.0/year (savings $180), medication to 40% prevalence (savings $90), and institutionalization delay affects 7% of users (savings $840), totaling $1,470 savings with net benefit $880/year (149% ROI). Break-even analysis calculates minimum healthcare utilization reduction necessary for cost-neutrality: 12% reduction across all categories maintains zero net cost, which meta-analyses suggest high likelihood of achieving given typical effect sizes (Cohen’s d = 0.4–0.8) from creative therapy interventions. Confidence in achieving at least breakeven exceeds 85% based on literature evidence, though optimistic scenario probability estimated only 35% and pessimistic scenario 15% based on expert panel assessments. Results confirmed that the proposed architecture successfully addresses key challenges in elderly care support systems while providing sustainable economic benefits through improved operational efficiency and reduced maintenance requirements. Conclusion This research successfully developed an innovative multimodal computer graphics-driven interactive art therapy platform that integrates resilient artificial intelligence adaptation mechanisms specifically designed for smart community home-based elderly care applications. The primary research achievements include the design of a four-layered hierarchical architecture that seamlessly integrates multimodal sensing technologies with adaptive learning algorithms, the implementation of personalized art therapy intervention generation systems that dynamically adjust to individual user preferences and capabilities, and the development of resilient adaptation mechanisms that maintain system performance and reliability under varying operational conditions. The platform’s application value in home-based elderly care extends beyond traditional service delivery models by providing comprehensive therapeutic interventions that address cognitive, emotional, and social dimensions of healthy aging . The integration of multimodal computer graphics with intelligent adaptation mechanisms creates opportunities for delivering personalized care services that can accommodate diverse user needs while maintaining cost-effectiveness and scalability. The social significance of this research lies in its potential to address the growing demand for innovative aging-in-place solutions that can support the increasing elderly population while reducing the burden on traditional healthcare infrastructure. Research limitations and ethical considerations This study presents several important limitations that must be acknowledged. First, the reliance on synthetic user models limits the generalizability of findings to real elderly populations, as synthetic models may not fully capture the complexity of human behavior, cultural preferences, and individual differences in technology adoption patterns. Our analysis indicates that users with elementary education levels required 2.3 times longer adaptation periods compared to those with higher education. Future research directions and clinical implementation Future development priorities include conducting randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 500 + elderly participants across multiple sites to validate therapeutic efficacy. The proposed RCT design will employ a waitlist control group with primary outcomes measured using standardized cognitive assessments (MoCA, MMSE) and secondary outcomes including quality of life indicators (SF-36) and caregiver burden scales. Sample size calculations indicate 80% power to detect medium effect sizes (d = 0.5) with α = 0.05. Large-scale deployment strategy Implementation will follow a phased approach beginning with pilot studies in 5 smart communities, expanding to 50 sites within 24 months. Each deployment phase will include comprehensive staff training programs, technical support infrastructure, and outcome monitoring protocols. Cost-effectiveness analyses will compare intervention costs ($180/user/month) against traditional care models, with projected healthcare savings of 23% based on reduced emergency interventions and delayed institutionalization. Cross-cultural adaptation studies Future research will examine cultural sensitivity across diverse populations, particularly focusing on Asian, European, and North American elderly communities. Cultural adaptation protocols will address language preferences, artistic traditions, social interaction norms, and family involvement patterns that influence therapeutic engagement and outcomes. The current 12-week intervention period, while sufficient for detecting short-term cognitive and emotional improvements (mean E_effectiveness increased from 1.8 ± 0.6 to 3.7 ± 0.8, Cohen’s d = 2.67), is inadequate for assessing sustained therapeutic benefits, potential disease-modifying effects, or long-term adherence patterns critical for chronic elderly care applications. Future research will implement extended longitudinal tracking following a 24-month protocol with assessment timepoints at baseline, 3 months, 6 months, 12 months, 18 months, and 24 months post-intervention initiation. Primary outcome will measure cognitive trajectory analyzing rate of decline via linear mixed-effects models comparing intervention group slope (−0.3 MMSE points/year projected based on meta-analytic evidence from creative therapy studies) against natural aging decline (−1.2 points/year for mild cognitive impairment populations), hypothesizing 75% slowing of decline rate. Secondary outcomes include functional independence measured by Activities of Daily Living (ADL) and Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADL) scales assessing practical life skills maintenance, healthcare utilization tracking emergency room visits, general practitioner consultations, and medication usage from National Health Insurance Service claims data, and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) calculation incorporating EQ-5D-5 L health utility scores for cost-effectiveness analysis. Exploratory neuroimaging substudy ( n = 50 volunteer subset) will employ structural MRI at baseline and 24-month timepoints measuring hippocampal volume, cortical thickness in frontal and parietal regions, and white matter integrity via diffusion tensor imaging, testing hypothesis that sustained cognitive engagement associates with preserved brain structure (expected effect size d = 0.35 based on exercise intervention literature). Anticipated temporal patterns based on creative therapy meta-analyses (Fancourt & Steptoe, 2019; Dunphy et al., 2019) include short-term gains (0–6 months) primarily in mood improvements and engagement metrics with rapid initial effect sizes (d = 0.6–0.9) plateauing around 4-month mark, medium-term phase (6–12 months) showing cognitive stabilization where intervention group maintains baseline cognitive performance while control group declines (difference-in-difference d = 0.4), and long-term phase (12–24 months) revealing potential slowing of cognitive decline rate with sustained engagement predicting better outcomes (correlation r = 0.35 between cumulative usage hours and cognitive trajectory slope). Statistical modeling will employ piecewise linear mixed-effects models allowing different slopes for each temporal phase, accounting for attrition using multiple imputation (m = 20 imputed datasets) under missing-at-random assumption justified by auxiliary variable inclusion (baseline characteristics, early engagement patterns), and conducting both intention-to-treat analysis (primary, including all randomized participants) and per-protocol analysis (secondary, restricted to ≥ 70% session attendance) as sensitivity check. Anticipated attrition of 30% by 24-month follow-up (common in elderly longitudinal studies) necessitates initial recruitment of 643 participants to maintain 80% power for detecting primary outcome difference. Participant advisory board comprising 8 elderly users will convene quarterly providing input on retention strategies, acceptable assessment burden, and protocol modifications based on participant feedback. Sensitivity analyses will vary key parameters (± 30% intervention costs, ± 20% healthcare savings, discount rate 0–5% for future costs) examining result robustness. This comprehensive long-term evaluation framework will provide definitive evidence regarding sustained therapeutic value, identifying critical engagement thresholds (minimum hours/week), optimal intervention intensity (session frequency and duration), and cost-effectiveness necessary for policy recommendations and widespread implementation in aging-in-place programs. For practical implementation, this research recommends establishing pilot deployment programs in representative smart community environments, developing standardized evaluation frameworks for therapeutic effectiveness assessment, and creating comprehensive training programs for caregivers and community support staff. The platform’s modular architecture facilitates gradual implementation and customization according to specific community requirements and resource constraints. Cross-cultural adaptability research agenda The current validation focuses exclusively on Korean elderly population with cultural context shaped by Confucian values emphasizing respect for authority and family-centric care, technology adoption rates of 45% smartphone ownership in 65 + age group (Korea Internet & Security Agency 2024 data), and art preferences favoring traditional ink painting (sumi-e), calligraphy (seoye), and folk music (gugak using traditional instruments like gayageum and daegeum). This cultural specificity limits generalizability necessitating systematic cross-cultural validation addressing international deployment. Planned cross-cultural studies employ three-phase approach spanning 2025–2028 examining effectiveness across diverse cultural contexts. Phase 1 East Asian Comparison (2025–2026, 18 months) will recruit n = 150 participants per country from South Korea, Japan, and China (total n = 450, ages 65–85, balanced gender, stratified by education level) examining cultural variations within collectivist East Asian context. Cultural adaptations include art style localization (Japanese sumi-e using minimalist brushwork, Chinese guohua emphasizing landscape painting, Korean minhwa featuring folk art motifs), traditional music integration (Japanese koto 13-string zither, Chinese guzheng 21-string zither, Korean gayageum 12-string zither with culturally-appropriate repertoires), color symbolism adjustments (red signifying luck in Chinese context requires prominent use vs. Japanese contexts favoring subdued earth tones, white representing mourning in some Southeast Asian cultures necessitates careful usage), and interface language requiring full localization beyond direct translation capturing idiomatic expressions (e.g., Korean “fighting” encouragement translates poorly, requiring culturally-appropriate equivalents like Japanese “ganbatte” or Chinese “jiayou”). Primary outcome measures MoCA cognitive score changes, GDS depression score changes, and user satisfaction (SUS scores), hypothesizing equivalent therapeutic effectiveness across East Asian cultures (non-inferiority margin 15% difference in primary outcomes) given shared collectivist values, with expected 12-month completion date December 2026. Phase 2 Western Cultural Contexts (2026–2027, 18 months) will recruit n = 100 participants per country from United States, United Kingdom, and Germany (total n = 300) examining individualistic Western cultures with anticipated challenges: individualism versus collectivism requiring adjustment of social features from group-focused collaborative activities (emphasis in East Asian version) toward individual achievement tracking and personal customization options, privacy expectations particularly stringent in Germany requiring enhanced data protection transparency (GDPR compliance with explicit consent for each data type, right to object to processing) and anticipated higher opt-out rates (projected 15% vs. 3% in Korean sample), artistic traditions requiring content expansion to include Impressionist painting techniques, realistic rendering styles, and abstract art movements unfamiliar to East Asian participants, and generally higher technological literacy (65% tablet ownership vs. 45% in Korea) enabling higher baseline difficulty settings. Cultural competence review panels ( n = 5 experts per country: geriatricians, cultural anthropologists, art therapists) will evaluate localized versions for cultural appropriateness, with iterative refinement based on pilot testing ( n = 20 per country, 4-week pilots) before full deployment, expected completion September 2027. Phase 3 Diverse Global South Contexts (2027–2028, 18 months) will recruit n = 75 participants per country from India, Brazil, and Nigeria (total n = 225) ensuring representation from Global South populations with unique considerations: multilingual support adding Hindi, Portuguese, Yoruba, and Igbo language interfaces alongside English (total 8 languages supported vs. initial Korean-only), socioeconomic factors necessitating lower-cost hardware options (evaluating $150 Android tablets vs. $450 iPad requiring software optimization for lower-spec devices with 2GB RAM vs. 8GB standard), community structures incorporating extended family involvement protocols where grandchildren often serve as technology mediators (designing family account features enabling shared progress tracking, remote assistance from family members via smartphone apps),

will recruit n = 75 participants per country from India, Brazil, and Nigeria (total n = 225) ensuring representation from Global South populations with unique considerations: multilingual support adding Hindi, Portuguese, Yoruba, and Igbo language interfaces alongside English (total 8 languages supported vs. initial Korean-only), socioeconomic factors necessitating lower-cost hardware options (evaluating $150 Android tablets vs. $450 iPad requiring software optimization for lower-spec devices with 2GB RAM vs. 8GB standard), community structures incorporating extended family involvement protocols where grandchildren often serve as technology mediators (designing family account features enabling shared progress tracking, remote assistance from family members via smartphone apps), and varying health literacy requiring simplified health information presentation using more illustrations and less text (target 6th-grade reading level vs. 8th-grade for Western contexts). Anticipated challenges include limited reliable electricity (implementing offline mode with local data storage, battery optimization achieving 6-hour runtime) and intermittent internet connectivity (designing content delivery network edge caching, background synchronization when connectivity available). Expected completion March 2028 with comparative effectiveness analysis across all 9 countries (total n = 975 participants, mean age 74 years, 60% female target). Cultural Adaptation Framework employs four-step systematic methodology: (1) Content localization partnering with local artists (commission 50 culturally-appropriate art assets per country at $50/asset budget, 250 traditional music compositions at $200/composition totaling $50,000 per country localization cost), color palette adjustments based on cultural color associations (e.g., purple signifying royalty in Western contexts vs. death in some Asian contexts), and narrative elements reflecting local storytelling traditions (Indian epics, Brazilian carnival themes, Nigerian proverbs); (2) Interaction paradigm adaptation distinguishing high-context cultures (East Asia) requiring implicit communication with non-verbal cues and subtle interface feedback versus low-context cultures (USA, Germany) needing explicit instructions, direct feedback, and detailed tooltips, with uncertainty avoidance dimension addressed by providing more structured guidance for high-uncertainty-avoidance cultures (Japan, Germany scoring 92 and 65 respectively on Hofstede’s uncertainty avoidance index) versus flexible exploratory interfaces for low-uncertainty-avoidance cultures (USA scoring 46); (3) Social feature customization emphasizing group activities, shared family galleries, and community competitions for collectivist cultures versus personal achievement badges, individual customization, and privacy controls for individualistic cultures; (4) Validation strategy employing cultural competence review by 5-person local expert panels per country, pilot testing with 20 participants per cultural context, ethnographic home observation visits (10 per country, 2-hour visits documenting home environment, family dynamics, technology usage patterns), iterative design-test-revise cycles (3 rounds at 4-week intervals incorporating user feedback from each round), and quantitative effectiveness comparison using mixed-effects models with Country as fixed effect examining effect size heterogeneity (hypothesis: therapeutic effectiveness varies 15–25% across cultures with core mechanisms universal but magnitude culture-dependent). Expected outcomes include cultural adaptation playbook (150-page manual with implementation guidelines for new country deployments covering translation protocols, cultural sensitivity checklists, partnership development with local organizations, regulatory compliance pathways, and cost estimation tools), modular design architecture implementing plug-in content modules (art assets, music libraries, language packs, cultural narratives as independently loadable components averaging 500 MB per module enabling customization without core system redesign), effectiveness comparison revealing anticipated 15–25% variance in therapeutic outcomes across cultures (e.g., collectivist cultures may show 20% higher social engagement benefits while individualistic cultures demonstrate 15% greater self-efficacy gains), and identification of universal design principles working across all cultures (hypothesized core features: adaptive difficulty, multimodal interaction, positive reinforcement, progress visualization, personalization based on 12-culture pilot data). Budget requirements estimate $2.8 million total across three phases ($400K per country for recruitment, assessment, localization, data management, analysis) with funding applications submitted to National Institutes of Health (NIH) International Research Grant Program (R01 mechanism, $500K/year for 5 years) and European Union Horizon Europe funding program (€3.5 M requested, 50% co-funding rate yielding €1.75 M, decision expected Q2 2025). This comprehensive cross-cultural research program will establish platform’s global applicability, identify culture-specific optimization strategies, and generate evidence for international dissemination supporting World Health Organization’s Decade of Healthy Ageing (2021–2030) initiative promoting accessible aging-in-place technologies worldwide.

documents.title: Practice guideline pharmacologic treatment of chorea in Huntington disease

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Huntington disease (HD) is the most frequent neurodegenerative chorea in adults, caused by an autosomal dominant inherited CAG trinucleotide expansion in the gene HTT (Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man: 613004) that encodes for the huntingtin protein on chromosome 4. HD is characterized by striatal degeneration that leads to thalamocortical hyperactivation due to an imbalance in the dopaminergic striatal pathway [ ]. Additionally, in HD early hypothalamic degeneration occurs, as shown by postmortem studies [ , , ] and neuroimaging studies through brain magnetic resonance imaging, which revealed gray matter density loss in the hypothalamus occurring up to 1 decade before clinical diagnosis [ , ]. Through positron emission tomography studies, using a D2–D3 receptor‐specific tracer and a marker of microglial activation, Politis et al. [ ] demonstrated the downregulation of D2 and/or D3 receptors in the hypothalamus. These findings partly explain the dysautonomic symptoms (e.g., thermoregulatory defect) along with dysregulation of wake–sleep cycle, increased thirst and hunger, progressive weight loss, and endocrine dysfunction [ , , ]. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is characterized by central hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, autonomic nervous system instability, and changes in mental status [ ]. The most used diagnostic criteria for NMS are outlined in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DMS‐5; Table ). Disrupted dopamine transmission is pivotal in the pathogenesis of NMS. Dopamine depletion in the tuberoinfundibular pathway causes body temperature dysregulation, and its effect on the nigrostriatal system results in rigidity; alterations in the mesocortical circuit impact mental status. The circuits are not always involved at the same degree, and NMS may have atypical presentations (more frequently caused by second‐generation antipsychotics) without hyperthermia or rigidity [ ]. Dopamine receptor blocking agents (DRBAs) and tetrabenazine (TBZ) are commonly used in treating hyperkinetic movement disorders, including HD [ , ]. NMS is a rare side effect of DRBAs, but other compounds affecting dopaminergic transmission such as TBZ have also been linked to this condition [ , , ]. It remains uncertain whether the risk of developing NMS in patients with HD is higher compared to the general population [ ]. The aim of this study was to explore the prevalence of NMS in a large cohort of HD patients and describe its clinical characteristics and associated risk factors in cases reported in the literature and in our case report. CASE REPORT We present the case of a 45‐year‐old woman (Table ), who developed the first symptoms of HD by the age of 29 years. The symptom onset consisted of gait disturbances and frequent falls. In the course of the disease, she presented rigidity, bradykinesia, involuntary movements, and psychiatric disturbances (bipolar disorder). She progressively developed severe dystonia, insomnia, cognitive decline, and dysphagia. The clinical diagnosis of HD, Westphal variant, was confirmed genetically at the age of 41 years. She was initially treated with quetiapine 25 mg once daily (qd). From 2022, she was treated with valproic acid 200 mg twice daily (bid), olanzapine 5 mg bid, quetiapine 50 mg qd, and zolpidem 10 mg qd. At home, the patient was not autonomous in daily activities; she was unable to walk, her movements were limited to a few steps from the bed to the chair with assistance, and her speech was unintelligible. She suffered from insomnia and agitation. After an occasional administration of five drops of haloperidol 2 mg/mL for psychomotor agitation, she developed fever up to 40°C, severe muscle stiffness, profuse diaphoresis, tachypnea (up to 35 breaths per minute), tachycardia (100 beats per minute), and stupor within a few hours. After initial stabilization, alternative causes of acute change in mental status with generalized hypertonia and hyperthermia were considered. Chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound imaging showed no signs of infection. Blood, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid cultures were normal. Brain computed tomography was unremarkable. Thus, infections and parenchymal brain abnormalities were ruled out. Laboratory tests showed elevated creatine phosphokinase (CPK; up to 11,000 IU/L), lactate dehydrogenase (821 IU/L), alanine aminotransferase (224 IU/L), and aspartate aminotransferase (133 IU/L). It is relevant to note that, in the week prior to the hospitalization, the patient was treated with antibiotics for influenzalike symptoms and diarrhea; the infectious state, and dehydration, due to dysphagia and diarrhea, were probably the precipitating factors of NMS. Neuroleptic drugs were discontinued and intravenous (IV) diazepam (10 mg three times daily), IV dantrolene sodium (150 mg/day for 10 days), and high‐volume IV fluids were administered. Fever regressed and muscle rigidity improved in 1 week. In 3 weeks, CPK levels dropped to the normal value. During hospitalization, the patient manifested frequent episodes of psychomotor agitation and insomnia, managed by gradual introduction of clonazepam, zopiclone, phenobarbital, and quetiapine (the latter reintroduced after 15 days since discontinuation). Hospitalization lasted approximately 1 month, during which she underwent surgery for percutaneous gastrostomy due to dysphagia and the resulting

At discharge, the patient was transferred to a nursing home. MATERIALS AND METHODS This paper encompasses a narrative review of the literature and the retrospective study of the data from the fifth dataset of the Enroll‐HD study (PDS5). We described the clinical presentation and potential risk factors of NMS in HD patients through a case report and through a narrative review of the literature (Table ). For the publication of the clinical case, we received approval from the caregiver. Furthermore, we explored the prevalence of NMS in a large cohort of HD patients reported in the Enroll‐HD registry. The literature review was conducted by two authors (A.F. and B.R.), under supervision of a senior neurologist (M.P.). The search was performed on PubMed and Embase using the keywords “Huntington's disease,” “neuroleptic malignant syndrome,” “malignant hyperthermia/hyperpyrexia,” and “tetrabenazine AND neuroleptic malignant syndrome.” We included patients who satisfied the following criteria: (i) genetically confirmed diagnosis of HD; (ii) ongoing DRBA and/or TBZ treatment at the time of NMS onset; (iii) presented with hyperthermia and/or rigidity, which represent the cardinal features of NMS according to DMS‐5, thus including both typical and atypical forms. We reviewed six case reports and one case series [ , , , , , , ], identifying 10 patients for whom we collected demographic and clinical data. We investigated NMS prevalence in HD patients through the collection of data generously provided by the participants in the Enroll‐HD study ( https://www.enroll‐hd.org ), version PDS5 (periodic dataset 5). Enroll‐HD is a global, multicenter clinical research platform funded by the CHDI Foundation, where data are collected annually from all research participants as part of a longitudinal observational study, including manifest and premanifest HD gene carriers, genetically negative subjects, and family controls. Data are monitored for quality and accuracy using a risk‐based monitoring approach. This study did not require institutional review board (IRB) approval because it utilized precollected, deidentified data from the Enroll‐HD database. Each study site that collected data received its own approval for the study from the local or national coordinator site IRB, and all participants, or their authorized representatives in the case of inability, gave their written informed consent for participation in the study and the distribution of deidentified data for research purposes. Dataset access can be requested by qualified researchers at https://enroll‐hd.org/for‐researchers . Participants enrolled into the study attend a yearly assessment of motor, cognitive, functional, and psychiatric conditions, in addition to comorbidity and pharmacological/nonpharmacological treatment updates. Reportable events are also registered, but only suicide attempts, completed suicide, mental health events requiring hospitalization, and death are systematically captured in Enroll‐HD [ ]. The data contained in Enroll‐HD PDS5 was extracted from the Enroll‐HD electronic data capture database on 31 October 2020. It contains data on 21,116 Enroll‐HD participants from 55,975 Enroll‐HD visits (baseline and follow‐up from July 2012 to October 2020). Most participants in Enroll‐HD PDS5 are diagnosed with HD (10,947 at baseline and 11,569 at last follow‐up), but others are subjects carrying HD gene expansion not yet HD symptomatic. The database also includes HD‐negative family members and family members not HD related who did not contribute to our analyses. Of these 11,569 HD symptomatic patients, we selected patients undergoing DRBA (first/second generations of antipsychotic drugs) and/or TBZ treatment. A flowchart illustrating the selection of patients from the Enroll‐HD PDS5 dataset is shown in Figure . To identify NMS cases in this cohort, we used the keywords "neuroleptic malignant syndrome," "NMS," "rigidity," "hyperthermia," and "fever" as filters, to include both typical and atypical forms of NMS. The keywords were searched both in the “comorbidity” section and in the “events” section. The first reports patient comorbidities, whereas the latter reports reasons for hospitalization, which mainly include psychiatric causes, suicide, suicide attempts, or other undefined causes. Among the cases of fever, we only included cases of unspecified fever, excluding all infectious, rheumatic, or other causes of fever. RESULTS From the analysis of Enroll‐HD PDS5 data, we identified 5108 of 11,569 HD patients who were undergoing DRBA and/or TBZ treatment. Using the keywords "neuroleptic malignant syndrome," "NMS," "rigidity," and "hyperthermia," we found only one correspondence in the “comorbidity” section, which referred to an episode of NMS occurring before Enroll‐HD PDS5

the “events” section. The first reports patient comorbidities, whereas the latter reports reasons for hospitalization, which mainly include psychiatric causes, suicide, suicide attempts, or other undefined causes. Among the cases of fever, we only included cases of unspecified fever, excluding all infectious, rheumatic, or other causes of fever. RESULTS From the analysis of Enroll‐HD PDS5 data, we identified 5108 of 11,569 HD patients who were undergoing DRBA and/or TBZ treatment. Using the keywords "neuroleptic malignant syndrome," "NMS," "rigidity," and "hyperthermia," we found only one correspondence in the “comorbidity” section, which referred to an episode of NMS occurring before Enroll‐HD PDS5 registration; no keywords were identified in the “events” section. The patient in question was a Caucasian man of 46 years, with a psychiatric onset of disease at age 28 years, who developed NMS while undergoing treatment with clozapine 300 mg qd and valproate 1500 mg qd. The time interval between the onset of NMS and the diagnosis of HD has not been reported. Furthermore, we found five cases of unspecified fever in the “comorbidity” section; all patients were undergoing polytherapy with drugs that included tetrabenazine, DRBA, and others (olanzapine, haloperidol, tiapride, quetiapine). DISCUSSION The loss of dopamine D2 and D3 receptors in the basal ganglia and in the hypothalamus [ ] may expose HD patients undergoing treatment with DRBA or/and TBZ to an increased risk of developing NMS. However, according to the available data, it is unclear whether the prevalence of this condition is higher in these individuals compared to the general population [ , ]. In the Enroll‐HD dataset, only one of 5108 HD patients treated with DRBAs and/or TBZ was diagnosed with NMS, while undergoing treatment with clozapine. In this database, all psychiatric events that lead to hospitalization are systematically collected (suicide attempts, suicide, mental health events including depression, psychotic disorders, aggression). Despite the frequent use of antipsychotics and TBZ to treat both motor and psychotic symptoms, the adverse events associated with these therapies, including NMS, are not systematically reported. Furthermore, it is important to note that some patients, mostly those treated with second‐generation neuroleptic agents and/or TBZ, may present an atypical form of NMS (i.e., hyperthermia without rigidity) [ , , , ], overlooked due to the incomplete manifestation of symptoms. For instance, five HD patients treated with DRBAs and/or TBZ reported unspecified fever, raising the possibility of an atypical form of NMS. Another potential reason for a missed diagnosis is that hyperkinetic movements such as chorea, dystonia, myoclonus, or a pre‐existing rigidity may mask tardive motor side effects. Therefore, systematically recording adverse events related to neuroleptic treatment would help avoid underestimation and underdiagnosis of this dangerous condition. Unexplained fevers should be thoroughly investigated and categorized to ensure they are not a result of the medications used. For instance, in the Enroll‐HD PDS5 dataset, we found the term “neuroleptic malignant syndrome” in the “comorbidity” section, reported as an episode that occurred before dataset registration and not in the “events” section, which included reasons for hospitalization. The main reported reasons for hospitalization include psychiatric causes, suicide, or suicide attempts but other events are not systematically described, including NMS, which is a rare but potential cause of hospitalization. This can partly explain the very low rate of NMS diagnosis in the dataset. In the general population, the main risk factors that lead to NMS are both clinical and environmental, such as physical restraint, dehydration, high temperature, iron deficiency, and the type and management of pharmacological treatment [ ]. Considering the patient from our case report and the data obtained through the literature review, we identified 11 cases of NMS in HD patients (mean age at HD onset = 33 years), three with the Westphal variant (Table ). On average, they had a long clinical history and an advanced stage of HD at the onset of NMS (mean NMS onset time after HD diagnosis = 12.8 years); almost all patients (9/11) were either bedridden, dysphagic, or dehydrated, showed signs of akinetic rigidity, were undergoing polytherapy, or showed a combination of these conditions. The remaining two presented only mild HD signs; however, one of the patients had a long clinical history of HD and oncologic comorbidity [ ]. The clinical characteristics described in this cohort are all known risk factors of NMS; however, compared to the general population, multiple risk factors are often present in late stage HD patients. Antipsychotics block D2 dopamine receptors with different affinity and potency [ ]. There is no clear epidemiological data showing that atypical antipsychotic drugs have a lower risk of inducing NMS [ , ]. Furthermore, even if higher doses are correlated with increased risk of NMS, it can occur even with low doses, indicating that possibly the risk is related more to individual susceptibility than to DRBA dosage [ , ]. The development

described in this cohort are all known risk factors of NMS; however, compared to the general population, multiple risk factors are often present in late stage HD patients. Antipsychotics block D2 dopamine receptors with different affinity and potency [ ]. There is no clear epidemiological data showing that atypical antipsychotic drugs have a lower risk of inducing NMS [ , ]. Furthermore, even if higher doses are correlated with increased risk of NMS, it can occur even with low doses, indicating that possibly the risk is related more to individual susceptibility than to DRBA dosage [ , ]. The development of NMS is also time‐independent, as it can develop immediately after the administration of the drug or after many months at the same dosage. Based on the data gathered from the literature review and our case report, only three patients developed NMS within hours or days after drug treatment modification, whereas the majority of patients did after at least 2 weeks and up to months after. This can hinder clinicians from identifying the causal link between the treatment switch and the first signs of NMS. TBZ has weak affinity toward D2 receptors, selectively depletes VMAT2, with higher affinity for dopaminergic vesicles, and is approved for the treatment of choreic dyskinesias in HD [ ]. Although TBZ has a different mechanism of action and has fewer side effects than DRBAs, cases of tardive syndromes and NMS under TBZ treatment have been described [ ]. In patients described in literature, five developed NMS associated with TBZ, either during long‐term treatment and after dosage modification or after introduction of TBZ. Two of five developed atypical NMS, without rigidity. As highlighted by our case and the literature review, all but the aforementioned patient manifested NMS during drug therapy modification, especially change of drugs, or even slight dose increases of a drug already in use. Moreover, four of 11 patients were under polytherapy. These observations confirm that treatment manipulation is one of the main pharmacological triggers of NMS, in addition to polytherapy, particularly when combining antipsychotic agents, tetrabenazine, antiseizure medication, mood stabilizers, and/or other antidepressants [ ]. Atypical NMS forms must be taken into consideration, as they can manifest with only one of the two core symptoms; this was the case in three patients who manifested hyperthermia without rigidity. Rigidity, isolated hyperthermia, altered mental status, mutism, catatonia, and dysautonomia are all part of a wide range of clinical manifestations with which NMS can manifest itself [ ]. That these symptoms may occur individually makes their detection more challenging. In patients with a long history of HD, there is progressive dysregulation of dopaminergic pathways and concurrent degeneration of the hypothalamus, a critical structure for autonomic functions such as thermoregulation, thirst, hunger, and circadian rhythm regulation, significantly increasing their risk of developing NMS [ , , , , , , , , ]. These pathophysiological changes not only contribute to an increased susceptibility to clinical risk factors such as immobility, rigidity, dehydration, and weight loss, but also make them more vulnerable to dopaminergic agents due to the underlying degeneration. Consequently, therapeutic changes must be cautious and gradual, and made under close monitoring, especially in patients with a long clinical history. Polypharmacy, or the use of multiple medications, should be minimized when possible, and potential drug interactions should be carefully evaluated. Addressing physical stressors such as dehydration and malnutrition is essential; ensuring patients maintain adequate hydration and receive proper nutrition can significantly reduce the risk. Regular checkups and a multidisciplinary approach can help mitigate these risk factors effectively. The main limitation of this study is the relative scarcity of the information obtained, which does not allow generalizability of the results. Probably this scarcity of reported information is partly explained by the absence of well‐defined criteria for NMS spectrum and thus the clinical challenge in recognizing it, and partly because these events are not carefully transcribed in the Enroll‐HD register. Consequently, this leaves little space for the analysis of the characteristics of NMS in HD. Given the potential danger of this condition for patients, larger studies are necessary to gain a better understanding of the prevalence and risk factors of NMS in HD patients. CONCLUSIONS HD patients have increased risk of developing NMS due to progressive dysregulation of dopaminergic pathways and hypothalamic degeneration. The prevalence of NMS in this population is unknown, mostly due to underdiagnoses and underreporting of atypical presentations, and partly to the masking effects of HD symptoms. Systematic recording of adverse events and thorough investigation of unexplained fevers are essential to increase sensitivity to this condition. Finally, the data highlight the importance of careful review and management of medications throughout the disease course, avoiding abrupt changes, and addressing clinical risk factors such as dehydration and malnutrition to reduce the risk of NMS in HD patients. Ellis University of Western Ontario, London, Canada Introduction: A hallmark of sepsis is early onset microvascular dysfunction. However, the mechanism responsible for maldistribution of capillary blood flow is not understood. Evidence suggests red blood cells (RBC) can sense local oxygen (O2) conditions and signal the vasculature, via adenosine triphosphate (ATP), to increase capillary flow. We hypothesized that sepsis impaired microvascular autoregulation over the entire capillary network, within a capillary and within the RBC. Study objectives were to: 1) measure capillary response time within hypoxic capillaries (capillaries with RBC hemoglobin oxygen saturation (SO2) < 20 %), 2) test the null hypothesis that sepsis had no effect on RBC O2-dependent ATP efflux and 3) develop a pathophysiological model. Methods: Hypotensive sepsis was studied in male Sprague-Dawley rats using cecal ligation and perforation, with a 6-hour end point. Rat hindlimb skeletal muscle microcirculation was imaged using a dual wavelength spectrophotometric intravital microscopy system, and capillary RBC supply rate (SR = RBC/s), RBC SO2 and oxygen supply rate (qO2 = pLO2/s) were quantified. Arterial NOx (nitrite + nitrate) and RBC O2-dependent ATP efflux were measured using a nitric oxide (NO) analyzer and gas exchanger, respectively. Results: Compared to control, sepsis increased capillary stopped flow and plasma lactate (p < 0.05). Increased plasma NOx (p < 0.001) was related to increased capillary RBC SR (p = 0.027). Analysis of 30-second capillary SR-SO2-qO2 profiles, revealed a shift towards decreased (p < 0.05) oxygen supply rates in some capillaries. Moreover, capillary response time within hypoxic capillaries (time to restore capillary RBC SO2 > 20 %) increased 3-4 fold (p < 0.05). And, consistent with impaired microvascular autoregulation, the RBC’s response to a hypoxic environment, measured as RBC O2-dependent ATP efflux, decreased by 62.5 % (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Sepsis impaired microvascular autoregulation at the capillary and erythrocyte level. Impaired autoregulation was manifested by increased capillary stopped-flow, increased capillary response time within hypoxic capillaries, decreased capillary oxygen supply rate and decreased RBC O2-dependent ATP efflux. This loss of local microvascular control was partially off-set by increased capillary RBC supply rate, which correlated with increased plasma NOx. Methods: We studied 137 Spanish patients who developed flu (80.3 % by H1N1pdm virus). Results: Ninety-three patients were hospitalized and 49 required admission to intensive care unit. Sixty-four patients developed viral pneumonia and 26 acute respiratory distress syndrome. However no association of IgG2m genotypes and severity of flu was observed. Conclusions: In our study we have not been able to replicate previously reported observations. Ergin Ozcan<sup>1</sup>, E. Senturk<sup>1</sup>, C. Ugur Yilmaz<sup>2</sup>, N. Orhan<sup>3</sup>, N. Arican<sup>4</sup>, M. Kaya<sup>2</sup>, M. Kucukerden<sup>3</sup>, M. Giris<sup>3</sup>, U. Akcan<sup>3</sup>, S. Bilgic Gazioglu<sup>5</sup>, E. Tuzun<sup>3</sup> <sup>1</sup>Istanbul University; Medical Faculty of Istanbul, Anesthesiology and Intensive Care, Istanbul, Turkey; <sup>2</sup>Istanbul University; Medical Faculty of Istanbul, Physiology, Istanbul, Turkey; <sup>3</sup>Istanbul University; Institute of Experimental Medicine, Neuroscience, Istanbul, Turkey; <sup>4</sup>Istanbul University; Medical Faculty of Istanbul, Forensic Medicine, Istanbul, Turkey; <sup>5</sup>Istanbul University; Institute of Experimental Medicine, Immunology, Istanbul, Turkey Introduction: Intravenous(IV) immunoglobulin(Ig) treatment is known to alleviate behavioral deficits in the experimentally induced model of sepsis. To delineate the mechanisms by which IVIg treatment prevents neuronal dysfunction, an array of immunological and apoptosis markers was investigated. Methods: Sepsis was induced by cecal ligation perforation(CLP) in rats. The animals were divided into five groups; sham, control, CLP + saline, CLP + immunoglobulin G IgG(250 mg/kg,iv), and CLP + immunoglobulins enriched with immunoglobulin M- IgGAM(250 mg/kg,iv). Blood and brain samples were taken in two sets of experiments after CLP to see the early(24 hrs) and late(10 days) effects of treatment. Total complement activity, complement 3(C3) and soluble complement C5b-9 levels were measured in sera of rats using ELISA-based methods. Cerebral complement content was analyzed by Western Blot. Immune cell infiltration and gliosis were examined by immunohistochemistry using cluster of differentiation 3, CD4, CD8, CD11b, CD19 and glial fibrillary acidic protein antibodies. Apoptotic neuronal death was investigated by TUNEL staining and Western Blot-based semi-quantitative evaluation of brain homogenates by bax and bcl-2 antibodies. Results: IV IgG and IgGAM administration significantly reduced systemic complement activity but increased serum C3 and soluble C5b-9 levels. Likewise, Western Blot data showed slightly increased C5b-9 expression and significantly reduced C1q expression in brain samples of IgGAM-treated but not IgG-treated septic rats especially in the first day of administration. No cerebral cellular infiltrates were observed in treated and non-treated septic rats. By contrast, IV IgG and IgGAM treatment induced considerable amelioration in glial cell proliferation which was increased in non-treated rats. IgG and IgGAM treated rats exhibited significantly reduced numbers of apoptotic neurons and cerebral expression levels of bax and bcl-2 as compared to non-treated rats. Conclusions: We suggest that IV IgG and IgGAM administration ameliorates neuronal dysfunction and behavioral deficits by reducing apoptotic cell death and glial cell proliferation. IgGAM treatment might be suppressing classical complement pathway by reducing C1q expression. Douvdevani<sup>2</sup> <sup>1</sup>Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Beer-Sheva, Israel; <sup>2</sup>Soroka Medical Center, Beer-Sheva, Israel Introduction: Most patients survive the initial hyper-inflammatory phase of severe sepsis and reach an intensive care unit with immunosuppression. Adenosine, a potent modulator of in fl;ammation and immunity is strongly elevated in blood of septic patients. We have previously shown that adenosine A1 receptor (A1R, Gi receptor) dominates the pro-inflammatory phase of bacterial peritonitis and that activation of this receptor by a specific agonist induces A2AR (Gs) expression and dominance during the resolution phase of inflammation. Methods: Polymicrobial severe sepsis was induced in C57BL/6 mice by cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) with an 18G needle. Blood and bone marrow (BM) cell counts, as well as flow cytometry were performed at 24 h post sepsis induction. Results: CLP-treated mice exhibited significantly lower number of WBC compared to sham controls (9.15 ± 2.65 vs. 3.21 ± 1.58 cells x10^3/μl). Similarly, desensitization of A1R by agonist (CCPA) or elimination of A1R with A1R antagonist (DCPCX) were associated with leukopenia. Takegawa<sup>1</sup>, H. Yoshida<sup>1</sup>, T. Hirose<sup>1</sup>, N. Yamamoto<sup>1</sup>, H. Hagiya<sup>1</sup>, M. Ojima<sup>1</sup>, Y. Akeda<sup>1</sup>, O. Tasaki<sup>2</sup>, K. Tomono<sup>1</sup>, T. Shimazu<sup>1</sup> <sup>1</sup>Osaka University Graduate School of Medicine, Suita, Japan; <sup>2</sup>Nagasaki University Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences, Nagasaki, Japan Introduction: Neutrophil play an important role as the first line of innate immune defense. Activated neutrophils become segmented and cytoplasm grows larger including granules. However, sometimes it is difficult to diffentiate whether the segmented neutrophils are on the process to grow up or not, and to decide to stop antibiotics or not. There are some reports that hyper spectral imaging (HSI) is available for analysis including diagnosis of malaria infected cells and distinction of the cells to produce antibody. In this study, we evaluated serial changes of HSI spectrum in patients with infection, and examined whether we could distinguish activated neutrophils or not. Methods: Sputum and urine samples were collected from the clinically ill three patients with pulmonary infection(n = 2) and urinary tract infection(UTI; n = 1). These samples were smeared on glass slides and gram stain was conducted. We observed the slides with HSI to get the hyper spectral data 10 times from each cytoplasm of neutrophil, and analyzed hyper spectral data with the software system, MultiSpec®. Results: We could find that neutrophils have different spectrum in each infectious stage, especially during from 400 to 700 nm wavelength. Representative image of a patient with UTI was shown in Fig. . When the neutrophils became segmented and had phagocytosis, the cytoplasm of neutrophil enlarged and showed strong intensity (black lines) compared to when microorganism disappeared and the size of cytoplasm decreased (blue and red lines). IB BRAHMS PCT, a new point of care (POC) test, has been developed for a fast PCT measurement of whole blood and EDTA samples with a measuring range of 0.08 - 10 μg/L. The objective of this evaluation study was to determine the correlation of the Samsung IB BRAHMS PCT test to established reference methods. Methods: This study was conducted to examine the correlation of the Samsung IB BRAHMS PCT to the established reference methods BRAHMS PCT sensitive Kryptor and BRAHMS PCT Elecsys at two German Laboratories. The design was based on the related CLSI Guidelines EP09-A3 (Measurement Procedure Comparison and Bias Estimation Using Patient Samples). The study compared PCT values using EDTA plasma determined with reference methods with results determined with Samsung IB BRAHMS PCT using EDTA whole blood and EDTA plasma over the whole measuring range of the assay in patients undergoing routine care PCT measurement. Results: 256 patients were included over a 6 weeks period. The correlation between EDTA whole blood or plasma and the reference method was r- = 0.97, the correlation of plasma and whole blood samples, both determined on the Samsung analyzer, was r = 0,98. The clinical concordance was 94 % related to a 0.5 μg/L threshold in whole blood. No significant bias was observed (0.033 and 0.034 for venous whole blood and plasma respectively, compared to the reference method). No difference was observed comparing imprecision of whole blood and plasma. The total CV was < 14.5 % for concentrations between 0.45 and 4.54 μg/L. The time to result of the Samsung IB BRAHMS PCT was 20 min. Conclusions: This study found an excellent correlation and diagnostic accuracy of the new, sensitive POC device for rapid measurement of procalcitonin. The Samsung IB BRAHMS PCT test allows an accurate measurement of PCT at a point of care, where near patient testing is practical, that is comparable to established lab based BRAHMS PCT assays. P011 Infection biomarkers in primary care patients with acute respiratory tract infections – Comparison of procalcitonin and C-reactive protein M. M. Meili, P. S. Schuetz Kantonsspital Aarau, Aarau, Switzerland Introduction: There is a lack of studies comparing the utility of C-reactive protein (CRP) with procalcitonin (PCT) for the management of patients with acute respiratory tract infections (ARI) in primary care. Our aim was to study first the correlation between these markers, and second to compare their predictive accuracy in regard to clinical outcome prediction. Methods: This is a secondary analysis using clinical and biomarker data of 458 primary care patients with pneumonic and non-pneumonic ARI. We used correlation statistics (spearman’s rank test) and multivariable regression models to assess association of markers with adverse outcome, namely days with restricted activities and ongoing discomfort at day 14. Results: At baseline, CRP and PCT did not correlate well in the overall population (r2 = 0.16 and r2 = 0.04) and particularly in the subgroup of patients with non-pneumonic ARI. Low correlations were also found comparing cut-off ranges, day seven levels and biomarker changes from baseline to day seven. High admission levels of CRP (>100 mg/dL, regression coefficient 1.7, 95%CI 0.6 to 2.8) as well as PCT (>0.5ug/L regression coefficient 2.3, 95%CI 0.3 to 4.3) were significantly associated with days with restricted activities. There were no associations of both markers regarding ongoing discomfort at day 14. Conclusions: CRP and PCT levels do not well correlate and have both have moderate prognostic accuracy in primary care patients with ARI to predict clinical outcomes. The low correlation between both markers calls for interventional research comparing these markers head to head in regard to their ability to guide antibiotic decisions. Methods: PSP/reg biosensors were analyzed in the abioSCOPE to determine the analytical performances of the test. Results: High analytical specificity was showed in a competitive inhibition study. Analytical sensitivity of the test is inferior to the mean PSP/reg value of a cohort of healthy individuals and the test is linear up to 1000 ng/ml of PSP/reg, thereby meeting clinical requirements. In a small-size comparison study, a good agreement was observed for PSP/reg values measured in microtiter ELISA and in the abioSCOPE. Conclusions: The analytical performances of the PSP/reg test in nanofluidic biosensors highlight that rapid and accurate quantitative measurement of low abundance proteins can be achieved at no quality costs. More data is however needed to better evaluate the diagnostic performance of PSP/reg in various settings. Quantification of PSP/reg in 5 minutes in the abioSCOPE, together with the evaluation of other specific clinical signs performed at the bedside, will hopefully improve the decision-making process of patient with suspected sepsis and improve patient’s management in various clinical scenarios. P036 Does zero heat flux thermometry more accurately identify sepsis on intensive care? J Johnston, R Reece-Anthony, A Bond, A Molokhia Lewisham and Greenwich NHS Trust, London, UK Introduction: Temperature measurement is an essential component for decision making on intensive care both in the context of identifying and treating sepsis and also in accurate calibration of blood gas analysis. SpotOn™ a Zero Heat Flux Cutaneous thermometer has been validated as a non-invasive, continuous and accurate method of measuring temperature in patients undergoing cardiac surgery in the operative and peri-operative period.1 We compared SpotOn™ with Axilla thermometers, our current method of non-invasive temperature monitoring, to establish how inaccurate our current practice was. Methods: 25 acute patients were selected on admission to intensive care at Lewisham Hospital, 17 male, 18 female, 16 medical and 9 surgical. Temperatures were recorded for an average of 47 hours on each patient using Covidien Fillac™ Axilla probes and SpotOn™ forehead probes as and when our current clinical practice indicated. Results: A total of 435 comparative values were recorded over a range of 34.4C to 38.5C. On average the SpotOn™ thermometer recorded temperatures 0.14C above the Axilla (95 % CI +/-0.04 with a Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test p < 0.0001). The average difference between SpotOn™ and Axilla over a normal range (36-37.4C) was 0.07 (95 % CI +/- 0.04) p = 0.0028. The average difference between SpotOn™ and Axilla at hypothermic temperatures (<36C) was -0.1 (95%CI +/-0.11 p = 0.13). The average difference between SpotOn™ and Axilla at hyperthermic temperatures (> = 37.5C) was 0.53C (95%CI +/- 0.11 p < 0.0001). There were 12 occasions when the SpotOn™ thermometer identified a SIRS defined temperature (<36 or > =38.3C) that the Axilla temperature did not, affecting 10 of the 25 patients. Conclusions: Zero Heat Flux Cutaneous thermometers have separately been shown to accurately record core temperatures. We have highlighted that axilla probes are inaccurate in comparison to SpotOn™. The Axilla probe appears to under-read at hyperthermic temperatures and over-read at hypothermic temperatures. The difference between the two methods appears most marked at hyperthermic temperatures. As a consequence it is likely that axilla probes could fail to identify sepsis in patients on intensive care. Reference 1. Alenezi, Y. Arabi King Saud bin Abdulaziz University for Health Sciences and King Abdullah International Medical Research Center, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia Introduction: Preclinical and clinical studies have investigated the role of β -blockers in sepsis, especially in early sepsis, which characterized by elevated sympathetic response. The purpose of this study was to examine the association between a previous prescription for β -blockers and mortality rate among septic patients. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study from January 1, 2003, to December 31, 2013, in a tertiary care academic medical center. We included all patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) with severe sepsis and septic shock who were > =14 years of age. Patients were defined to have a previous prescription of β -blockers if the prescription was active for the 3 months prior to hospital admission. Results: We identified 4,629 patients with severe sepsis and septic shock, 623 of whom had a previous prescription for β -blockers before hospital admission and 4006 of whom were not previously taking β -blockers. Common medications used by patients were metoprolol (77 %) and carvedilol (13 %). The overall mortality rate was 30 %. Among patients who were previously taking β -blockers, 181 (29.1 %) died in the ICU and 442 (70.9 %) were discharged alive. Of the patients who did not have a previous prescription for β -blockers, 1,231 (30.7 %) died in the ICU and 2,775 (69.3 %) were discharged alive. There was no statistically significant association between patients having a previous prescription for β -blockers and ICU mortality (risk ratio 0.94; 95 % confidence interval [CI] 0.82 to 1.08; p = .39). We further stratified patients on the basis of highest heart rate in the first 24 hours of ICU admission into those with a heart rate >95 beats per minute and those with a heart rate of < =95 beats per minute. There were no statistically significant association between patients who had a previous prescription for β -blockers and ICU mortality in either group (risk ratio 0.91; 95 % CI 0.77 to 1.06; p = 0.22) and (risk ratio 1.095; 95 % CI 0.78 to 0.1.54; p = 0.60) respectively. Conclusions: Our study demonstrated no significant association between previous prescription for β -blockers and ICU mortality. This held true even after further stratification of patients on the basis of highest heart rate in the first 24 hours of ICU admission. This result may be due to lack of effect of β -blockers or short-term action of medication use. Mann Ben Yehudah Assaf Harofeh MC, Beer Yaakov, Israel Introduction: There is paucity of data concerning the group of patients with a clinical syndrome of sepsis, suspected clinical infection and negative cultures regarding disease severity, end organ failure and outcomes. It is also not clear whether patients with only negative blood cultures (BCs) but other positive cultures have a different disease entity than patients who have no growth in all of the cultures taken. Our study attempts to further define true culture negativity and its effect on disease severity and outcomes. Methods: All blood cultures results taken in the Detroit Medical Center ICUs from December 2012 to March 2013 were collected. Any patient who had a negative BC was reviewed. All cultures taken within 10 days of the negative BCs were further reviewed. Patients were then divided into 3 groups: 1.BC positive group- BCs within 10 days of the negative BC were positive. 2. Non BC positive group - other cultures within 10 days of the negative BC were positive. 3. All culture negative. The 3 groups were compared. Results: During the study period, 300 patients had at least one negative blood culture. 132 had all cultures negative, 76 had positive BCs, and 92 had other positive cultures. The BC positive group resembled the negative group in all baseline characteristics. There was a significant difference in the admission scores, with higher SOFA and APACHE2 scores of the BC positive group. SOFA score was higher for the positive group throughout the ICU stay. There was no difference in SIRS in both groups. However, there was more shock, need for vasopressors, renal failure, respiratory failure and neurological alterations in the BC positive group. The BC positive group was more frequently started on antibiotics and had more antibiotic days then the negative group. They also had worse outcomes with a higher mortality in the ICU (40 % in the positive vs. 6.8 % in the negative, p < 0.0001) and in the hospital (47.4 % vs. 9.9 % respectively, p < 0.0001). In a multivariate analysis of ICU death predictors, the only independent predictors were APACHE2 > 25 and positive BC group. Disease severity was also worse in non-blood positive culture group when compared with the negative group; scores were higher, there was more end organ dysfunction, antibiotic treatment was longer and Outcomes were worse. Conclusions: We have shown that the culture negative patients have lower disease severity, end organ failure and better outcomes, and therefore should be considered for shorter antimicrobial treatments and early de-escalation.
