Funding information and disclosures deemed relevant by the authors, if any, are provided at the end of the article. 11 6 2013 80 24 225475 2250 2257 06 8 2012 12 2 2013 11 06 2014 11 06 2014 20 05 2014 15 02 2024 © 2013 American Academy of Neurology 2013 American Academy of Neurology Protecting the brain in sports: what do we really know? 80 24 18 3 2013 2178 2179 Neurology 23508729 Objective: To update the 1997 American Academy of Neurology (AAN) practice parameter regarding sports concussion, focusing on 4 questions: 1) What factors increase/decrease concussion risk? 2) What diagnostic tools identify those with concussion and those at increased risk for severe/prolonged early impairments, neurologic catastrophe, or chronic neurobehavioral impairment? 3) What clinical factors identify those at increased risk for severe/prolonged early postconcussion impairments, neurologic catastrophe, recurrent concussions, or chronic neurobehavioral impairment? 4) What interventions enhance recovery, reduce recurrent concussion risk, or diminish long-term sequelae? The complete guideline on which this summary is based is available as an online data supplement to this article. Methods: We systematically reviewed the literature from 1955 to June 2012 for pertinent evidence. We assessed evidence for quality and synthesized into conclusions using a modified Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation process. We used a modified Delphi process to develop recommendations. Results: Specific risk factors can increase or decrease concussion risk. Diagnostic tools to help identify individuals with concussion include graded symptom checklists, the Standardized Assessment of Concussion, neuropsychological assessments, and the Balance Error Scoring System. Ongoing clinical symptoms, concussion history, and younger age identify those at risk for postconcussion impairments. Risk factors for recurrent concussion include history of multiple concussions, particularly within 10 days after initial concussion. Risk factors for chronic neurobehavioral impairment include concussion exposure and APOE ε4 genotype. Data are insufficient to show that any intervention enhances recovery or diminishes long-term sequelae postconcussion. chunks.content: Background High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy emerged as an essential tool in the management of acute hypoxemic respiratory failure during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic [ ]. As a frontline treatment for moderate-to-severe COVID-19 pneumonia, HFNC offered a non-invasive alternative that could deliver oxygen at high flow rates (up to 60 LPM) with controlled fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO₂). This capability significantly reduced reliance on invasive mechanical ventilation at a time when ventilator availability was critically limited [ , ]. Beyond its clinical efficacy, HFNC proved to be a cost-effective solution, especially in resource-constrained settings [ ]. Indian COVID-19 management protocols highlighted the value of early intervention at lower oxygen thresholds, which helped to mitigate rapid respiratory decline. Moreover, it allowed patients to remain conscious, mobile, and communicative, reducing the need for sedation and physical restraints [ ]. The widespread use of HFNC during the pandemic reinforced its role in managing not only COVID-related respiratory distress but also broader conditions such as community-acquired pneumonia and acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. This experience catalysed updates in treatment protocols and spurred innovation aimed at retaining the therapy’s benefits while overcoming challenges related to training, infection control, and affordability [ ]. High flow nasal cannula device has been proven to effectively decrease intubation rates for patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF) [ ], avert post-extubation respiratory failure [ ], and reduce patients’ hospital stay duration [ ]. Meanwhile, high flow nasal cannula (HFNC) device has likewise displayed an influence in non-hospitalised patients with severe breathing illnesses by minimising the acute exacerbation rate at 1 year, rising the 6-minute distance of walking [ ], stabilising the status of life [ ], and improving the dynamic activity performance and capacity [ – ]. It can also be non-inferior to non-invasive ventilation in order to avoid reintubation among patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) [ , ]. Better patient outcomes related to HFNC are attributed to its physiological impacts, including enhancement of oxygenation, ventilatory efficiency [ – ], prevention of patient self-inflicted lung injury, and patient comfort and tolerance improvement [ ]. HFNC flushes out dead space in the upper airway, and its benefits are optimised when the delivered gas flow is equal to or greater than the patient’s peak inspiratory flow, leading to stable FiO 2 and a degree of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) [ ]. Hence, flow settings become an important aspect in HFNC oxygen therapy [ ]. The TrueOxy+ HFNC Device is a novel, indigenously developed system (Patent application no: 202411032907) designed to deliver precise and high-flow oxygen therapy with flow capabilities up to 60 LPM, exceeding typical peak inspiratory demands (30–40 LPM). This device ensures that the prescribed FiO₂ reaches the lungs without dilution from ambient air. Its integrated heated humidification system warms the gas to 37 °C and maintains nearly 100% relative humidity. These features help to reduce airway resistance and inflammation, preserve muco-ciliary clearance, and improve patient comfort and compliance [ ]. Preliminary preclinical evaluations have shown promising results in terms of flow rate, humidification, maintenance of temperature and FiO 2 delivered. This proof-of-concept study aims to assess the clinical performance and subjective safety of the TrueOxy+ HFNC device in healthy individuals. The research question was: Does the TrueOxy+ device increase the partial pressure of oxygen as expected from an HFNC device (with change in flow and FiO 2 ) in healthy human volunteers? Findings from this study will support further clinical trials in critically ill patients and contribute to regulatory approval of this indigenously developed HFNC device. It will expand caregivers’ selection of existing high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) device options. Despite the established benefits of HFNC therapy, most commercially available HFNC systems are imported, with marginal acquisition costs, and often in short supply in low- and middle-income countries. During the COVID-19 pandemic, these constraints led to critical shortages, delayed therapy initiation, and inequitable access to respiratory support. There remains a clear unmet need for a locally manufactured HFNC device/system that meets international safety and performance standards while being scalable for widespread use in resource-limited healthcare settings [ , ]. The TrueOxy+ HFNC device was developed indigenously to address this gap by providing functional characteristics consistent with and technical specifications comparable to those of existing HFNC systems. It includes high-flow delivery up to 60 LPM, precise FiO₂ control, and integrated heated humidification. This study was therefore designed as a first-in-human physiological validation to assess whether the device performs as expected under controlled conditions prior to broader clinical evaluation. Accordingly, this investigation was intentionally designed as a first-in-human physiological validation study rather than a comparative effectiveness trial, with the objective of confirming expected oxygenation behaviour and subjective safety prior to head-to-head evaluation against commercial HFNC systems. The indigenously developed TrueOxy+ high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) is a system that delivers heated and humidified oxygen–air mixtures at high flow rates via a nasal interface. The device operates on a demand-responsive gas-delivery principle to maintain stable output despite variable flow requirements. Methods Study objective The primary objective of this proof-of-concept study was to physiologically validate the performance of the TrueOxy+ HFNC device by assessing the arterial partial pressure of oxygen (PO₂) response to graded increases in delivered FiO₂ at fixed flow rates in healthy adult volunteers. Secondary objectives included evaluation of device safety, participant tolerability, and the effects of varying FiO₂ and flow rates on other physiological parameters, including pH, pCO₂, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation. Study design and setting This was a single-centre, participant-blinded, randomised trial conducted between February and March 2024 at the Phase I Unit (Clinical Pharmacology Unit (CPU)) of our institute. The study received prior approval from the Institutional Ethics Committee ‘Institute Ethics Committee, Post Graduate Institute of Medical Education and Research’ (PGI/IEC/2023/EIC001372, dated: 15.11.2023) and was registered with the Clinical Trials Registry of India (CTRI/2024/02/062209, dated: 01/02/2024). This study was reported in accordance with the CONSORT 2025 checklist [ ], and Fig. depicts CONSORT flow diagram. Participant recruitment and eligibility Healthy volunteers aged 20–50 years of either sex were recruited through word-of-mouth referrals and from the Phase I Unit’s CPU’s healthy volunteer registry. All participants were provided with detailed study information in their local language, and their queries were addressed before obtaining written informed consent. During screening, a comprehensive medical background and physical examination were performed. Laboratory investigations included a complete blood count (with haemoglobin threshold of 13 g/dL) and a Triple Marker Test (HIV 1 & 2 antigen, HBsAg, and HCV antigen) to exclude infectious conditions. The volunteers were considered eligible if they met all inclusion criteria and consented to participate. History of smoking, blood donation within the past 3 months, and participation in another clinical trial within the last 6 months were exclusion criteria. In the absence of national or international guidelines for clinical validation of respiratory therapy devices, at the time of this trial the present new device has passed the ISO80601-2-90:2021 [ ], IEC60601-1:2005 + AMD:2012:Ed:3.1 [ ], IEC606O1-1-2:2014 [ ], IEC60601-1-6:2010 + AMD1:2013 + AMD2:2020 [ ], IEC 60601-1-8:2006 + AMD1:2012 + AMD2:2020 [ ], IEC60601-1-12:2014 + AMDl:2020 [ ] standards for basic safety and essential performance of respiratory high-flow therapy equipment from an established national accreditation board for testing and calibration laboratories (NABL) approved/accredited conformity assessment body (Laboratory). We decided to take the approach of phase 0 (pre-phase 1) trials and limit the sample size to 21 healthy volunteers [ ]. Study procedures Participants reported to the CPU on the morning of the study after consuming a light breakfast (caloric value recorded but not standardised). Eligibility was reconfirmed, and informed consent was reaffirmed. The volunteers were monitored closely throughout the procedure and for one-hour post-procedure. They were discharged only after clinical evaluation confirmed their well-being. The volunteers were randomised in a 1:1:1 ratio into one of three HFNC flow-rate groups: 20 LPM, 40 LPM, or 60 LPM. Randomisation was performed using sealed opaque envelopes to ensure allocation concealment with participant-blinding. Each participant was seated comfortably and connected to standard monitoring equipment, including ECG, pulse oximetry (SpO₂), and non-invasive blood pressure (NIBP). Emergency resuscitation equipment was readily available on-site. Under all aseptic precautions and local anaesthesia, a radial artery catheter was inserted for serial arterial blood sampling. After a 5-minute rest period on room air, a baseline arterial blood gas (ABG) sample was obtained (T1pre). The HFNC device was then applied with FiO₂ of 0.40 for 20 min, followed by a second ABG sample (T1post). A 10-minute washout period followed, during which a third ABG sample was collected (T2pre). The HFNC was reapplied at FiO₂ of 0.60 for 20 min, followed by T2post sampling. This protocol was repeated sequentially for FiO₂ levels of 0.80 and 1.00, with corresponding pre- and post-intervention samples collected for each phase (Fig. ). We chose to randomise volunteers into 3 flow rates to minimise the number of blood samples collected. Each flow condition was maintained for 20 min to allow arterial blood gases and ventilation to reach a near steady state [ ].

The HFNC was reapplied at FiO₂ of 0.60 for 20 min, followed by T2post sampling. This protocol was repeated sequentially for FiO₂ levels of 0.80 and 1.00, with corresponding pre- and post-intervention samples collected for each phase (Fig. ). We chose to randomise volunteers into 3 flow rates to minimise the number of blood samples collected. Each flow condition was maintained for 20 min to allow arterial blood gases and ventilation to reach a near steady state [ ]. After each condition, a 5-minute room-air washout was used to permit return to baseline respiration [ ]. Vital signs (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂) and physical status were continuously monitored and recorded at each sample time point according to the study protocol. Predicted arterial oxygen partial pressure (pO₂) values were calculated for each FiO₂ level. Figure shows the indigenously developed ‘TrueOxy+ HFNC device’ used in this study. Table highlights technical specifications of the ‘TrueOxy+ HFNC Device’. Post-study care Following completion of the HFNC protocol, participants were observed on room air for 2 h. The radial artery catheter was removed after confirming hemostasis. Participants were discharged following a final clinical assessment and provided with post-study care instructions and follow-up guidance. Statistical analysis and sample size calculation Continuous variables have been presented as mean (SD) or median (IQR) and compared using t-tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, or ANOVA as per the nature of the distribution and number of groups. Categorical variables have been represented as numbers (percentages) and have been compared using the chi-square test/Fisher’s Exact test. The effect of FiO 2 and flow when controlled for room air pO 2 has been assessed as part of a generalised linear mixed effects model while accounting for repeated measures using Bonferroni’s adjustment. For comparison, the predicted (estimated) pO 2 with each FiO 2 change was calculated using the room-air pO 2 /FiO 2 (PF) ratio and using the formula [ ]. The association between the measured and the estimated pO 2 was assessed using the Spearman rank correlation coefficient. A p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results A total of 32 volunteers were screened, and 21 were randomised into one of three groups (Flow: 20 LPM, 40 LPM and 60 LPM). There were no significant differences in the baseline parameters across the groups. The mean (SD) age was 31.71 (7.89), 29.29 (3.86) and 30.29 (5.28) years, respectively. The mean (SD) of BMI was 26.56 (1.06), 26.11 (1.30) and 25.54 (1.29) kg/m 2, respectively. The baseline pO 2 was 102.33 (9.92), 101.06 (10.95) and 101.71 (10.73) mmHg, respectively, across the groups (Table ). There was one female participant in the 40 LPM flow group; all the others were male volunteers. Correlation between measured pO<sub>2</sub> and predicted pO<sub>2</sub> In Fig. , we demonstrate the strong linear correlation between the measured pO 2 values and the predicted (estimated) values as per the Al-Otaibi formula (spearman correlation coefficient of 0.74 [95% CI, 0.60–0.84]) as well as the predictions based on baseline p/f ratio (spearman correlation coefficient of 0.73 [95% CI, 0.57– 0.84]). Relationship between FiO<sub>2</sub>, flow and pO<sub>2</sub> A generalised linear mixed-effects model accounting for within-subject repeated measures revealed a linear increase in pO 2 with increasing FiO 2 , which was statistically and clinically significant (Supplementary Table 1). There was no statistically significant change in pO 2 with a change in flows. Biologically, this is expected, as these were healthy volunteers, and flow does not affect pO 2 by a large margin. This, however, will not be the case with postoperative or critically ill patients. In Fig. A, demonstrates that as FiO 2 increases, the pO 2 also increases linearly in each setting of flow in the HFNC device. Figure B demonstrates that the 95% confidence intervals (purple bars) of the mean difference in pO 2 between the baseline room air exposure and room air exposures (room air 2, 3 and 4) before each FiO 2 change cross the line of no difference (red dotted line). Relationship between FiO<sub>2</sub>, flow and other variables In Table , it is seen that FiO 2 appears to have a statistically significant effect on the pH. Figure shows that this is due to the presence of outliers in the 40 LPM flow group at FiO 2 values of 0.4 and 0.6. These were the blood samples of a single volunteer, which showed bicarbonate values at the upper limit of normal (27.7 and 28, respectively) with pH at 7.538 and 7.509. This was due to a calibration error in the blood gas machine, which was observed after data analysis. The outlier was removed post hoc. The pH and bicarbonate in the rest of the blood gases of this volunteer were in

statistically significant effect on the pH. Figure shows that this is due to the presence of outliers in the 40 LPM flow group at FiO 2 values of 0.4 and 0.6. These were the blood samples of a single volunteer, which showed bicarbonate values at the upper limit of normal (27.7 and 28, respectively) with pH at 7.538 and 7.509. This was due to a calibration error in the blood gas machine, which was observed after data analysis. The outlier was removed post hoc. The pH and bicarbonate in the rest of the blood gases of this volunteer were in the normal range. Removing this sample from the analysis changed the p-value to 0.097. There was no statistically or clinically significant difference between the flow rates and across FiO 2 ranges in any of the other blood gas parameters (supplementary Fig. 1). Supplementary Fig. 2 and Table show that there was no statistically significant difference in the heart rate with change in FiO 2 ; however, there was a statistically significant difference across different flows. All of these values were, however, within clinically acceptable ranges, and there was no significant change from the baseline within each group. Supplementary Fig. 3 and Table show that there were no major differences in the blood pressure, oxygen saturation and respiratory rate throughout the trial at different FiO 2 and flow rates. Discussion We intended to evaluate whether our indigenously developed device would raise the pO 2 as expected in healthy human volunteers using the P/F ratio or the expected pO 2 as per the Al-Oitabi formula [ – ]. The strong correlation between the measured and expected pO 2 , as shown in Fig. (Spearman Rho > 0.7), demonstrates this objective. The pO 2 values prior to each adjustment in the FiO 2 had achieved baseline levels (The 95% CIs cross the line of no difference at 0 in Fig. B), which indicates the absence of a carryover effect from prior FiO 2 exposure within the same subject. There was no statistically significant change in pO 2 with changes in flow rates. This finding is biologically plausible, as changes in flow are not expected to substantially influence oxygenation in healthy individuals. In contrast, flow-dependent effects on pO₂ have been reported in postoperative and critically ill patients, where respiratory physiology is altered [ ]. To the best of our professional knowledge, this is the first study to explore the physiological effects of an indigenously developed high-flow nasal cannula device in healthy awake volunteers at flow rates up to 60 LPM. Respiratory rate remained unchanged across different FiO₂ levels and flow settings. While using an HFNC device in critically ill patients with high work of breathing, the respiratory rate is expected to decrease substantially with increasing HFNC flow rates [ ]. This was absent in our experiment as the participants were healthy volunteers with normal work of breathing at rest. There was no statistically or clinically significant variation in flow rates or FiO2 across the other blood gas parameters, as under normal circumstances HFNC is not expected to alter these parameters [ ]. We observed that all participating awake healthy volunteers in this study reported that the air was moist and comfortable. This observation indicates that the indigenously developed ‘TrueOxy+ HFNC Device’ had generated the desired humidified flow [ ]. There was no statistically significant variation in the heart rate with changes in FiO 2 , but there was a statistically significant variation with different flows. All these values, however, were within clinically acceptable limits, and there was no significant variation from the baseline in each group. There were no significant variations in blood pressure, oxygen saturation, or respiratory rate during the trial at varying FiO 2 and flow rates [ ]. All volunteers completed the study without any complaints, indicating good compliance. There were no cases of barotrauma (subcutaneous emphysema), new onset respiratory distress, or nasal ulceration/irritation among the participants. This suggests that the indigenously developed device is clinically safe. It was also observed that the HFNC device primarily improves oxygenation [ ] via anatomical dead-space washout and low-level positive pressure [ ]. For example, HFNC flushes expiratory gas from the upper airway, effectively reducing dead space, and raises alveolar O₂. It generates modest positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) (≈ 1 cmH₂O for every 10 LPM when the mouth is closed), and almost ~ 7 cmH₂O nasopharyngeal pressure at 60 LPM flow. These effects expand end-expiratory lung volume and improve V/Q matching, but mainly in hypoxemic lungs [ ]. In healthy volunteers with near-normal pO₂, the additional flow-dependent gains are minimal. This study has some drawbacks. The sample size was small, and the majority of the healthy volunteers were males. To the best of our knowledge, no published trial has evaluated a similar device; therefore,

These effects expand end-expiratory lung volume and improve V/Q matching, but mainly in hypoxemic lungs [ ]. In healthy volunteers with near-normal pO₂, the additional flow-dependent gains are minimal. This study has some drawbacks. The sample size was small, and the majority of the healthy volunteers were males. To the best of our knowledge, no published trial has evaluated a similar device; therefore, we chose to follow a phase 0 trial design, for which a sample size of 21 was deemed adequate [ ]. Although most participants were male, physiologically, the performance of respiratory therapy devices is not expected to differ between genders. Comfort was assessed subjectively rather than using a validated scale. Future work should use standardised instruments such as Visual Analog Scale or the General Comfort Questionnaire for adults to quantify tolerability [ ]. Further clinical studies are essential to evaluate the performance of this indigenously developed HFNC device in various clinical subject populations. The absence of a commercially available comparator and of investigator blinding reflects the device’s early developmental phase. It should be interpreted within the context of an initial phase-0 evaluation rather than as a methodological limitation. Although a formal cost-effectiveness analysis was not undertaken. The device incorporates an indigenous design and locally sourced, fully compatible consumables, which may affect acquisition and operational costs relative to existing HFNC systems. The design approach emphasises local manufacturing and the use of non-proprietary components, aiming to improve deployment feasibility in settings with varying resource availability. Conclusion From this trial, we may conclude that the indigenously developed HFNC device produces an increase in oxygenation (pO 2 ) as expected, without any untoward adverse events in healthy human volunteers and device failure. The overall compliance of healthy volunteers with the indigenously developed HFNC device was positive and acceptable. All volunteers were reported with normal clinically acceptable physiological changes at the beginning and end of each session, and there were no major differences in the blood pressure, oxygen saturation and respiratory rate throughout the trial at different FiO 2 and flow rates. chunks.content: Overview of Sodium Channels and Neurophysiologic Role in Pain Transmission Voltage-gated sodium channels (NaV) are integral transmembrane proteins critical for the initiation and propagation of action potentials in excitable cells, including neurons. These channels are pivotal in pain transmission, mediating the rapid depolarization phase of action potentials in nociceptive neurons. Consequently, a comprehensive understanding of their structure, function, and role in human pain is essential for the development of targeted therapeutic strategies. Among the nine isoforms of human NaV, NaV1.7, NaV1.8, and NaV1.9 are centrally involved in the neurophysiologic transmission of pain. Their distinct biophysical properties and expression patterns are fundamental to both normal and pathological pain processing. Continued advancements in understanding sodium channel function and developing isoform-specific inhibitors hold significant promise for novel pain therapies, with the potential to improve outcomes for patients suffering from various acute and chronic pain conditions. Structure and Function of Sodium Channels NaV are comprised of a large α-subunit, which forms the ion-conducting pore, and one or more auxiliary β-subunits that modulate channel gating and trafficking. The α-subunit consists of four homologous domains (I–IV), each containing six transmembrane segments (S1–S6) ( ). The S4 segment functions as a voltage sensor, while the pore is formed by the S5–S6 segments. In humans, nine α-subunit isoforms (Nav1.1–Nav1.9) are encoded by the SCN1A–SCN11A genes, each exhibiting distinct tissue distributions and biophysical properties. Of the nine subtypes (NaV1.1–NaV1.9), NaV1.1, NaV1.2, NaV1.3, and NaV1.6 are preferentially expressed in the central nervous system, while NaV1.7, NaV1.8, and NaV1.9 are expressed in the peripheral nervous system. NaV activate in response to membrane depolarization, facilitating the influx of sodium ions and triggering an action potential. Following activation, the channel undergoes rapid inactivation, which prevents further ion flow until the membrane repolarizes. This cycle is crucial for the efficient propagation of electrical signals along axons and across synapses within the pain pathway. Multiple sodium channel isoforms are expressed in nociceptive neurons, particularly within dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons and trigeminal ganglia, which are central to pain sensation. The key isoforms implicated in pain transmission, which are NaV1.7, NaV1.8, and NaV1.9, differ in terms of their primary location, kinetics, tetrodotoxin (TTX) sensitivity, and, most importantly, their clinical relevance ( ). NaV1.7 Encoded by the SCN9A gene, NaV1.7 is highly expressed in peripheral sensory neurons, including nociceptors. Its fast activation and inactivation kinetics are necessary to establish the threshold for action potential firing. By amplifying sub-threshold depolarizations, NaV1.7 facilitate the initiation of pain signals. NaV1.8 NaV1.8, encoded by SCN10A, is predominantly expressed in DRG neurons and is resistant to TTX, a potent sodium channel blocker. It generates slowly inactivating currents, which contribute to repetitive firing in nociceptors during sustained depolarization. NaV1.8 is upregulated in inflammatory pain states, leading to enhanced neuronal excitability. Its functional role in cold pain sensation has also been reported, as it remains active at lower temperatures compared to other isoforms. NaV1.9 Encoded by SCN11A, NaV1.9 generates persistent, TTX-resistant currents with slow activation and inactivation kinetics. It is expressed in small-diameter DRG neurons and contributes to the resting membrane potential and sub-threshold depolarization, which amplifies pain signals. Mutations in NaV1.9 are linked to both painful and painless phenotypes, highlighting its complex role in nociception. Neurophysiologic Role in Pain Transmission Pain transmission is initiated by the activation of peripheral nociceptors, by noxious stimuli ( eg , thermal, mechanical, or chemical). NaV within these sensory neurons generate and propagate action potentials along sensory axons to the spinal cord. In the dorsal horn, these signals are relayed to second-order neurons, which project to the brain for pain perception. At the peripheral terminals of nociceptors, NaV1.7 amplifies generator potentials and lowers action potential initiation thresholds. NaV1.8 sustains high-frequency firing during intense or prolonged stimuli, while NaV1.9 maintains sub-threshold depolarization, enhancing neuronal excitability. Collectively, these channels ensure the efficient transmission of pain signals from the peripheral to the central nervous system. In pathological pain states, such as neuropathic or inflammatory pain, sodium channel expression and function are dysregulated. For example, nerve injury upregulates NaV1.8 and NaV1.3 (another isoform implicated in neuropathic pain), which increases neuronal excitability and causes spontaneous depolarizations, generating early neuropathic symptoms which contribute to hyperalgesia or allodynia. These alterations contribute to chronic pain establishing sodium channels as key therapeutic targets. Therapeutic Implications of Sodium Subtype Selection Given their fundamental role in pain transmission, sodium channels represent potential targets for analgesic drug development. Non-selective sodium channel blockers, such as lidocaine and carbamazepine, are used to treat neuropathic pain but are limited by off-target side effects due to their lack of isoform specificity. Recent research has focused on developing selective inhibitors for NaV1.7, NaV1.8, and NaV1.9 to achieve pain relief with a more favorable side effect profile. Selective NaV1.7 inhibitors have demonstrated preclinical potential in models of inflammatory and neuropathic pain; however, clinical trials have encountered

sodium channels as key therapeutic targets. Therapeutic Implications of Sodium Subtype Selection Given their fundamental role in pain transmission, sodium channels represent potential targets for analgesic drug development. Non-selective sodium channel blockers, such as lidocaine and carbamazepine, are used to treat neuropathic pain but are limited by off-target side effects due to their lack of isoform specificity. Recent research has focused on developing selective inhibitors for NaV1.7, NaV1.8, and NaV1.9 to achieve pain relief with a more favorable side effect profile. Selective NaV1.7 inhibitors have demonstrated preclinical potential in models of inflammatory and neuropathic pain; however, clinical trials have encountered challenges with efficacy or off-target effects. NaV1.8 inhibitors such as suzetrigine and others are also under investigation, particularly for their potential in treating chronic inflammatory pain conditions. , Furthermore, gene therapy approaches, such as CRISPR-based modulation of SCN9A , are being explored to address genetic pain disorders. Among the subtypes, NaV1.8 is considered a highly favorable target due to its specific expression and direct role in pain signal transmission. NaV1.8 is the most prevalent sodium channel in small dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, mediating rapid upstroke of action potentials and sustaining the high-frequency firing essential for pain signal propagation. , The inhibition of NaV1.8 effectively blocks the sustained sodium current required for these neurons to fire, disrupting pain signaling without significantly affecting other physiological functions, beneficially minimizing off-target side effects. Unlike NaV1.8, the use of NaV1.7 and NaV1.9 inhibitors presents greater challenges. NaV1.7 functions as a “threshold channel” in pain signaling but is also found in olfactory sensory neurons. Broad inhibition could therefore lead to undesired side effects such as anosmia. NaV1.9 amplifies weak pain stimuli and helps regulate the membrane potential in nociceptors. However, its role in both painful and painless conditions, along with technical difficulties in drug development, has hindered its exploration as a therapeutic target. Disease States Associated with Sodium Channel Dysfunction Dysfunction within NaV, whether due to inherited mutations or acquired conditions, can lead to disorders of nociceptive processing. (see ). Specifically, alterations to NaV1.7, NaV1.8, and NaV1.9 isoforms have been identified in the development of well defined pain syndromes. Primary Erythromelalgia Primary erythromelalgia is a disease associated with NaV dysfunction characterized by a triad of redness, warmth, and burning pain, most commonly affecting the extremities. It typically manifests within the first two decades of life, with an estimated incidence ranging from 0.25 to 2 per 100,000 people annually. The condition may be idiopathic or inherited. In inherited cases, neuropathy develops from an autosomal dominant mutation to NaV1.7. This mutation causes allodynia as a result of NaV hyperexcitability, leading to the firing of nociceptive neurons in response to sub-threshold stimuli. While most cases occur prior to the age of 20, a novel NaV1.7 Q10R mutation has been identified in patients with later onset. This mutation is associated with decreased DRG excitability, which may contribute to the delayed symptom presentation. Paroxysmal Extreme Pain Disorder Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder (PEPD) is a pain syndrome caused by a mutation in the SCN9A gene, which affects NaV1.7. The condition is characterized by neonatal or infantile onset of autonomic manifestations, including skin flushing, patchy or asymmetric color changes, tonic non-epileptic attacks, and syncope with bradycardia. Subsequent disease progression can lead to symptoms such as severe rectal burning, ocular pain, and submandibular pain with associated erythematous skin changes. PEPD is exceptionally rare, with an incidence of less than 1 in 1,000,000 and fewer than 500 documented cases. Pain episodes often begin abruptly and can last from seconds to hours. These events are frequently precipitated by triggers such as defecation, perineal wiping, eating, or temperature changes. Although pain typically originates focally in the rectum, it often radiates to the abdomen. Small Fiber Neuropathy Small fiber neuropathy has also been linked to sodium channel dysfunction. Gain-of-function mutations in NaV1.7 or NaV1.8 can lead to an increased frequency of action potential firing in response to supra-threshold stimuli, as well as an increase in spontaneous neuronal firing within the DRG. , The median age of onset is 52 years. This condition is more prevalent in women, who constitute 67% of affected individuals. The disorder can present with sensory changes, autonomic dysfunction, or a combination of both. , Patients commonly report fatigue, cognitive disturbances, headaches, and widespread musculoskeletal pain, which can significantly impair their quality of life. Familial Episodic Pain Syndrome Familial episodic pain syndrome is associated with mutations in the NaV1.7, NaV1.8, or NaV1.9 voltage-gated sodium channels, which can cause enhanced evoked excitability, a reduced current threshold for action potentials, and a higher firing frequency. Due to the rarity of the disease, precise demographics are not well-defined; however, cases have been reported in three Chinese families, one family of mixed European ancestry, one family from South America, and six families from Japan. Common clinical features include

, Patients commonly report fatigue, cognitive disturbances, headaches, and widespread musculoskeletal pain, which can significantly impair their quality of life. Familial Episodic Pain Syndrome Familial episodic pain syndrome is associated with mutations in the NaV1.7, NaV1.8, or NaV1.9 voltage-gated sodium channels, which can cause enhanced evoked excitability, a reduced current threshold for action potentials, and a higher firing frequency. Due to the rarity of the disease, precise demographics are not well-defined; however, cases have been reported in three Chinese families, one family of mixed European ancestry, one family from South America, and six families from Japan. Common clinical features include an early childhood onset, with symptoms primarily affecting the lower extremities and joints. Fatigue and cold temperatures are common triggers, while warming the extremities and applying compresses provide pain relief. Congenital Insensitivity to Pain In contrast to the aforementioned gain-of-function disorders, congenital insensitivity to pain is a condition of sodium channel dysfunction caused by a loss-of-function mutation in NaV1.7. This mutation results in an inability to perceive pain from birth. Affected individuals do not feel pain from any noxious stimuli, including inflammation and heat. Consequently, self-inflicted injuries to the fingers and oral cavity, such as lacerations and tooth avulsions, are common, as are cuts, bruising, and burns. Older individuals frequently experience painless fractures and joint damage, which can lead to permanent complications, including bone deformities and Charcot joints. All affected individuals are at risk for corneal injuries due to absent corneal reflexes. Corneal scarring may develop and is best evaluated by slit-lamp examination. Corneal transplants in these patients carry an increased risk of failure, likely due to the absence of nociceptive innervation in both the transplanted cornea and the surrounding conjunctiva. Developmental and intellectual delays or disabilities are also present in some cases. Current Medications Affecting Sodium Channels for Pain Current sodium channel inhibitors are categorized into three primary classes: local anesthetics, antiarrhythmics, and anticonvulsants (See ). The local anesthetics include lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, levobupivacaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine, procaine, tetracaine, and chloroprocaine. Antiarrhythmics used for pain include disopyramide, mexiletine, flecainide, procainamide, propafenone, quinidine, and phenytoin. Lidocaine is classified as both a local anesthetic and an antiarrhythmic. Anticonvulsants include carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, lacosamide, zonisamide, topiramate, eslicarbazepine, and valproate. Most of these medications are non-selective sodium channel blockers and have been implicated in managing neuropathic pain, particularly in disease states associated with abnormal sodium channel function. Local Anesthetics Local anesthetics are widely utilized, particularly in strategies aimed at reducing opioid use and implementing multimodal analgesia. While generally safe, their use carries a risk of local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST). Although rare, LAST can be life-threatening, with case reports indicating mortality rates approaching 10%. Local anesthetics are weak bases composed of a lipophilic aromatic ring, an intermediate ester or amide chain, and a terminal amine. Their classification as amides or esters is based on this intermediate chain; amides undergo hepatic metabolism via cytochrome P450, whereas esters are hydrolyzed by plasma esterases. The various local anesthetics differ in their potency, lipophilicity, protein binding, onset time, and pKa. The pharmacological profiles of bupivacaine, prilocaine, tetracaine, and chloroprocaine highlight the diversity among local anesthetics. Bupivacaine, an amide local anesthetic discovered in 1957, is a long-acting agent widely used for intraoperative anesthesia, postoperative analgesia, and chronic pain management. However, reports of severe systemic toxicity associated with bupivacaine prompted the development of levobupivacaine and ropivacaine. Both are pure levo-isomers, and their stereochemical configuration contributes to a lower potential for cardiac and central nervous system toxicity compared to bupivacaine while offering longer duration of analgesia compared to other local anesthetics but shorter duration compared to bupivacaine. In contrast, prilocaine is an intermediate-acting amide local anesthetic suitable for procedures requiring moderate duration anesthesia. It is also notable for causing less vasodilation than other agents during neuraxial anesthesia, which reduces the need for vasoconstrictor use. Tetracaine, a long-acting ester, is highly potent due to its strong protein binding. Conversely, chloroprocaine, a fast-acting ester, has a very rapid onset and low potency, making it particularly useful for neuraxial anesthesia during brief surgical procedures or emergent situations requiring a quick anesthetic effect, such as an emergency cesarean section. The differences in onset, duration, and metabolism underscore the importance of selecting the appropriate local anesthetic for specific pain management needs. Antiarrhythmics All class I antiarrhythmics target the cardiac NaV1.5, with subgroups A, B, and C delineated by their specificity to various sodium channel states and dissociation rates. Among the Class IB antiarrhythmics, lidocaine, mexiletine, and phenytoin have been widely recognized for their therapeutic potential in managing neuropathic pain due to their non-specific sodium channel inhibition. Lidocaine, synthesized in 1943, was the first sodium channel blocker identified and functions as an amide local anesthetic that inhibits NaV. , Intravenous administration of lidocaine has demonstrated significant analgesic effects in both central and peripheral neuropathic pain, particularly in

for specific pain management needs. Antiarrhythmics All class I antiarrhythmics target the cardiac NaV1.5, with subgroups A, B, and C delineated by their specificity to various sodium channel states and dissociation rates. Among the Class IB antiarrhythmics, lidocaine, mexiletine, and phenytoin have been widely recognized for their therapeutic potential in managing neuropathic pain due to their non-specific sodium channel inhibition. Lidocaine, synthesized in 1943, was the first sodium channel blocker identified and functions as an amide local anesthetic that inhibits NaV. , Intravenous administration of lidocaine has demonstrated significant analgesic effects in both central and peripheral neuropathic pain, particularly in cases in which opioid therapy is ineffective or contraindicated. Lidocaine is also FDA-approved for topical use as a local anesthetic and for the treatment of post-herpetic neuralgia. , Clinical evidence further supports its use in conditions such as diabetic neuropathy. However, lidocaine’s limited oral bioavailability and narrow safety margin prompted the development of mexiletine. Mexiletine, an oral analogue of lidocaine, was developed in the late 1960s and has a longer half-life, making it suitable for effective oral administration. , Like lidocaine, mexiletine has been used for neuropathic pain management, with clinical studies highlighting its benefits in diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia, and erythromelalgia. , Phenytoin can be utilized to treat arrythmias but is also considered an anticonvulsant. Along with carbamazepine, they were among the first anticonvulsants studied in controlled clinical trials and were demonstrated to be effective treatments for neuropathic pain in diabetic neuropathy and trigeminal neuralgia. , Currently, phenytoin is being investigated in topical formulations for the treatment of neuropathic pain in conditions such as chronic idiopathic axonal polyneuropathy and chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy. Anticonvulsants The molecular changes and neuronal hyperexcitability seen in neuropathic pain resemble the cellular changes observed in certain forms of epilepsy. This pathophysiological overlap supports the use of anticonvulsants, originally developed for seizure control, as effective agents for neuropathic pain management. The carboxamide class of sodium channel blockers, which includes carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine, is also used for neuropathic pain management. This subclass consists of non-selective sodium channel inhibitors that bind to the α-subunit of voltage-gated sodium channels. In 1968, the FDA approved carbamazepine for pain associated with trigeminal neuralgia and glossopharyngeal neuralgia. Subsequently, evidence has supported its benefits for neuropathic pain in other conditions, including reducing pains, post-sympathectomy neuralgia, and diabetic neuropathy. However, carbamazepine is associated with serious side effects, such as cognitive impairment, hepatotoxicity, agranulocytosis, hyponatremia, syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), and Stevens-Johnson syndrome. , , , To mitigate these adverse effects, oxcarbazepine, a carbamazepine derivative, was developed and FDA-approved in 2000 to avoid the formation of the 10,11-epoxide metabolite believed to contribute to many of these side effects. , , , Despite this, oxcarbazepine has not received FDA approval for trigeminal neuralgia, although it is recommended as a reasonable first-line option by the American Academy of Neurology. , Oxcarbazepine has been determined effective in treating neuropathic pain in diabetic neuropathy, allodynia, paroxysmal symptoms in multiple sclerosis, and peripheral neuropathy. , , Valproate, a simple branched-chain fatty acid structurally unrelated to other antiepileptic drugs, was first approved by the US FDA in 1978. It has limited utility in neuropathic pain due to adverse side effects, including weight gain, pancreatitis, hepatotoxicity, and teratogenicity. For example, new evidence suggests a potential increased risk of neurodevelopmental issues in the offspring of males taking valproate three months prior to conception. It is occasionally used in chronic pain settings, such as migraine prophylaxis, but is not considered a first-line option for neuropathic pain. Topiramate, first licensed in the UK in 1995 for adjunctive treatment of intractable partial epilepsy, is now approved globally. It has multiple mechanisms of action, including the blockade of NaV. These diverse mechanisms suggest a potential role in neuropathic pain management, particularly in conditions such as intercostal neuralgia, diabetic neuropathy, and trigeminal neuralgia. However, topiramate is known for its side effects, such as sedation, cognitive impairment, nausea, vomiting, narrow angle glaucoma, and kidney stones. , While not a first-line analgesic, topiramate can be considered for chronic neuropathic pain in certain patients. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, newer sodium channel inhibitors, lacosamide and lamotrigine, were developed. Lamotrigine has a complex mechanism of action involving the inhibition of both sodium and specific calcium channels. It has been determined to be effective in the treatment of neuropathic pain in central post-stroke pain, HIV-related neuropathy, spinal cord injury patients with incomplete transections, and diabetic neuropathy. , , However, lamotrigine is associated with the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, which occurs at an incidence of 0.04% when the dose is increased too quickly. Lacosamide has also demonstrated effectiveness in managing neuropathic pain in diabetic neuropathy. , , Lacosamide, which binds to a novel site, is recognized for its non-use-dependent mechanism and is the first anticonvulsant identified for its selective enhancement of slow

both sodium and specific calcium channels. It has been determined to be effective in the treatment of neuropathic pain in central post-stroke pain, HIV-related neuropathy, spinal cord injury patients with incomplete transections, and diabetic neuropathy. , , However, lamotrigine is associated with the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, which occurs at an incidence of 0.04% when the dose is increased too quickly. Lacosamide has also demonstrated effectiveness in managing neuropathic pain in diabetic neuropathy. , , Lacosamide, which binds to a novel site, is recognized for its non-use-dependent mechanism and is the first anticonvulsant identified for its selective enhancement of slow sodium channel inactivation. , , This differentiates it from other sodium channel inhibitors (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin, and lamotrigine), which affect both fast and slow inactivation in a dose-dependent manner. , Current sodium channel blockers are limited primarily by their narrow therapeutic margin, which is a consequence of their non-selective binding to various sodium channel subtypes. As a result, optimizing efficacy often increases the risk of central nervous system side effects, including seizures. Furthermore, these pharmacological agents are associated with adverse side effects (eg, carbamazepine carries a risk of bone marrow suppression). Consequently, considerable effort has been dedicated to the development of selective inhibitors that target specific sodium channel isoforms. However, progress has been slow, and only a few subtype-selective sodium channel blockers have been identified and characterized in the scientific literature. One such medication is suzetrigine which received FDA approval for the treatment of moderate-to-severe acute pain on January 30, 2025. A NaV1.8 specific inhibitor that preferentially binds to NaV1.8 at the Voltage Sensing Domain 2 (VSD2) along the transmembrane segments 3 and 4 in the NaV closed state, suzetrigine has a mechanism of action that is distinct from local anesthetics which preferentially bind the sodium channel in the open and inactivated states. By stabilizing the closed state, suzetrigine uniquely inhibits the channel from transmitting pain signals to the central nervous system. Notably, NaV1.8 is not expressed in the central nervous system and is primarily localized to the peripheral nervous system and the DRG. Suzetrigine for Acute Pain Current evidence for suzetrigine use is in the acute pain post-surgical literature. Initially two Phase 2 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were performed evaluating the efficacy of this medication in treating patients with either post- abdominoplasty or -bunionectomy associated pain. A total of 303 abdominoplasty and 274 unilateral bunionectomy patients were enrolled in the studies. Patients in the abdominoplasty study were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to 100 mg oral loading dose of suzetrigine followed by 50 mg dose every 12 hours (high dose regimen), 60 mg oral loading dose of suzetrigine followed by a 30 mg dose every 12 hours (medium dose regimen), hydrocodone – acetaminophen (5 mg- 325 mg) every 6 hours, or placebo every 6 hours. Patients in the bunionectomy study were assigned in a 2:2:1:2:2 ratio to receive suzetrigine high dose regimen, suzetrigine medium dose regimen, 20 mg loading dose suzetrigine followed by 10 mg dose every 12 hours (low dose regimen), hydrocodone – acetaminophen (5 mg- 325 mg) every 6 hours, or placebo every 6 hours. All bunionectomy patients received a popliteal nerve block catheter for perioperative regional anesthesia which was stopped on post-operative day 1. Study results demonstrated a least-squares mean difference in sum of the pain-intensity difference over 48 hours (SPID48) of 37.8 (95% CI, 9.2 to 66.4) after abdominoplasty and 36.8 (95% CI, 4.6 to 69.0) after bunionectomy when suzetrigine high dose regimen was compared to placebo. Meanwhile low dose and medium dose regimens fared no better than placebo for treatment of post operative pain. Subsequently, two Phase 3 RCT was performed in the same surgical cohorts to evaluate the efficacy of the suzetrigine high dose regimen compared to hydrocodone-acetaminophen (5 mg – 325 mg) every 6 hours and placebo every 6 hours. In this study, 1,118 abdominoplasty patients were included while 1,073 unilateral bunionectomy patients were included and randomized in a 2:2:1 ratio of the aforementioned medication regiments. With similar study parameters as the Phase 2 trials, bunionectomy patients underwent a popliteal nerve block catheter which was stopped on post operative day 1. In these studies, the SPID48 was 48.4 (95% CI, 33.6 to 63.1; P < 0.0001) after abdominoplasty and 29.3 (95% CI, 14.0 to 44.6; P = 0.0002) after bunionectomy when comparing suzetrigine to placebo. Neither study found suzetrigine to be superior to the hydrocodone study arm for pain relief. However, suzetrigine was found to have a more rapid onset of clinically meaningful pain relief compared to placebo after abdominoplasty (119 min vs 480 min; nominal P < 0.0001) and bunionectomy (240 min vs 480 min; nominal P = 0.0016). 71 A phase 3, open-label study was subsequently conducted to assess the safety and effectiveness of suzetrigine for moderate-to-severe acute pain

to 63.1; P < 0.0001) after abdominoplasty and 29.3 (95% CI, 14.0 to 44.6; P = 0.0002) after bunionectomy when comparing suzetrigine to placebo. Neither study found suzetrigine to be superior to the hydrocodone study arm for pain relief. However, suzetrigine was found to have a more rapid onset of clinically meaningful pain relief compared to placebo after abdominoplasty (119 min vs 480 min; nominal P < 0.0001) and bunionectomy (240 min vs 480 min; nominal P = 0.0016). 71 A phase 3, open-label study was subsequently conducted to assess the safety and effectiveness of suzetrigine for moderate-to-severe acute pain from various surgical and non-surgical conditions. Suzetrigine was generally safe and well-tolerated among the 256 participants with a range of acute pain conditions including orthopedic surgery, breast surgery, plastic surgery, colorectal surgery, gynecologic surgery, and urologic surgery. The majority of adverse events (AEs) were rated as mild (71 participants; 27.7%) or moderate (21 participants; 8.2%). The most common AEs (occurring in at least 2% of participants) were headache, constipation, nausea, falls, and rash. The only AE occurring in at least 5% of participants was headache (18 participants; 7.0%). Most participants (213 participants; 83.2%) rated the effectiveness of suzetrigine as good, very good, or excellent on a patient global assessment. Nevertheless, as a new medication for this clinical indication, its introduction has raised certain considerations. Physicians should be aware of several potential issues. One concern is the slower onset of action of suzetrigine (4–6 hours to peak plasma concentration) compared to opioids (1–2 hours). Another potential issue is the ceiling effect of non-opioid medications, whereas opioids can provide additional pain relief with dose escalation, limited primarily by adverse events. Finally, as the FDA approval was based on pain relief results at 48 hours, the authors appropriately noted the benefit of evaluating outcomes beyond this timeframe to determine if suzetrigine can reduce the progression to chronic pain. As the medication has only been recently approved, further research and clinical trials, particularly post-market Phase 4 surveillance studies, will be essential to continue to demonstrate its efficacy as an effective, non-opioid acute pain treatment option for clinicians. The Potential Role of Suzetrigine in Chronic Pain As previously highlighted, suzetrigine preferentially binds to NaV1.8 at the Voltage Sensing Domain 2 (VSD2) along the transmembrane segments 3 and 4 in the closed state, which is distinct from local anesthetics that preferentially bind the sodium channel in the open and inactivated states. By stabilizing the closed state, suzetrigine uniquely inhibits the channel from transmitting pain signals to the central nervous system. Notably, NaV1.8 is not expressed in the central nervous system and is primarily localized to the peripheral nervous system and the DRG. Although the available Phase 3 data for suzetrigine are for acute postoperative pain, its unique mechanism of action suggests a potential for its use in chronic pain management. To date, two phase 2 randomized, double-blind clinical trials are evaluating the use of suzetrigine for chronic pain management, specifically in patients with lumbar radiculopathy and diabetic peripheral neuropathy (See ). Both studies are ongoing, and preliminary data have been presented at national conferences, including the American Academy of Neurology. Although the data are nascent, NaV1.8 inhibition shows promise, particularly in the management of chronic neuropathic pain. The diabetic neuropathy study included patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus with a hemoglobin A1c ≤ 9.0% who suffered from lower extremity neuropathic pain with a numeric rating score (NRS) ≥ 4 for over one year and who had normal renal function, defined as a creatinine clearance > 60 mL/min. Patients were randomized into four treatment groups: low-dose suzetrigine (23 mg daily), mid-dose suzetrigine (46 mg daily), high-dose suzetrigine (69 mg daily), and pregabalin (100 mg three times daily) for 12 weeks. Before starting their assigned therapy, patients discontinued all chronic pain medications for at least 14 days, with the exception of acetaminophen, which was allowed (up to 500 mg every 4–6 hours as needed). The average baseline NRS was 5.70, 5.88, 5.79, and 5.98 in the aforementioned groups, respectively (see ). After 12 weeks of treatment, the within-group reductions of NRS from baseline were 2.18, 2.11, 2.26, and 2.09, respectively. Although the study was not powered for across-group comparisons, the preliminary data demonstrate a statistically significant within-group reduction in NRS in patients treated with suzetrigine, similar to that observed with pregabalin. The pain reduction began at week 1 and reached a steady state by week 5. Adverse event rates were similar to those of pregabalin across all three dosages of suzetrigine, although none of the suzetrigine-treated patients experienced dizziness or weight gain, which were observed in the pregabalin group. The lumbar radiculopathy study evaluated patients with a 3-month history of lumbar radicular pain with an NRS ≥ 4 and a body mass index ≤ 40

powered for across-group comparisons, the preliminary data demonstrate a statistically significant within-group reduction in NRS in patients treated with suzetrigine, similar to that observed with pregabalin. The pain reduction began at week 1 and reached a steady state by week 5. Adverse event rates were similar to those of pregabalin across all three dosages of suzetrigine, although none of the suzetrigine-treated patients experienced dizziness or weight gain, which were observed in the pregabalin group. The lumbar radiculopathy study evaluated patients with a 3-month history of lumbar radicular pain with an NRS ≥ 4 and a body mass index ≤ 40 kg/m 2 , without a history of moderate-to-severe painful neuropathy or lumbar spine surgery. Enrolled patients also stopped all pain medications for 14 days prior to the first dose, with the exception of over-the-counter ibuprofen (up to 1,600 mg/24 hours) or naproxen (up to 440 mg/24 hours). Patients were randomized to either high-dose suzetrigine (69 mg daily) or placebo for 12 weeks. The baseline NRS was 6.05 for the placebo group and 6.33 for the suzetrigine group. Interestingly, both the placebo and Suzetrigine cohorts experienced a similar reduction in NRS of 1.98 and 2.02, respectively. This may be attributed to the study design, which effectively compared suzetrigine to an active control group rather than a true placebo, given that the placebo cohort received nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) throughout the study period. This may account for the similar reductions in NRS observed in both groups. The incidence of adverse events was similar between the suzetrigine and placebo cohorts. The development of chronic pain is a complex process often attributed to peripheral sensitization caused by persistent nociceptive (somatic or visceral) or neuropathic pain. This can lead to subsequent central sensitization, resulting in pain hypersensitivity due to decreased neural activation thresholds and abnormal pain signal amplification. Studies have shown that suzetrigine inhibits sensory action potentials at the DRG. The DRG, as a sensory signal amplification center, is implicated in the development of certain forms of chronic pain. It is currently a target for treatment, in which low-frequency stimulation has been effective in treating specific pain conditions. It is plausible that suzetrigine’s role in treating chronic pain is due to a combination of its ability to inhibit pain signal transduction at the peripheral nerve, thereby reducing the incidence and severity of peripheral and central sensitization, and its direct inhibitory effect on NaV1.8 at the DRG, which may modulate the DRG’s role in pain signal propagation. This may explain why a peripherally mediated condition such as diabetic neuropathy appears to be better controlled than a centrally mediated condition such as lumbar radiculopathy, in which the insult is typically at the spinal cord or spinal nerve level rather than a peripheral nerve. However, further studies of suzetrigine in both peripherally and centrally mediated pain conditions are required to further evaluate this theory. Conclusion Voltage-gated sodium channels’ role in the initiation and propagation of pain signals is well-established, with distinct isoforms such as NaV1.7, NaV1.8, and NaV1.9 representing key factors in both physiological and pathological nociception. Current pharmacological strategies for pain management often rely on various medications including non-selective sodium channel blockers, which are limited by a narrow therapeutic index and dose-limiting adverse effects due to their broad off-target activity. The advent of suzetrigine marks a significant advancement in this field, offering a novel, non-opioid approach to pain relief by selectively targeting NaV1.8 in its closed state, a mechanism distinct from traditional agents. Amid the global opioid crisis and unmet need for safe, effective chronic pain therapies, suzetrigine’s selective NaV1.8 inhibition offers a non-addictive alternative with fewer off-target effects, addressing a critical gap in pain management. The preliminary data from suzetrigine’s clinical trials for acute and chronic pain conditions, particularly its favorable safety profile and efficacy in diabetic neuropathy, underscores the potential for isoform-selective inhibitors to provide effective pain management with fewer adverse events. While further research is warranted to fully evaluate its long-term efficacy and potential in reducing chronic pain progression, the data collected thus far suggest that suzetrigine may represent a new frontier in targeted, non-opioid pharmacotherapy. This provides a compelling rationale for continued investigation into NaV1.8 as a highly specific and viable therapeutic target for the clinical management of a range of painful conditions.

Published by John Wiley & Sons, Ltd. 10.1002/14651858.CD010764 Abstract Background The estimated likelihood of lower limb amputation is 10 to 30 times higher amongst people with diabetes compared to those without diabetes. Of all non‐traumatic amputations in people with diabetes, 85% are preceded by a foot ulcer. Foot ulceration associated with diabetes (diabetic foot ulcers) is caused by the interplay of several factors, most notably diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN), peripheral arterial disease (PAD) and changes in foot structure. These factors have been linked to chronic hyperglycaemia (high levels of glucose in the blood) and the altered metabolic state of diabetes. Control of hyperglycaemia may be important in the healing of ulcers. Objectives To assess the effects of intensive glycaemic control compared to conventional control on the outcome of foot ulcers in people with type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Search methods In December 2015 we searched: The Cochrane Wounds Specialised Register; The Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) ( The Cochrane Library ); Ovid MEDLINE; Ovid MEDLINE (In‐Process & Other Non‐Indexed Citations); Ovid EMBASE; EBSCO CINAHL; Elsevier SCOPUS; ISI Web of Knowledge Web of Science; BioMed Central and LILACS. We also searched clinical trial databases, pharmaceutical trial databases and current international and national clinical guidelines on diabetes foot management for relevant published, non‐published, ongoing and terminated clinical trials. There were no restrictions based on language or date of publication or study setting. Selection criteria Published, unpublished and ongoing randomised controlled trials (RCTs) were considered for inclusion where they investigated the effects of intensive glycaemic control on the outcome of active foot ulcers in people with diabetes. Non randomised and quasi‐randomised trials were excluded. In order to be included the trial had to have: 1) attempted to maintain or control blood glucose levels and measured changes in markers of glycaemic control (HbA1c or fasting, random, mean, home capillary or urine glucose), and 2) documented the effect of these interventions on active foot ulcer outcomes. Glycaemic interventions included subcutaneous insulin administration, continuous insulin infusion, oral anti‐diabetes agents, lifestyle interventions or a combination of these interventions. The definition of the interventional (intensive) group was that it should have a lower glycaemic target than the comparison (conventional) group. Data collection and analysis All review authors independently evaluated the papers identified by the search strategy against the inclusion criteria. Two review authors then independently reviewed all potential full‐text articles and trials registry results for inclusion. Main results We only identified one trial that met the inclusion criteria but this trial did not have any results so we could not perform the planned subgroup and sensitivity analyses in the absence of data. Two ongoing trials were identified which may provide data for analyses in a later version of this review. The completion date of these trials is currently unknown. Authors' conclusions The current review failed to find any completed randomised clinical trials with results. Therefore we are unable to conclude whether intensive glycaemic control when compared to conventional glycaemic control has a positive or detrimental effect on the treatment of foot ulcers in people with diabetes. Previous evidence has however highlighted a reduction in risk of limb amputation (from various causes) in people with type 2 diabetes with intensive glycaemic control. Whether this applies to people with foot ulcers in particular is unknown. The exact role that intensive glycaemic control has in treating foot ulcers in multidisciplinary care (alongside other interventions targeted at treating foot ulcers) requires further investigation.

Plain language summary Controlling blood glucose in treating diabetic foot ulcers (sores) Background: People with diabetes can develop foot ulcers (sores) for a number of reasons. This includes nerve damage and reduced blood flow to the feet and legs. Having high blood glucose may affect the ability of foot ulcers to heal and therefore intensively controlling blood glucose may be beneficial. Review question: This Cochrane review aimed to answer the question; how does controlling blood glucose more intensively compared to conventional blood glucose control influence foot ulcer healing in people with diabetes? What we found: We did not find any trials which have been completed on this topic with available results. The only trial which met our criteria for inclusion had been terminated due to encountering difficulties with recruiting participants. Therefore we cannot be sure whether controlling blood glucose intensively when people have diabetic foot ulcers is beneficial or harmful. The lack of evidence however should not deter efforts to achieve optimal glycaemic control in people with diabetic foot ulcers to encourage healing as is current practice. We believe there are currently two trials underway which may provide some evidence on this topic once completed. This Plain Language Summary is up to date as of 7 December 2015. chunks.content: La toxina botulínica es una proteína producida por bacterias de la familia Clostridium spp. Su administración intramuscular genera una parálisis química reversible de las fibras al bloquear la liberación de acetilcolina en la unión neuromuscular . En 1989, la Food and Drug Administration (FDA) aprobó su uso para el tratamiento del estrabismo. Desde entonces, se han creado once formulaciones de toxina botulínica, seis de ellas aprobadas por la FDA , y, al menos, 30 indicaciones terapéuticas en diferentes especialidades médicas , . Si bien la toxina botulínica es utilizada ampliamente en la medicina estética para reducir las líneas de expresión causadas por la hiperactividad muscular y el envejecimiento, también tiene otras indicaciones en diferentes especialidades médicas. En neurología, se utiliza para el tratamiento de distonías focales, espasmos hemifaciales y espasticidad; en oftalmología, para estrabismo y nistagmos; y en urología, para la hiperactividad del músculo detrusor y la incontinencia urinaria. Además, se ha demostrado su eficacia en el manejo de la migraña crónica, el dolor neuropático y la sialorrea, lo que refleja su amplio potencial terapéutico (Du X, Patel D. Use of botulinum toxin in the treatment of neuropathic pain: A case series (P10-13.009). Neurology. 2022;98(Suppl. 18). Abstracts: AAN 74 th Annual Meeting, Seattle, May 03, 2022. https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.98.18_supplement.864 ) - . En cuanto a las indicaciones terapéuticas no estéticas, existen cuatro formulaciones diferentes de la toxina botulínica aprobadas por la FDA para diversas enfermedades: Botox ® para el tratamiento de blefaroespasmo, espasmo hemifacial, estrabismo, distonía cervical, migraña, espasticidad de miembros superiores e inferiores (estos últimos en adultos), hiperactividad neurogénica del músculo detrusor, vejiga hiperactiva y arrugas de la frente; Xeomin ® como opción terapéutica para blefaroespasmo, distonía cervical, líneas de expresión, espasticidad de miembros superiores y sialorrea en adultos; Dysport ® para la distonía cervical, líneas de expresión y arrugas, espasticidad de miembros superiores en adultos y espasticidad de miembros inferiores en general; y Myobloc/Neurobloc ® para tratar la distonía cervical . En Colombia, el Instituto Nacional de Vigilancia de Medicamentos y Alimentos (Invima) es la institución gubernamental responsable de emitir las aprobaciones de los medicamentos y los registros sanitarios en el país , . Las preparaciones activas de la toxina botulínica aprobadas por el Invima en Colombia para indicaciones no estéticas, incluyen: Magnion®, Botox ® , Dysport ® , Neuronox ® , Siax ® y Xeomin ® ( . Sus registros Invima se muestran en el . Por otra parte, existen múltiples reportes que respaldan el uso de la toxina botulínica para indicaciones no aprobadas ( off-label ) , . Entre ellas, se encuentran: el dolor posterior a accidentes cerebrovasculares, la neuralgia posherpética, el bruxismo, la hipertrofia maseterina, y el dolor neuropático, miofascial o vesical, entre otros. La carencia de aprobación por parte de instituciones reguladoras de medicamentos, parcialmente debida a la discordancia entre los diagnósticos registrados ante el Invima y aquellos utilizados en la práctica clínica (Clasificación Internacional de Enfermedades, 10 a edición, CIE-10), hace que el uso de la toxina botulínica en estos casos sea controvertido. Aunque hay estudios en Latinoamérica que documentan la experiencia de la toxina botulínica en contextos clínicos específicos e indicaciones puntuales - , hasta la fecha no existe una caracterización integral de su uso en diferentes indicaciones, especialidades médicas e instituciones con recursos limitados, donde su disponibilidad es escasa. Algunos factores que limitan la disponibilidad de la toxina botulínica en las instituciones prestadoras de servicios de salud podrían estar relacionados con una subestimación del cálculo de la unidad de pago por capitación destinada a esta intervención. Esta subestimación puede deberse a insuficiencias en el control y la vigilancia del uso de la toxina y, por lo tanto, su demanda real en este contexto. Lo anterior resulta en una asignación ineficiente de los recursos financieros destinados al acceso y la distribución de la toxina botulínica, y en un incremento de los gastos de los colombianos que buscan alternativas fuera del sistema de salud . Además, en Colombia, el proceso para la prescripción de medicamentos suele estar sujeto a las indicaciones aprobadas por el Invima, y, por lo general, las que están fuera de la ficha técnica (según los diagnósticos disponibles en el CIE-10), tienen un gran riesgo de no ser cubiertas por las aseguradoras, lo que limita aún más el acceso a la toxina botulínica en el sistema de salud público del país. Por lo tanto, el objetivo de este estudio fue, en primer lugar, describir el perfil de los usos terapéuticos de la toxina botulínica en una institución de salud de la Red Pública Distrital de Bogotá, en la cual existen algunas limitaciones para acceder a estos compuestos; y, en segundo lugar, explorar los posibles riesgos de interacciones farmacológicas y la carga anticolinérgica para proporcionar una visión completa del uso de la toxina botulínica en Colombia. Materiales y métodos Este estudio corresponde a un análisis farmacoepidemiológico que utilizó un enfoque de prescripción-indicación dentro de un diseño observacional transversal. Se recopiló información retrospectiva sobre la prescripción de la toxina botulínica a partir de la base de datos “Mi prescripción” (MIPRES), correspondiente a pacientes atendidos en las instituciones públicas de salud de la Subred Integrada de Servicios de Salud Norte E.S.E. en Bogotá, Colombia, entre el 2019 y el 2020. La plataforma MIPRES es la herramienta virtual de prescripción del Ministerio de Salud y Protección Social del gobierno colombiano, mediante la cual se autoriza la dispensación de medicamentos de alto costo financiados con recursos públicos del Sistema Nacional de Seguridad Social . Muestreo y recolección de datos Se utilizó un método de muestreo por conveniencia para seleccionar la información de la base de datos MIPRES de pacientes a quienes se les recetó toxina botulínica en la Unidad de Servicios de Salud Simón Bolívar. Posteriormente, se obtuvieron las historias clínicas del sistema electrónico de información de la institución. Para recopilar los datos necesarios, se creó un instrumento mediante el s oftware Microsoft Excel™. Se extrajeron datos sociodemográficos, clínicos y farmacoepidemiológicos de la plataforma MIPRES y de la historia clínica de los pacientes. Variables Se consideraron las siguientes variables: sexo, edad, antecedentes farmacológicos, tipo de toxina botulínica utilizada, dosis empleada, vía de administración, especialidad correspondiente a la prescripción, diagnóstico para el que se indicó su uso y concordancia entre el diagnóstico y las indicaciones estipuladas por el Invima para la toxina botulínica. Para efectos de este estudio, la “administración efectiva” del medicamento se definió como el registro de la prescripción del medicamento en el sistema MIPRES y la administración documentada de la toxina botulínica al paciente, respaldada por la historia clínica en la que se describa la aplicación del medicamento. Para caracterizar el riesgo de interacciones farmacológicas, cada medicamento consignado en los antecedentes farmacológicos de los pacientes se clasificó según el sistema de clasificación ATC ( Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical ) . El riesgo de interacción se determinó con la herramienta de búsqueda de interacciones entre medicamentos Lexicomp Drug Interactions , que hace parte de la plataforma UpToDate . La carga anticolinérgica se estimó con la calculadora ABC ( Anticholinergic Burden Calculator ) . Se ingresaron los antecedentes farmacológicos utilizados en el momento de la prescripción de la toxina botulínica y reportados en la historia clínica de cada paciente. Los pacientes se clasificaron según la puntuación obtenida en la herramienta ABC como: “sin carga anticolinérgica” (puntuación ABC = 0), “posible carga anticolinérgica” (puntuación ABC = 1) y “carga anticolinérgica definitiva” (puntuación ABC ≥ 2). Análisis descriptivo Las variables cuantitativas, ordinales y nominales, se describieron utilizando proporciones. Después de realizar la prueba de normalidad de Kolmogorov-Smirnov, se identificó una distribución no paramétrica en las variables continuas, por lo tanto, estas se presentaron mediante medianas y rangos intercuartílicos (RIC). Análisis exploratorio Se hizo un análisis bivariado exploratorio para comparar las diferencias entre los subgrupos de las variables de interés. Se aplicaron las pruebas de ji al cuadrado o la U de Mann-Whitney, según correspondiera. Se consideró como significancia estadística a un valor de p < 0,05. Para los análisis estadísticos se utilizó el software JAMOVI, versión 2.2.5. Consideraciones éticas Este estudio fue clasificado como una investigación de riesgo mínimo y fue aprobado por el Comité de Ética Institucional de la Subred Norte en Bogotá, Colombia, bajo el número de protocolo SNCEI-160 del 1 ° de julio del 2021.
